MOTHER'S GIRL. Sleeves to the dimpled elbow, Fun in the sweet blue eyes, To and fro upon errands, The little maiden hies. Now she is washing dishes,l Now she is feeding the chicks, Now she 15 playing with pussy, Or teaching 'Royer tricks. Wrapped in a big white apron, rinne I in a chequered shawl, Hanging clothes in the garden, Oh, were she only tall! Hushing the fretful baby, Coaxing his hair to curl; Stopping around so briskly, Because she is mother's girl. Bunting for togs in the haymow, Petting old 13rindle's calf, , Riding Don to the pasture, With many a ringing laugh; , Coming whene'er you call her, Running wherever cent, Mother's girl is a blessing, , And mother is well content. .--Leeds Weekly .Ifercury. The marl who always puts his "best foot forward "—The one-legged man. "I'm bound to get to the bottom of this," as a man said when he fell into the well. "About the greatest tail-bearer I know," said the farmer's boy, "is our old peacock." It is when a woman tries to whistle that the great glory of her mouth is seen without being very much heard. One of the most spirit-drooping things is to borrow an umbrella and rind the proprietor's name indelibly attached to the handle. "I have a great ear, a wonderful ear," said a conceited tnusjrclan, in the course of conversation. "So has a jackass," replied a bystander. What one of the Forgers said, when he acknowledged his fault to Mr. Shapira :—"Ma tear, itth a reglar Doo-too- wrong-o'-me.—Panch. Some wretch has the audacity to remark that the ladies deck their hats with flowers in memory of the men who have been killed by milliners' bills. Qnoth Pat of the Yankee—" Bedad, if he was cast away on a &white island he'd get up the next mornin' an' go round sellin' maps to the inhabitants." A gentleman, when asked why he went into bankruptcy, said because his liabilities were large, his inabilities numer- ens, and his probabilities unpromising. The prayer of the Norman might suit the spirit of our own time. It was, "Kind heaven,l do not ask for wealth; only to be placed within arm's length of some man who has

A shout went up in the House of Commons when Barry once grew eloquent after this fashion—"There—there is Boston. Cherish'her ; provoke here not to rebellion. She is your eldest son." When Dr. Lucas, a very unpopular man, ventured on speech in the Irish Parliament, and failed altogether, Grat- ton said," He rose without a friend, and sat down without an enemy." "What a tine-looking man that is !" said one gentleman to .anotloer, noticing a face and form that would attract atten- tion anywhere. " Yes," was the reply; "he looks like an encyclopaedia, but he talks like a primer." "Who wrote Wordsworth's poems?" asks a contemporary. We are not guilty, anyhow, unless we wrote them when we were asleep. The probabilities are that the same fellow who wore Wordsworth's shirt and pantaloons also wrote his poems. The theory at least is plausible. A man never loses anything by being polite. A gentle- man, waiting for a train, saw a woman slip upon something and nearly fall. He hurried to assist her and helped her to rise, and as he did so she dropped a valise which proved to be his own, which he had left in the depot a few minutes before, and which she was attempting to steal. "Is ais hea letter all right, boss?" asked a nigger, hand- ing the clerk a letter he wanted to send off in the mail. The clerk weighed the letter and returned it, saying—" You want to put another stamp on it; it weighs too much." " Ef I puts another stamp on de letter, dat won't make it no lighter. Dat's gwine ter make it weigh more." "The last time I saw defendant before to-day he was sit- ting on the kerbstone one night about eleven o'clock, wait- ing, as he said, for his house to come along that way and take him in." "Well," asked the prison 'a counsel, "and what did you infer from that ?" "1 inf -4° that the last place he'd been in wasn't a temperance mseting." How THE ' ORGAN GRINDERS LIVE.—It may naturally be askel whether the organ-grinders are able to earn a living, and the question may be answered strongly in the affirmative. Few, if any artisans, or even skilled workmen, can earn as much day by day as the Italian organ-grinder. Their takings, it is true, vary much according to the dis- tricts they work in, and the time of the year. Some organs too, set to new and popular tunes, are very liberally pa- tronised. But £1 a day is said to be the most that an organ. grinder ever takes, while, with some exceptions, five shil- lings is about the least, so that a London organ-grinder may be regarded as a fairly-prosperous man. An organ can be hired from the makers for eighteenpence a day, while the price of a new organ is £25. The cost of setting an organ to new Vallee is about £4, and since novelty is essential this is a frequent source of expense. They moreover possess habits that tend to enhance their pro3perity. Content to live on plain and scanty fare, their expenses are infinitesimal compared with those of the English artisan. Many of them live in gangs, with board and lodging at a fixed charge a head per diem. The lodging-houses they frequent are, for the most part, kept by men of their own nationality; and the fare provided is of the simplest description, often con- sisting of little more than bread and milk for breakfast, and maccaroni soup for supper; the whole, including bed, being provided at a charge of about sixpence a day. Their occu- pation is by no means such easy work as it seems, the piano or opera organs, as they are called, weighing from seventy to a hundred pounds—no light weight to drag about all day long.—Cassell's Family 21fagazine. WHERE THE BUTTONS COME FROM.—It is not easy to say where all the buttons go to, but we can tell where most of them come from. This is what was said on the subject in a recent number of St. Nicholas :—" Button, button, who has the button ?" asked a glove that had been dropped on a toilet table. "I've got it,' answered Jimmy's jacket. "I've got several buttons, in fact." "No," put in the closet door, "I have it myself; the carpenter gave it to me." "I had a dozen or so," said a boot, looking rather down at the heel. "And I have a hundred or more," yawned the easy-chair, "but they don't button anything • they don't belong to the working class." "Here's a bachelor's button," remarked a vase of flowers on the bureau. "There's a button-wood tree in the garden," said the button-hooker; "I suppose you all grew there." "I know better than that," pouted the closet door. "Mine grew in the veins of the earth, where all the precious metals are found. . It's a poor relation of theirs." "And we," added a pair of ivory sleeve-buttons, "we grew in the land of the elephant. We were carved from the tasks of the leader, who threaded the jungles and swam,the rivers at the head of his troops." "My buttons," said the glove, "were nearly related to the gem which Cleopatra dissolved for Antony. They were mother-of-pearl, grown in the shell of the pearl oyster, for which divers risk their lives." " T 's something a a fish story," thought Jimmy's jacket. 4d " uttons are only glass; but glttss is sometimes made of sa , and who knows but their atoms may have been swept down to the sea-shore from 'farthest India ?' " "And I," whispered the bachelor's button, "I sprang from a tiny seed, with all my splendour of blue and purple wings, like the Afrite from the jar which the fisherman found on the bh. It's a miracle how I was packed away there 1" BACITELons' Stryro9.—Dll yOu tver See a man in the solitude and privacy of his study attempt to sew on a but- ton himself? It is in all its details one of the most in- teresting performances in the world. First he hunts for a button. Generally, to secure it he robs Peter to pay Paul, and cuts one from another garment. This button may be much larger than the size he is wearing. Next he hunts for a needle. Probably he goes out and buys a paper of needles. He always chooses the laegest needles, having the impression that large needles will sew stronger than small needles. As to thread, he gets the coarsest he can find', and this he doubles. He would thread hit needle. He takes his big needle in one hand and his coarse black thread in the other. He bites off thread to the desirable length. Then he tries to twist it to a fine point. Generally, in this he succeeds in making two and sometimes three fine points of one cud. Of course he can't get all these points through the needle's eye at once. He tries hard to make that needle and thread get on friendly terms with each other, but they won't. They don't want to get acquainted. They do not wish to have anything to do with each other. Sometimes it is the needle that kicks ; sometimes the thread. Some- times he imagines he has threaded his needle. It is an ocular delusion. The thread has missed the needle's eye by half an inch. It is harder work than sawing wood. At last the needle is threaded. Now he tries to sew the but- ton without taking his trousers off, This proves a failure. Hejwists himself into an uncomfortable position, and so would sew. But he can't sew. He runs the needle into himself. And the contrary thread always insists on fouling or on doubling on the next button. Then one part of the doOled thread won't work harmoniously with the other part; one part draws through the button's eye first and leaves the other part behind. Then it gets hitched up, and the ambassador swears. Or the needle breaks. He has for- gotten all about the necessity of a thimble. He jams his thumb down into the needle, and it punctures his thumb or runs under the nail. By and by he sews the button's eye full of thread. His big needle won't pass through anyt:, more. He must stop. He ends by winding the thread as many times as it will go under the button. And perhaps he lea es off with two or three inches of thread sticking outs' A woman can, through many outward indications, tell 011 la a man has been trying to sew on a button. He doesn't know the sh4bboleth of needle and thread, and it catches somewhere every tin. At last the button is sewed on, and he is proud of his work. REMARKABLE DISAPPEARANCE!

div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTICULTURE, &e.
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &e.

Sir Joseph Pease, M.P., has returned his agricultural tenants 15 per cent. of their last half-year's rent. A PROFITABLE SOW.—Mr. Charles Grimes, of Eye, has a sow which lately farrowed and brought forth 19 pigs, all of which are alive and healthy. This is the fourth farrow of this sow during the last two years, the total of the four far- rows amounting to 79 pigs. THE POTATO CROP.—At one time it looked likely that there would be an extensive attack on the potato crop by the potato disease; but such does not appear to have been the case. The month of July afforded plenty of moisture, but not sufficient simultaneous heat, whereas the heat of the latter part of August has been singularly free from mois- ture. Present appearances are, consequently—or, at all events, actually—in favour of the crop, as a whole, being unusually free from disease. EARL NELSON ON COTTAGE GARDENING.—Speaking at a flower show at Salisbury on Thursday, Earl Nelson said the surest sign of a well-conducted and happy family among the agricultural community was the cottage window. If the windows showed an array of flowers and a clean gauze blind, they would find the kitchen clean and the children decent. The windows were the index to the character of the occupants. Flowers were a distinct factor in social ele- vation, and had an influence which conduced to civilisation. FIENDISH TORTURE OF A HORSE.—A valuable horse be- longing to Mrs. Lea, of Solihull, near Birmingham, was killed on Wednesday in a wanton manner. The animal, which was grazing in a field, was afterwards found tied tightly to a tree with a rope and lying on the ground in great agony, its head being swollen nearly double its size, and a leg fractured, the injuries having evidently been caused by blows from a stick or iron bar. The suffering animal, which was past recovery, was immediately after- wards killed. A RAM IN A NEW SITUATIO'N.—A ram in the stall of a countess at a bazaar seems almost as out-of-the-way a visit- ant as a bull in a china shop, but at the bazaar recently got up in aid of the funds of the Norwich Hospital one of Lord Walsingham's rams was eagerly welcomed, and the Countess of Leicester was, it is to be presumed, delighted to have him at her stall, for being the eon and grandson of the Royal prize winners, and having received a Royal high commenda- tion, he provedat valuable consignment, and, being submitted to public auction, realised 50 guineas, Mr. M. Wyatt, a London architect, being the purchaser. The Duke and Duchess of Connaught were present, and took great interest in the proceedings. Minx FRQM INFECTED FARMS.—The following query ap- pears in the Agricultural Ga:ette :—I milk some cows and send the milk away for sale. Foot and mouth disease is rapidly spreading all over here, and getting close to me. Suppose my cows get it, and my premises be declared an infected place, what course am I to take with the milk? Shall I have to throw away the whole of the milk during the whole period my premises are declared infected, which means a month after the last cow gets better? Or shall I be allowed to sell any of the milk, say, from those cows that have not had it, or from those that have got better, during any portion of that period, and, if so, when? Where can I get the information, so as to know what to do to be legally within the law ?—The reply is :—"The Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milk Shops Order' of January, 1879, is still in force. You may sell milk from healthy cows though in the same shed as the diseased cows, but you must not sell milk from the latter, or even give it to pigs before being boiled." FOOT AND Motrria DISEASE.—Mr. Priestman, M.R.C.V.S., of 426, Caledonian-road, Holloway, N., publishes the fol- lowing account of his preventive treatment of the disease : —" I have great pleasure in:Forwarding you my method of preparing and administering carbolic acid as a prophylactic treatment of foot and mouth disease. I mix 11b. best soft soap with 16 fluid ounces of carbolic acid. If occasionally shaken, the soap will soon become dissolved, and the mix- ture fit for use. Four measured ounces of this solution are mixed in eight quarts of cold water, and one quart given daily (as soon as the disease is observed) to every one of the herd for four consecutive days, continuing it daily to those only that show signs of the disease. The same strength as administered I find is the best dressing for the feet, a small portion being applied daily. Diet Is a very important item. I recommend pulped wurzel and wet bran only (and that in moderate quantities) until the disease has subsided. I order unslaked lime to be spread daily inside and around the entrance to all sheds, and outside the piggeries." LEARNING TO FARM—If there is anything which is praise- worthy in the system of teaching agriculture abroad it is that it is practical. Every young man has to go through the rou- tine of cattle and pig feeding, milking, mowing, harvesting, dairy work, &c., until he is proficient and able to show his own men when he becomes occupant of a farm of his own. With us the young man goes to a large gentleman farmer, who as a rule has to find him with horse and shooting. He does little or nothing; and if he sees the work that is about all he thinks necessary. Dairy work he never dreams abont, and as for feeding the cattle and pigs, it is quite out of the question. Practical experience has shown the writer that a young man must, if he is to succeed under the new condi- tions of farming, really go through the whole routine. Scores of times have I been at farms where the whole of the work is done according to the directions of the foreman, who is master of his own system, antiquated though it maybe, but who knows that his master has no system at all. In such a case, too, if the master comes home with a new idea, his men can seldom be induced to carry it out, knowing that he is not a practical man. It has been pointed out that scientific training is very good in its way, but that without the practical portion of the education it is thrown away upon a young man who is to become a working farm. If a man is to succeed he must be a worker, whether he occu- pies one hundred or a thousand acres. For instance, how many young men who have undergone their coarse of tuition at the College of Agriculture or with a farmer know whether a fence is well made or not—or how it is laid and headed—and yet this is work for which they may have to pay hundreds of pounds. How many can tie up a shock of wheat and arrange it against wet weather, or take to pieces or alter a plough, a chaff cutter, or mowing machine; and yet all of these implements and many more have to be manipulated by the labourers? Is there one young man in a hundred who receives instructions in rick building and in a knowledge of the condition of hay? Hundreds of ricks are annually tired or spoiled because of this want of know- ledge ; while thousands of tons of grain and pulse are strewn about the fields because of the stupidity of farmers in cut- ting or carrying too late. There are, indeed, scores of little practical matters which a young man can only learn by work- ing upon a farm, for he will never understand them by reading or seeing others carry them out. AN INGENIOUS SMUGGLEIt.—A lady and gentleman, seated in a plain, respectable-looking coupe, drawn by a good horse, and driven by a coachman in livery, were wont to drive out to the Bois de Boulogne every afternoon, returning usually about dusk. The gentleman was evidently an invalid. He was always enveloped in a fur-lined cloak, with a collar raised round 43 throat, and had a fur cap pulleddown over his brow ii while 11% little that could been seen of his coun- tenance was of sickly pallor. He was always reolining in a corner of the carriage, as if too feeble to sit erect, while his attentive wife sat beside him, evidently solicitous for his welfare being especially careful to keep his cloak well wrapped around him. The guardians of the '6 ctroi saw this vehiele and its inthastes pass by them daily without suspicion. One day, hoWever' after making the usual inquiry, "Have You anything to disclose ?" the customhouse officer on closing the door, struck the supposed invalid's foot. "I beg your pardon, sir!" said the officer. No response—not so much as an inclination of the head. Rather surprised, the officer repeated his remark in a louder tone, at the same time touching the sick man's shoulder. Atat moment the lady and the coachman leaped from their respective places and fled with surprising swiftness, leaving in the hands of the of4sers the horse, the carriage, and the invalid, which last was found to be made of tin and full of brandy, his face being most aristally constructed in wax. The space under the seat of the cOuPe and the coachman's box were also reservoirs of tin; so the smuggling t.rtursactions of the party had been practised on a rery extensive sMIT.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURDA.Y, SEPTEMBER 15, 1883.

COTTAGE GARDENING. LEEKS planted in shallow trenches should have the soil drawn to them, so that the ground is level. The soil ex- cludes the air, and the part which was green becomes white on that account, and makes the leek more esteemed for culi- nary purposes. Many prefer this esculent to the onion for soups and broths, because the flavour is not so strong, and it imparts a sweet, pleasant taste, and no part of it should be wasted. We are paying more attention than usual to the leek this season, because like many others, our crop of onions has suffered severely from the attacks of the grub. Thus the leek in the spring time will have to act as a sub- stitute. The leek is frequently cooked as a vegetable by those who know how; but many housewives spoil them in cooking. The leek should be sufficiently cooked in salt water and served with good gravy, or a little butter sauce, to which may be added a spoonful of cream. There is an expensive ring about these auxiliaries, but they are not so, and much more is frequently spent in producing a dish much inferi,or, and less wholesome. Such a dish, with any other vegetable, requires 'out little meat with it to make a dinner, or cold tea or beer to wash it down, and more of one and less of the other would no doubt diminish the number of dyspeptic cases. In making this statement we are allud- ing to other judiciously cooked vegetables as well as the leek.

ONIONS.—The tops of all that stand erect should be bent down, which we do by giving them a pinch near the bulb, and then turn them over. The flow of sap is checked by bruising the cells or their walls, and what would have still gone to form top is diverted to produce bulb. CAMOMILE.—AS we are frequently asked for a handful of _ . . - . .

the flowers of this herb, we take advantage of fine days to pick them, so as to have the flowers dry. We spread them thinly on a sheet of paper in a room, and shall finally store them in proper bags. FRUIT GATHERING.—We have been frequently grieved when witnessing the manner in which this has been done. Some shake the trees; others more considerate procure a ladder, and, as they pick the fruit, they carelessly throw it into abasket. When that is full they precipitately empty it into another basket. This process tells most disastrously on the condition of the fruit. Every time an apple or apea comes in contact with any substance as hard as itselr, bruising is the result. When an apple or a pear is cut it ivill be observed that the pulp has innumerable cells. When these divisional membranes are injured, putrefaction is sure to follow sooner or later, in proportion to the injury Sus- tained. In emptying fruit from one basket to another. damage is inevitable, and few escape. Those that do not come in contact with the side of the basket come in contact with each other more or less, and we would as soon allow the fruit to fall off the tree as serve it so, if we wished it to keep. Our practice is to pick each fruit separately and place it in "boat baskets," so called because they assume that shape, and are put together in a similar manner, with wood split very thin. There is no rough surface, which cannot be said of a wicker basket, which we entirely dis- card for conveying fruit, even to the storehouse. When our boat basket is full we hand them a few at a time into boxes or barrels, and for convenience the barrels can be placed on their sides till partially full; but with choice pears and some of the best late apples we prefer taking the boat bas- ket direct from the tree to the store-room, feeling convinced that the oftener they are moved and handled the worse they get. It may not in a season like this, when crops are heavy, be sufficiently remunerative to bestow such labour in pick- ing. When fruit has not been worth picking we have always gone over the trees and picked the best. The Wil- liams' Bon Chretien pear will soon be fit for gathering. If this pear is left on the tree till it turns colour or approaches ripeness, it will become mealy in a few days. We eat the finest fruit, and, if the seeds or pips are turning brown, we make a picking of the finest, and go over them again in a few days to gather the remainder. We never recollect plucking it too soon but we have been too Lite, and had to i pay the penalty by flaying to throw the fruit away. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Cuttings of pansies may now be put in. The shoots most likely to root are those near the base of the plant; the top or flowering shoots are fre- quently hollow, so that if they do form roots they are liable to die in the winter. We are surprised that these are not more grown, but beyond an odd stand of cut bloom at ' flower shows we see little of them. If properly attended to they may be sown at any time from March to September, but the earlier in the year the longer their season for flower- ing. Some sown last June in a frame and then pricked out are now producing their first flowers, and we are going to make another sowing at once with the view of having an early supply of bloom. We find there is an abundance of good cuttings attached to double rockets which were cut down in the middle of July, and if taken off and put in a shady corner they will soon root. Some that are near the ground will be found to be already forming young roots, and may have some soil placed up to them to encourage them, or they may be removed and sown as ordinary cut- tings. The flowering stems that were cut in pieces in July and inserted in cuttings have in some instances formed roots. Cuttings and pipings of pinks and carnations should be gradually inured by removing the glass or any other protec- tion they may have by degrees. All decayed leaves should be picked off, for if left they convey decay to the cuttings. Some of our earliest layers of the carnation are now well- rooted plants. THE WINDOW. —So soon as the pelargoniums that have been cut back have made a growth of half an inch they should be turned out of their pots and most of the soil, and, in the case of small plants, the whole of it should be shaken away, and one-fourth of the roots may be removed, which we do by clutching the whole in one hand and with the knife in the other shorten them. They can generally be -got into smaller pots than they have been in. The pots should be perfectly clean, especially inside, and they must be well drained by placing a crock over the hole, and halt an inch of broken crock over that for a 4in. pot, and pro- portionately for larger sizes. The soil most suitable is three-parts loam, one of leaf mould, with a sprinkling of sand. Some of the rougher portion of the soil should be placed over the crocks to prevent the smaller portion filling the interstices, and obstructing the free passage of theefl water supplied to the plants.

Modern Setting of an Old Saw.—" Mashers not Men." The King of Bavaria, the most uncompromising of all the Wagnerites, one day met a soldier without a leg, and asked him when he lost it. "In the war of 1866," replied the warrior gruffly. "Don't you know me ?" asked the King, somewhat piqued at the soldier's manner. " No; how should I?" was the reply. "You don't go to the wars, and I don't go to the opera." "Gentlemen, I can't lie about the horse; he is blind in one eye," said the auctioneer. The horse was soon knocked down to a citizen who had been greatly struck by the auc- tioneer's honesty, and, after paying for the horse, he said, "You were honest enough to tell me that this animal was blind in one eye—is there any other defect ?" "Yes, sir ; there is. He is also blind in the other eye," was the prompt reply. Mr. McManus is a very matter-of-fact farmer in Midland, Ontario, and the father of a number of very attractive girls. A young farmer, in every way eligible, was a suitor for the hand of the second unmarried daughter. "No, no," said old McManus, when the young man had confessed his tender passion," you cannot have the pick o' my flock." "But," ' objected the young man, "why should I be compelled to wait until after the eldest of your daughters is married?" "Oh, you need not wait until after," rejoined the farmer, "you can have the eldest; they must all be taken in their turn." The young man was confounded, but not dismayed. A few weeks after a double wedding was announced to take place at McManus's house. The young farmer had persuaded his brother to take the eldest, which, of course, left the way clear for him to the second. McManus says that there is nothing like making good, sensible rules, and sticking to them MARRIED FOLKS WOULD BE HAPPIER if they tried to be as agreeable as in courtship days. If they kissed and made up, at once, after every quarrel. If each would try to be a real support and comfort to the other. If household ex- penses were always proportioned to receipts. If each re- membered the other was practically a human being, not an angel. If women were as kind to their husbands as they are to their lovers. If men were as thoughtful for their w ;Nes as they were for them when sweethearts. If both parties remembered that they were married for worse as well as for better. If there were fewer silks and velvet street-costumes, and more plain, tidy house dresses i aria street ones too, for that matter. If there were fewer "My dears" and "Please darlings " in public and nlOrn common manners in private. If wives and hii3Lands would take their pleasure as they go along, and not degenerate into mere toil- ing machines. Recreation is necessary to keep the heart in its place, and to try and get along without it is a big mis- take.—Christian at Work.

A DANGEROUS QUIET.—They tell in the fables of Eastern lands that when a weary traveller lay down by the road- side to rest, a huge bird, without an:o rustle of flight, drew near, and, hovering above him, gently waved its wings and fanned him into a deep and not unwelcome slumber; and then, when Nature's sentry was gone, it darted its pointed beak into his heart and gorged upon his blood. In like manner do these spirits that deceive and mislead man's will, draw round, all silent as a rising star, and draw away the life which gave that will its energy. An arm and a side are often paralysed in the old. But before the gray hairs come, the will of man is paralysed against any effort for God. Days pass, and the will gives no further trouble. The reason has slid away, discomforted, long ago. Terrors have been quieted. Old alarums have grown weak through use. There is a complaisant qukt over the whole nature—but it is the quiet laid calm of death.—The Quiver.

TIIE AMERICAN NATIONAL FLAG.—It may be interesting to many readers to learn the origin of the "Stars and Stripes," which is none other than the coat of arms of the Washington family, who flourished in Northamptonshire in the sialteenth century. Laurence Washington, who was Mayor of Northampton in 1533, and again in 1546, was, on the dissolution of the mbnasteries, presented in 1538, by Henry VIII., with the manor of Sulgrave, in Northampton- shire, this having previously belonged to the priors of St. Andrew, Northampton; and to-day may be seen upon the porch of the Old Manor House two stone shields, one of which, in perfect preservation, has carved on it the "Stars and Stripes," or, in heraldic language—" Argent, two bars gules ; in chief three mulletts of the second." John Wash- ington, a great-grandson of the above Laurence, emigrated to Bridges Creek, in America, in 1657, and from him was descended George Washington, first President of the United States, who, during the days of his military career, presented I to Mrs. Ross, of Philadelphia, ideas for a national flag, and she adopted his own "Stars and Stripes." SOME NOTES ON VICTORIA. No. VI. Victoria in its form of government is more democratic than any other British colony. There are two Houses of I Parliament as there are at Westminster, but the resemblance goes little farther. The Lower House, or Legislative As- oembly, is elected by manhood suffrage, and the Upper House, or Legislative Council, under an Act which was passed as the result of a bitter political struggle, is practi- call), elected on the principle of household suffrage. Under I this new Act the reformed Council, both in the qualification for membership and the qualification of its electorate, may claim to be a thoroughly representative body, and there are thus two popular Chambers existing side by side—a state of things un:que in constitutional history. How long the present arrangement will work amicably no one can tell. Already, however, there are not wanting signs which appear to foreshadow a storm—when the new Council will dispute with the Assembly the control of affairs. The outcome of such a serious contest or contests may be another period of intense partisan turmoil, from which the colony is at pre- sent happily free. The members of the Council consider themselves much superior to the members of the Legisla- tive Assembly, in that while the former labour for the State without salary the latter are pecuniarily re-imbursed for their Parliamentary services. Another fact which is be- lieved to place the Legislative Council above the Legisla- tive Assembly is that while the latter body is dissolvable at the pleasure of the Governor, as representing the Crown, and cannot run longer than three years under any circum- stances, the former remains intact in spite of a dissolution, and the members are elected for six years. There is a fur- ther difference in the qualification of the two classes of members. Any man, who is of full age and has lived in the colony two years, can be elected to the Assembly, whereas candidates for the Council must possess freehold propertyof the annual value of £lOO or capital value of £l,OOO. Though it is the fashion here for those who are opposed to the pay- ment of members to run down the Legislative Assembly and correspondingly exalt the Council as a body of patriots, the Legislative Assembly is quite able to hold its own and to

compare favourably with the other Chamber. Nothwith- s'anding opinions expressed to the contrary, the writer of these notes holds that the Victorian Howe of Assembly at the present day, whatever its faults, is a fairly creditable instrument of legislation, and past Assemblies in Victoria

must have exercised wisdom and had foresight,or the colony would not now have been in the position it is. This remark is made without any partisan consideration and with- out urging any opinion on the merits or demerits of the payment of members system. It should be stated that the advocates of payment are not con- fined to one class of politicians. The party here which calls itself Radical or Liberal, but which is no more Liberal as the term is understood with the mother country than is the Constitutional party in Victoria, is mainly committed to the policy of payment; but there are several Constitution-

alists, and notably one of the leading men on that side, who believe in it, and it may be added that the instances of mem- bers of the Assembly refusing the £3OO a year, the salary stipulated, are very rare amongst those who most vigorously oppose the system. The act providing for payment on recently expiring, was renewed without much demur in the • Assembly and with only a feeble growl in the Council, showing, I think, that the people by their representatives do not feel very strongly averse to the existing arrange- ment. It is somewhat singular that there is not, in the paid. House, a single direct delegate from the weekly wage earn- ing classes, in whose interest payment of members is specially advocated. There are lawyers and bankers, merchants, doc- tors, newspaper men, auctioneers, farmers' and squatters in the Legislative Assembly, but within my knowledge, not a single member who in ordinary parlance would be styled a working man. It is made a reproach against the Parliament of Victoria that it occupies sadly too much of its time in haggling about small parochial questions, and disputing personal rather than public grievances. The blame for this should be cast to a large extent on the system and the circum- stances of government, rather than on the Members of Parliament themselves. Parliament has mainly to discuss what may appear to be trivial local matters viewed from an Imperial standpoint, because the Government of the colony, which is responsible to Parliament, has all kinds of little duties within its purview—doing, in fact, a multitude of things which elsewhere are left to municipal or other bodies. In Victoria, for instance, the State has the making and con- trol of the railways, the provision and management of the water supply, and it undertakes other duties which, when the colony gets older, will probably be left entirely to Local Boards. A stormy Parliamentary contention as to whether certain locomotives should be ordered in England or made in Victoria, or an exciting debate upon the locality of a State school, are not matters of high international moment, but they are of importance locally, and it is such matters as these which at present necessarily engage the attention of the people's representatives. The system of political patronage is rampant here; hence there are numerous wranglings in the Assembly about appointments and pro- motions, and charges of jobbery and corruption are bandied about somewhat frequently. At such times as these the Colonial Senators are not seen to advantage. It is hoped that when the purer system, which has for some time been promised, is brought into play that these scenes will be less frequent. Meantime, when occupied with its best and more important work, the Parliament of Victoria acquits itself fairly well, and it is but the barest justice to say of the manhood suffrage elected and paid member portion of it— the Assembly,—that it discharges its functions on the whole to the reasonable satisfaction of the community. There are in the Assembly, it must be acknowledged, some men of mean ability and vulgar manners, but the Legisla- tive Council has also its objectionable members. Ihave not heard of any member of the Victorian Legislature, of either House, entertaining his colleagues with a music- hall ditty after the fashion of a New Zealand M.P., and I have only once in the course of a pietty close acquaintance with the Victorian Parliament seen a member intoxicated in his place. On the other hand, if some of the stories one hears from New South Wales are not grossly untrue, drunkenness in that more Conservative Parliament is a vice rather prevalent on the part of a number of members. There are naturally, with the "screw" of £25 a month to tempt, a, number of public men described as "professional politi- cians" who make Pailiamentary membership their sole ithought. The electors provide such as these with a com- fortable billet in the Assembly. But they may, some of them, more than earn their salary and deserve their pay; and the class, much as it may be derided, includes such politicians as the Honourable Graham Berry, the present Chief Secretary, and the Honourable Duncan Gillies, the present Minister of Railways. These gentlemen would either of them stand to the front in any Assembly. It is light to add that they would probably be in the House if there was no Act to provide for their payment as members. When complaint is made that professional politicians crowd the field, it should be borne in mind that the arena is open to all, and that if the best men do not come forward it is their own fault. The opportunity is open to them to serve their adopted country if they will but display sufficient in- terest in public affairs. Speaking generally, I should say there was not much room for regret in this direction. The colony is as well served as most constitutionally governed communities. A few words should follow in reference to Parties in Parliament. Members usually are content to be described as Liberals or Constitutionalists. Not that there can to an impartial observer ise discovered any tendency to anarchy on the side of the so-called Liberals, or that the Conservatives or Constitutionalists in Victoria are slow to suggest reform like old-fashioned home Tories. The fact is that among the Constitutionalists are many men who are responsible in a large measure for the most democratic of Victorian Acts. The true definition of the terms " Liberal ' and "Constitutionalist" as applied here now, I think would be that the Liberal is a believer in protection and that the Constitutionalist is a free trader. This question of protec- tion is the onl g very serious one that divides Victorian poli- ticians at the present time, and, as by common consent, the subject is not to the front just now, they are able to work pretty amicably together. The Government now in office is, in fact, a union of both parties. So much for Parliament. A few particulars as to the electoral system. As everybody knows, voting here is by ballot, a point of the Charter gained in this part of her Majesty's dominions long before its introduction into an Act of 'Parliament in England. I have already mentioned that once at least in every three years t,t; itooso of Assem. "-- has to be dissolved, a"4t iresh one elected. In practice tllere is a General Election once in 18 months or two years. The decision of the people thus appealed to is given in one day, the oblect being in having all the elections occurring together to prevent plural voting as much as possible. The State defrays the whole of the expenses of the returning officers ; but, to prevent candidates coining forward who have not the slightest chance of success, it is.provided that failure to record a certain proportion of votes—one-fifth— will involve the forfeiture to the consolidated revenue of the deposit, which each candidate has to make on nomina- tion. The fear of seeing this deposit no more prevents many bogus candidates from putting in an appearance, though, as often happens to the disgust of the caucus in England, many constituencies have an embarrassing number of aspirants for Parliamentary honours, and the proper influence of the ma- jority of the voters is not, therefore, exerted. The counting up of the votes is done with greater expedition than in England. Instead of tkileallot papers being all taken to be counted at the central ;T Oiling booth of the electorate, they are in Victoria counted at each booth. The result is corn-

municated by quick despatch to the central place, and there the returns are totalled. Due precautions are taken in the subsequent collection of papers to verify the figures foi, official declaration a day or two after; but the system very ready and reliable, and ensures the outcome of the struggle being known in the metropolis and chief country towns by ten or eleven o'clock on the evening 04 the day of election. 4;04,6,161,w: inataniMiels

Local government in Victorians still in its infancy. There are city, borough, and shire councils, which are fitted to undertake for the municipalities much more important work than they door are allowed to do uncler the act which has given them life. Shire councils in particular have very restricted functions, but the time is coming when many of the matters now dealt with by the various departments of the Central Government will be left in the hands of the localities. An important step in this direction has recently been taken in providing for the formation of water trusts in the arid districts, and some of the more influential city and borough councils are asserting a position for themselves which will eventually be the death blot cif over centralisa- tion. At present everything, except the manaei it of the public roads, is done from the capital and out o i.e:e national exchequer. The railways I have already mentioned, as well as the psincipal works of water supply. The police force of the colony is under the sole control of the Chief Secretary's, Department, and the localities have therefore no say in the stationing of the men or their use. In the same way the

Education Department has the undivided care of the com- mon schools of the state, and the school teachers are answer- able to no one but their superiors in that department of the civil service. There are, it is true, local school boards of advice, as they are called. But they are invested with no powers, and their advice is more often respected than acted upon, and the public has come to look upon their existence as a farce. No doubt in earlier days this sort of paternal government was necessary, but is no longer so, and the pro- cess of decentralising may now be:Jollowed with advantage to the country.

PRESENTATION TO Mit. JAS. COOK, ST. HELENS. On Friday afternoon last, Mr. James Cook, solicitor, who is about to leave St. Helens for New Zealand, was presented with an illuminated address in the private office of Mr. Brewis, the town clerk. The chair was occupied by Mr. Brewis, and there were also present the Rev. J. M. Warns- ley, Dr. McNicoll, Messrs. R. F. Cook, Craik, Thomas, Mal- kin, W. Swift, Mearns, and Lomax. On Mr. Cook entering the room, Mr. Brewis said that before he, Mr. Cook, went away from his native town he (Mr. Brewis) had been re- quested to present to that gentleman a testimonial and fare- well address signed by a large number of the most influen- tial gentlemen in St. Helens. It would be some gratification to him to know that so many gentlemen in his own town bok an interest in his welfare. Mr. THOMAS read the address as follows :—" To James Cook, solicitor, St. Helens, Lancashire. We, the under- signed solicitors of the Supreme Court of Judicature in England, notaries, public commissioners, justices of the peace, town councillors, ministers, physicians, merchants, and burgesses of your native town of St. Helens, where you have for some years practised as a solicitor with credit to yourself and to the profession to which you have the honour to belong, hearing with regret of your intended departure to the distant colony of New Zealand, desire to express our best wishes for the welfare and happi- ness of yourself and family in the island of your adoption, and trust that you will have a fair and prosperous voyage and that on your arrival at your new home you will pursue with success the same upright, gentlemanly, and honourable course that you have hitherto done, and that when you look upon the signatures hereunder written you will think of the friends by whom you are esteemed in the old country." Mr. BREWIS' in making the presentation, said the address was signed by Colonel Gamble, the Mayor, and other magis- trates, all the solicitors of the town, and several ministers, physicians, and town councillors. He was sure that all who knew Mr. Cook would join in the good wishes the docu- ment expressed. He was sorry that Mr. Cook had not been so successful in his profession in the town as he deserved to be, and he was sure it had been through no fault of his own. He could speak for Mr. Cook's conduct during the eight or ten years be had been in his office, when serving his articles, and for about three years afterwards when he acted as managing conveyancing clerk. His conduct had been all that could be desired, and he transacted the business entrusted to his care with diligence and ability. He hoped, however, that in the new country to which Mr. Cook was going he would be more prosperous and happy. Mr. Brewis then handed Mr. Cook the address, saying that he hoped it would prove not only a material advantage to him in his profession, but also a remembrance of the friends he left behind him in St. Helens. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Rev. J. M. WAMSLEY said he felt that he should like to say a few words on that interesting occasion. He did not look upon it as a valedictory occasion. There was something in that word " valedictory " which was rather too sombre in its character to indicate the feelings upper- most in their minds and hearts. It was a little over two years since he had the pleasure of forming Mr. Cook's ac- quaintance, atd the little intercourse he had been enabled to have with him during that period had led him to form' a very high opinion of his Christian and general character. He deeply regretted the circumstances, or combination of circumstances, which seemed to render it necessary that Mr. Cook should leave his native town and enter upon life anew in a distant clime. He trusted in that bright and genial land Mr. Cook would be able to form many bright and genial associations, and that in his heart, in his home, in his profession, and in his general walk in life he might be favoured with the special tokens of the favour and blessing of God. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. W. H. THOMAS said as he had served his articles with Mr. Cook in the same office, sitting in the same room, he had had many opprcrtunities of judging of his character and his worth, and during the whole time he had known him he had always been 'exceedingly courteous, kind, un- assuming, and generous, and since he commenced practice in St. Helens he had obtained the respect, goodwill, and friendship of all the solicitors in the town. (Hear, hear.) He was informed that solicitors or barristers going to New Zealand were allowed to practice as native lawyers. He hoped that was so, and that Mr. Cook might be successful in his profession there—more successful than he had been in St. Helens. Dr. McNicoLL also made a few appropriate references to Mr. Cook's intended departure. He had heard it stated— but of course it was a libel—that a lawyer to be successful must have a bit of the devil about him. (Laughter.) Well, that was a quality Mr. Cook had not got, but after all a right-minded, fair-dettling wan had all those qualities which would ensure success. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Roar. COOK also added his testimony to Mr. Cook's ability. Dr. McNicoll had said that a lawyer required a little of the devil, but in his own opinion a lawyer could get on very well without a bit of the devil—(hear, hear)— and he hoped in his new country Mr. Cook would not im- port that element into his character, but would continue the same course he had pursued amongst them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. COOK responded in a feeling and appropriate man- ner. Several things, he said, had tempted him to leave England. One thing was of course that in having to begin a new practice there was a great deal to contend with, and besides it was not the best time to commence. At the same time he naturally had a hope that the new country .he was going to would realise all his expectations. The climate would be a healthy one, and he felt he and his family would enjoy better health than they had done. (Hear, hear). A vote of thanks to Mr. Brewis then brought the pro- ceedings to a close.

SUSPICIOUS DEATH- OF A SHEFFIELD INNKEEPER.—John Tyrer, a well-known publican in Sheffield, and formerly a member of the Corporation, died on Wednesday under sus- picious circumstances. He was found in the smoke-room unconscious and his face cut and bruised, and it is alleged that he received his injuries at the hands of his nephew, John Tyrer, with whom he was quarrelling the night before, The nephew has been arrested, and was on Thursday re- manded for a week.

THE BANKRUPTCY ACT.—At a conference of county court judges, held at Birmingham on Thursday, a general opinion was expressed that the new Bankruptcy Act was perfectly workable, and it was resolved to ask the Lord Chancellor to allow county court judges to see a draft of the new rules before adoption. It is stated in the Daily News that the applications for the office of Receiver in Bankruptcy under the new Act are so numerous that they have all been referred to a departmental committee of the Board of Trade. THE DISCOTERY OF STOLEN MONEY IN DUBLIN.—A Dublin correspondent says it has transpired that the sum of money found by the four artisans concealed near the bank of the Grand Canal, Dublin, amounted to nearly £4,000. It was contained in a leather bag, which was brought to light by a dog tugging at the string which was attached. The four finders, after dividing the iiioney, Separated. One got married, and left Australia. Another hollowed in his wake, and a third has sailed for America. The fourth, a labouring man, remains in Dublin. The landlord of an hotel at Southport entered, in an angry mood, the sleeping apartment of a boarder, and said, "Now, sir, I want you to pay your bill, and you must. I've asked you for it often enough ; and tell yol now that you don't leave my house till you pay it!" "Good!" said his lodger, "just put that in writing; make a regular agreement of it; I'll stay with you as long as I live!"

Mr. Hare, on going along the line, was surprised to find Sterling at the rivex:end of it, up to his waist in the water, and re- proached him for his thoughtlessness in risking: injury tol his health, which was weak. And this was the answer which Mr. Hare received—" Somebody mist be in it; N_vjag, not I as well as Another ?"—From "Little Folks" Ilfaaiflffe. A LITTLE RUSSIAN'S BATIL—The little mouschik is taught to be very clean—once a week. The Russiaa creed requires him to bathe evsry Saturd/y, and he does so reli- giously, but does not see much water between times, and sleeps by night in the clothes he wears by day. Even the Russians of better families often content theniselves with a dry polish instead of a wash. Little Iwan's bath Would be a trying thing for an English child. First he is steamed , till he is half suffocated in a i ole under the stove, or In' one of the vapout-baths constr ted in rude manner in ali* Russian villages. Then he craw a out, and his mother half drowns him with pailfuls of hot water. Then she pours ice-cold water over him, or sends him (fat to have a roll in the snow; after which little Iwan dresses with pride, hiving had all the cleaning he will get for a week.—Lettle Folks Magazine. ,1

ST. HELENS AND THE ARTISANS' DWELLINGS ACT. An interesting and valuable report on the "Artisans' Dwellings Act," with special reference to its application to St. Helens, was on Wednesday submitted to the St. Helens Health Committee by Dr. McNicoll, the medical officer. The following is a copy of the report :—" You are aware that in the session of 1875 Parliament passed a measure for facilitating the improvement of the dwellings of the work- ing classes in large towns, called the Artisans' Dwellings Act,' and it has appeared to me that the best way of get- ting rid of the plague spots in the town is to apply this Act to such places, and so improve St. Helens at once. In the newest districts, where the houses have been well built, it is enough to deal with the nuisances as they arise, but in the older parts where the original defects of the buildings have been increased by age and bad usage, the best way is for the sanitary autbority to use the powers it possesses and pull down such infected portions or blocks of buildings and erect a better class of cot- tages in their places. If the houses in such infected areas are tolerated, and only such individual cases are dealt with as are positively unfit for human habi- tation, then the present generation of inhabitants must con- tinue to suffer all the direful effects that flow from living in low *class tenements. The part of the town to which I would call your attention is Parr-street, which has for many years shown a high state of mortality. This street is only of moderate length, and contains 102 houses and about 600 tenants, yet we find that the death rate has been excessive year by year. In the last seven years*. less than 191 deaths took place in the street, being twice too many at least. During that period the death rate has been 45 per annum, and fever and diarrhoea and other zymotics have caused a mortality of 110, which is high indeed. When the houses which comprises this district are examitied no wonder is entertained at this shocking state of things. The houses which form Parr-street are very old and dilapidated, and to make matters worse they were undermined some 20 years ago and the whole of them at that time settled down about six feet below the former level. In consequence of this many of the houses are leaning, and the walls are kept from falling by props and braces applied within and without, and in some instances the floors and the bedrooms are leaving the walls. As a general statement, we may say that the street is in a tumble-down , and filthy state. The reofs and spouts on the houses and ! the pantries are defective, and, of course, the walls inside are damp and frequently wet; and broken down stairs are I not uncommon. All the houses on the Parr side of Parr- street, between Warrington New-road and Frazer-street, are deficient in yard spaces. Indeed, the bask yards are miser- able specimens, and, of course, the privies are close to the houses. Two of the houses, Nos. 28 and 30, have yards without any outlet whatever, so that the contents of the ashpits have to be brought through the houses, which is an abominable contrivance, and no longer to be endured. On the other side of the street—that is the Windle side—the defects are apparent—spouts and roofs in bad repair and radically defective. On this side there is not a separate yard to each house, but large open spaces of ground un- drained and unpaved; and in these spaces cottages have been built with small and cramped rooms, with no sanitary surroundings to the houses. The inspectors and myself have been over every house in that portion and the street between Warrington New-road and Frazer-street. This is the part that requires dealing with first. So far I have given you a general summary of the defects, but if your committee wish to hear the character and condition of each house separately, given I will read over the list which includes 47 houses. Only five of these are in fairly good con- dition. It is now generally acknowledged that providing better accomodation for working people, is a matter of the greatest importance. There are several diseased portions of the town—plague spots—that ought to be stamped out, and I thought it well to begin with Parr-street as being very old awl worn-out, and very dirty. If your committee cannot see its way to erect new buildings in the place of these worn-out ones, a number of the houses will have to be closed as unfit for human habitation and the people driven elsewhere, and the houses which remain must be made habitable, but will be poor specimens of dwellings after all. Such piecemeal improvement may lessen the rate of mortality, but it is not likely to reduce the rate to anything like an average. And as the power of providing accommodation for the working classes has been conferred on municipal authorities, I venture to hope that your committee will see its way to take steps in this direction by makiag a beginning at Parr. Besides the detailed account of each house I have a map, showing the particulars of each, and the whale district or area. I bring this question before you now because the lonthe of September, October, and November, are men- tioned in the Act as the proper time for taking steps to ob- tain a provisional order for this improvement scheme from the Local Government Board; and if the present season is allowed to go by no steps can be taken for twelve months in which case the improvement of the district by reconstruc- tion cannot be effected till 1885.—The consideration of this report was left over to a special meeting of the committee to be held next Friday.

The Marquis of Lorne, the Princess Louise, and Prince George of Wales arrived at Toronto on Wednesday, and formally opened the Industrial Exhibition.
Private Sweeney, Royal Marines, was, on Thursday, sen- tenced by court-martial, at Portsmouth, to five years' penal servitude for assaulting a Marino sergeant.

FATAL LAMP ACCIB-ENTS.-4 wom-an nained Welter met with a fearful death at LiVerpool on Wednesday. She was going upstairs with a lighted paraffin lamp, when the lamp broke, and the oil igniting, ran on her clothes and enveloped her in flames. She was terribly burned, and died shortly , after admission to the Royal Infirmary.—As Susannah Wie- ' terick, of 5, Fashion-street, Spitalfields, was filling a lamp with paraffin oil on Tuesday, it suddenly exploded and set fire to her clothes, burning her so seriously that she died in the Metropolitan Free Hospital soon after admission. A BRAVE GIRL ATTACKED BY COWARDLY RUFFIANS.-At Sudbury, on Thursday, two brothers, named Wallace, silk weavers, and George Amos were committed for trial on charges of murderously assaulting Frank Gayfer, a plate- layer, and stabbing a girl named Wright, on the 27th ult. Amos challenged the prosecutor to fight, and being refused all the prisoners set upon him, dragged him ihto a public road, and kicked him in a brutal manner in the presence of a number of men, none of whom interfered. The girl , Wright, however, pluckily interposed, and, standing over the injured man, prevented further ill-treatment by putting her clothes round his head. Whilst in this position she was severely stabbed in her shoulder. EXPERIENCE OF ASIITON PUBLICANS AT DONCASTER.— Rumour has been pretty busy as to the doings and expe- riences'of certain well-known Ashton publicans at Doncaster on the St. Leger day. It is freely asserted that many Ash- tonians had bad an intimation from somebody or some- where that the horse Elzevir, owne4 by the Hon. W. Gerard, son of Lord Gerard, of Ashton, could not possibly fail to secure the St. Leger stakes, and consequently the publicans in question—so it is said— followed the " tip " by backing the horse named to the uttermost farthing they possessed. Their speculation proved a losing one, however, as Elzevir did not even secure a " place," but landed the fourth—and also landed the hard- earned funds of the Ashtonians into the pockets cf some- body else. Tales as to the penniless condition of certain Ashton persons have been spread abroad, and it is whis- pered that some difficulty existed in one or two instances as to how they were to get back to their native heath. One gentleman left behind him a valuable gold watch—said to be worth .05—some "light-fingered" gentleman having succeeded in extracting it during the absorbing interest which was centred in the great race. Surely a warning is to be seen in this, and a wholesome lesson to be gained therefrom!

SUICIDE IN A COAL MINE: SAD CASE.—A most peculiar and sad case of suicide occurred at Ashton on Sunday morning last. It Seems that on last Friday a young man named John Thomas Johnson, 20 years of age, residing at Platt Bridge, was before the Wigan County Magistrates in connection with an illegitimate child case. An order was made for Johnson to contribute a certain sum of money per week towards the support of the child, and this appears to have upset and troubled the young fellow a great deal. He was employed as the night furnace man at the Mesnes Col- liery, belonging to Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co., and went down the mine as usual about two o'clock on Saturday afternoon. All other men had left —he simply stytying to keep the fires in ready for the resumption of work on the Monday. Shortly after six o'clock on the following morning John Hilton, one of the firemen, went down the mine for the purpeise of making his customary inspection, and discovered Johnson suspended by a chain from a beam in the ceiling. The deceased had unhooked the chain from a waggon, and from all appearances had de- liberately hanged himself with it. The body was released from its position and afterwards removed to the deceased's regidence. What makes the oeteurrence all the more sad is the fact that the deceased was well connected, and had al- ways borne a steady and good character —An inquest on the body was held at the Bryn Hall Hotel, on Wednesday, when the jury returned a verdict of "Suicide while in a state of temioorary insanity."
