div.p: THE EXAMLNEB, SATURDA_Y, SEPTEMPErt 15, 1883.
PERSONAL.

The Rev. E. Bradley, better known as "Cuthbert Bede," author of " Verdant Green." has been presented to the vicarage of Lenton, Lincolnshire, worth £7OO a year. Mr. NV. E. Forster, accompanied by Mr. 11. 0. Arnold- Forster, left London on Tuesday night for Vienna, and does not, expect to return to England until the end of October.

The Prime Minister, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone and other members of his family and friends, left Barrow on Saturday morning in Messrs. Donald Currie and Co.'s steamer Pembroke Castle, on a cruise round the coast of Scotland. Sir Wm. Harcourt, the Home Secretary, artived at Oban on Tuesday. He is the guest of Sir Wm. Collins, in whose yacht, the Fingal, be will proceed in the wake of the Pem- broke Castle, containing Mr. Gladstone and party. Sir William will also make a trip round the west coast of Scot- land. ,

the station and cheered him, and, addressing a few words !o them, Mr. Davitt said the Land League had sounded the th.,athknell of landlordism, and the present azit,ition would see its fall. On re:aching •Cahir Mr. Davit: was presented within address of w(lcome from the people of Cishel. He afterwards drove from Gallic. to Cashel, calling at Rockwell College, where he lunched, and where addresses were read from the Cashel Town Commissioners and the Mechanics' Institute.

NEW ON COMMISSIONERS' MEETING. A meeting of the members of the 13,)ar.1 uf Improvement Vormnissioners tor the township of Newton was held in the Board Room, Town Hall, on Monday afterut on, when there were present Messrs. W. F. G.uch (in the chair), T. J. Gillespie, T. Stone, T. Forster, B. B Glover, J. E. Wore- ley (law clerk), and It. Brierley (sarveyor). THE RE-ELECTION OF THE CHAIRMAN. Mr. Goocn (on takiog his sit for the Ii et tnne since his re-election as chairm in of the Board) slit; : I hive to thank you for the confidence you have uut in no in re-electing inc chairman for the ensuing year. To have the support of the ni•rnb,i•rs of the Board will make my du:iel light: and pleasureable.

HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Highways," Public Works, and Sani- tary Committee, held on the 20th August, Mr. Firclough was re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. Dr. Watkins attended to confer with the committee upon his report, and the ccst of providing a disinfectant apparatus. It was ordered to await the. report of the medical officer and sur- veyor upon the best apparatus they could recommend. Dr. Watkins reported the necessity for a supply of water to Mercer's cottages, Newton Common, and to the Gib cottages, near Haydock, and that the Haydock Local Board were willing to supply the latter. It was or- dared that the Haydock Local .Board have authority to arrange with the owners of the -Gib cottages to lay on the necessary supply of water, and that the Surveyor report to the Water Committee on the necessity and cost of carrying the water mains to Mercer's cottages. An amended block plan for 14 cottages in Leigh-street, for Mr. John Elliott, and plan of •eight cottages, in Hfoughton-street, for Mr. Thomas Forster, were submitted and approved—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. STONE, seconded by Mr. GILLESPIE. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. Mr. B. B. Glover was elected chairman of the Gas, and Water Committee, at a meeting of the committee held on 20th ult. Tile gasworks carbonizing account for the Past month ge.vo fuel used 81 tons 19 cwt., gas made 846,500 cubic feet, averaging 10,333 feet nor ton of fuelaised. Mr. Brierley reported that the district had been irregula,rly and insufficiently supplied with water by the railway company between Thursday 16th to Saturday the 18th of August. It was ordered that Mr. Brierley communicate with Mr. Webb enquiring the cause of the short supply of water, and urging that steps might be taken to avoid a recurrence.—Mr. STONE moved, and Mr. FORSTER seconded, the passing of the minutes. Carried. —Mr; GLOVER asked if Mr. Brier:ey had communicated with Mr. Webb as to the supply of water 7—Mr. BatErinEy replied that he wrote to Mr. Webb according to the instruc- tions of the committee, ' but he had not had any reply. He had since indirectly ascertained that the short supply of water was caused through a breakdown at the Viaduct Works, and not at Parkside as was reported.—Mr. GILLESPIE : Has we a full supply of water now ?—Mr. BRIERLEY : Save and except such occurrences as these.—Mr. GILLESPIE : Have they got the breakdown made right yet?—Mr. BRIERLEY : Yes; a few hours was all that was required, I believe.—'The CHAIR- MAN: Has there been any complaint since ?—Mr. BRIERLEY : No, not since then.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Finance Committee was held on the 20th ultimo, and Mr. T. Stone was elected chairman for the ensuing year. The application of Mr. Houghton collector, for an increase of salary was considered, and referred to a special committee, consisting of the chairman of each com- mittee; and in the meantime the clerk to ascertain his salary as assistant overseer and collector of poor rates. Accounts amounting to £363 15s. sd. were examined and passed for payment. At a meeting of the special committee referred to, held on the 27th ult , the committee considered Mr. Houghton's application, and recommended that an advance of £l4 per year be given to him, making £l3O to be paid by the Commissioners, out of which Mr. Hough- ton must continue to provide an office youth.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. GILLESPIE. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. A meeting of the School Attendance Committee was held on the 20th ult., at which Mr. Pardey was re-elected chair- man of the committee. The School Attendance Officer (Mr. Ball) read his report explaining his inability to submit a copy of the school registers in the new form, which could not be made up by the school teachers until after the receipt of the inspector'S report.—lt was resolved that Mr. Ball be requested to submit at the next meeting a copy of the register of each school, made up as far as possible.—Mr. Bars, explained his inability to get summonses signed, owing to the absence of magistrates gem the district, and it was ordered that legal proceedings be, for the present sus- pended.—Mr. Fortman moved that the minutes be passed. Mr. GILLESPIE seconded the motion, which was carried. THE RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. Mr. WORSLEY reported the receipt of a letter -from the I Local Government Board, dated the 18th August, confirm- ing the re-appointment of Dr. Watkin as medical officer of health for the district for the year ending the sth August, 1384. THE PROPOSED ENCLOSURE OF LAND IN SOUTHWORTH- ROAD. With regard to the proposed enclosure of land in South- worth-street, Mr. WORSLEY stated that no tracing had been sent in by Mr. Shortrede and having had no communication from Mr. Shortrede he (Mr. Worsley) did not attend the committee meeting. Mr. Shortrede had, however, seen Mr. Brierley on the ground, and probably by the next committee meeting he would be in a position to advise upon the mat- ter.—Mr. &rotes stated that he had that morning received a letter from Mr. Shortrede, which was to be read at that meeting.—Mr. WORSLEY then read the letter as follows: " Winstanley Estate Office, Wigan, Ssptember Bth, 1883. Southworth-road, My dear sir,—When the new fence is put down along the above it will make a great improve- ment if the sharp turn near the Bull was rounded off. If the Newton Commissioners are inclined to do the work I shall be glad to arrange for them having sufficient land to make a good sweep instead of the present nasty sharp angle. Will you he good enough to lay this before the Commissioners ?—Yours very truly, T. SHORTREDE.—Thos. Stone, Esq., Newton Park. Newton-le-Willows." Mr. GLOVER moved that the letter be referred to the Highway Committee, and the motion haying been seconded by Mr. Fons-rER, was carried. THE MAIN ROADS QUESTION : A "DECISIVE ANSWER" BY

THE COUNTY AUTHORITIES. • Mr. WORSLEY stated that he had received the fol- lowing letter with reference to the main roads question "Preston, 10th August, 1883.—Main roade.—Dear Sir,—ln reply to your letter of yesterday, I beg to say that I brought your letter of the 26th June before the County Highway Committee at their meeting held on the 31st ult., and was instructed to say in reply thereto that the committee do not feel justified at the present time in recommending the dourt of Annual General Session to make any order decl tring high- ways in this county to be main roads under section 15 of the Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act, 1878. You may take this to be the decisive answer' of the com- mittee.—Yours faithfully, CAMPBELL H. SADLER, Deputy Clerk of the Peace.—James E. Worsley, Req., solicitor, Warrington."—Mr. GILLESPIE aslad if there were no other steps they could take in the matter to enforce their idea.— Mr. WORSLEY observed that the only steps they could take would be to apply for a mandamus to compel the justices to make an order under the section. They seemed to have re- fused all through the county to make any order under the section. When he and Mr. Gooch saw the Clerk of the Peace at Preston, the latter said if they granted their request they would have to repair the high-ways of the whole county.—Mr. GILLESPIE: That has nothing to do with it.—Mr. WORSLEY said they did not know anything about that question.—The CHAIRMAN: We want them te I repair ours.—Mr. WORSLEY : They will evidently not do so so long as it is possible to keep out of it.—Mr. GILLESPIE: Shall we press the matter any further at present or let the thing rest ?—Mr. WORSLEY remarked that there was a con- siderable loss going on in connection with the highways.— The CHAIRMAN: Something like £.OO a year.— Mr. GLOVER: What are neighbouring townships doing ? Mr. WORSLEY replied that sometime a joint memorial was sent to the Local Government Board but nothing came of it.—The CHAIRMAN asked who took the active part in that matter.—Mr. WORSLEY : The active part at that time was taken by the Atherton Local Board.—The CHAIRMAN: Won't they follow it up P—Mr. WORSLEY : They don't Seem to be doing much now.—Mr. BRIERLEY understood that the Atherton Local Board would be willing to join other locel boards in any action on the matter.—Mr. GLOVER moved that the Clerk write to the Atherton Local Board asking them what they were doing in the matter. Mr. WOHSLEY expressed the opinion that it would be better to have counsel's opinion.—After some further discussion Mr. GILLESPIE moved that the Law Clerk write to other local boards and see if they were willing to act with the Newton Commissioners in taking legal opinion upon the question.— Mr. GLOVER seconded, and the motion was carried. BURIAL ACCOMMODATION IN EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. IMPORTANT DETAILS. Mr. WORSLEY said: Dr. Hoffman, inspector of burial grounds, attended and inspected the burial grounds of the district on Wednesday, the 29th August. He first of all visited the Congregational burial ground, and he found that they were restricting interments to those of their own denominatiqn, and that the ground would last for a few years longer by thtt means. He greatly approved of the soil there. and said that as the burials were being restricted he should make no order as to closing that graveyard. He then went on to the Roman Catholic burial ground and found the soil very suitable inde;cl for interments, and he also found that at their present rate of interment they would have room for interments for very many years to come ; so he decided be make no order whatever as to that burial ground. He then came down and inspected the additional burial ground belonging to St. Peter's church, and he con- demned that ground very strongly. Ile said the land was very suitable for interments, but in consequence of the crowded state of it and the evidence that he had of the smell —which was very disagreeable indeed and very injurious to health—he made an order that that ground should be closed on the Ist September, 1884, vvith certain reservations as to the existing rights. The first reservation reserved the rights in vaults and brick grava until those were filled up ; and then was the reservation of rights to inter in graves where there was room for the relatives to fill up the vacant spaces in the graves.. And there was a reservation to the vicer and churchwardens to allot the remeining land, at present unused, until that land should be filled up. That is to say, that the retneining land can be allotted now, and be used in the period for which the grave- yard'will'be closed.HMr.- GILLESPIE asked if that applied to the present burial ground alone, or the ground round the church as well?—Mr. WORSLEY :He Made these remarks as

ito the additioaal burial gromadee-Mr. GILLESPIE: Supposing the other is not already filled up P—Mr. WORSLEY : We then went to the churchyard, and he reserved there tbe righte to the Vaults. I believe he found there were no (nick graves, but practically the set e reservations were made as to the add itioual gra veee-va id Mr. GIL- LESPIE : I am under the impression that there are brick graves tbere.--Mr. WORSLEY: I must be wrong then. , He then went to the Parish Church at Wargrave, and found , that the ground there was very unsuitable indeed.--Mr. Gier.wei: Heavy clay, I suppose.—Mr. Wceosewe : He condemned it very strongly, and pointed out two evils. In the first place if a carpse was buried on a dry day, the clods of earth thrown into the grave formed blocks, through which the gas from the body escapes to the top, which is a very great source of danger. He then 'mid that if a corpse was buried on a wet day, the clay hermeticilly sealed the coffin anti stopped the process of decemposition. He condemned that ground very strorg:y, but found, however, that there ' was room for interments for some yeafs to come there. . He said he should make no orderl as to thee— Mr. GILLESPIE: Did he examine the piece of land which we propose taking for a cemetery ?—Mr. WORSLEY: It was shown to 13im.—Mr. GILLESPIE: But did he not examine it P—Mr. WORSLEY: It is no part of his duty. He will come when the cemetery is finished and laid out. He does not inspect sitese—Mr. GILLESPIE; Is there not some lAA' to whom we shall show the ground first P—Mr. Woosexe : That will be another affair. Dr. Watkins acc3mpanied the ' Inspector, and he wee met at the various graveyards by the clergy and persons in charge of the churchyards. His report has not been received yet, but that is what he said 1 it would be.—Mr. GILLESPIE: If on the let September , next year St. Peter's churchyerd has to be closed it behoves ' us to be getting on with the cametery.—Mr. WORSLEY : Yee.—Mr.'GILLESPIE: It Will become a very serious ques- tion if we don't mind.—The CHAIRMAN: What ie beioge done now?—Mr. WORSLEY: We have waited for this-4,1 I report as to the closing of the cemeteries is everything. 1 Supposing. the Inspector had found that 'he, could , not rtkommend the closing of the graveyards we could not have got a cemetery then.— Mr. STONE:. From what you say, I take it that there is ample accommodation for some time ,at all the other grave yards except St. Peter's?—Mr. WORSLEY: No, air. There is ample accommodation at the Roman Catholic ground for some years.—Mr. GILLESPIE: And Wargrave.—Mr. WORS- LEY: For two or three years, and the Congregational ground will be tilled by their own people.—Mr. GLOVER: Not in the next 20 years, Mr. Worsley.—The CHAIRMAN: What is the next step—to get some official down to examine the site?—Mr. WORSLEY: Yes; the next step is to' proceed as we were doing. Now that an inspection has been made we have to apply for an inquiry as to our borrowing money. We should have no inquiry if we did not want to borrow money. As we want to borrow money we shall have to hold an inquiry for its sanction.—Mr. GILLESPIE: Ir appears to me that we have allowed the thing to lie over too long' already. The sooner we get it done the better.—Mr. WOES- LET: rhe delay has been since April last in correspondence to get the inspector to come down.—Mr. GILLESPIE: I sup- pose all difficulties with regard to the .taking of the hind have been got over now ?—Mr. WORSLEY: Practically. There are the usual formalities to be gone through, that is all.—Mr. GILLESPIE moved that the clerk be instructed to write for an inspector to come down and hold an inquiry.— Mr. GLOVER thought it would' be a hardship for the rate- payers to provide a new cemetery for simply one church in the district. From their law clerk's report the Congrega- tionalists were provided for for some years, seri also at Wargrave; and the ratepayers were asked to provide a burial ground for St. Peter's alone. From what he had heard that afternoon there were even some reservations . made even in regard to that ground—the brick graves and the vaults not having to be closed for some time ; while the churchwardens and the clergy were at liberty to sell the spaces not taken up to a certain date. It was.unfair to the ratepayers at large that they should be called upon to buy a churchyard, and then the people in authority to put the whole of the money in their private pocket. He thought it would have been better if the con- gregation and churchwardens of St. Peter's had themselves provided the extra burial ground and thereby prevented a rate of 4d. or 61. coming upon the township so soon as was likely to be the case through their wants. Everybody else had supplied themselves, and it was only as much as could have been expected if St. Peter's had done as other bodies had done.—Mr. GILLESPIE remarked that the other bodies were only supplied for a very limited number of years, and would very soon have to fall back on the new cemetery.— Mr. WORSLEY: The inspector found that Wargrave would not certainly last for more than two or three years.—Mr. GLOYER: They are even allowed to bury in St. Peter's for the next 18 months.—Mr. WORSLEY: That is of course be- cause there is no cemetery. If there was a cemetery I sup- pose it would have - been closed at once.— The CEAIRMAN thought the question raised by Mr Glover ought to have been discussed at an earlier stage of the matter.—Mr. Geovan: We have only bad the facts 1 before Us this afternoon.—The CHAIRMAN: Well, we had ' the means of ascertaining them for ourselves.—Mr. Geovett always understood that §t. Peter's Churchyard was on the point of being closed.—Mr. BRIERLEY suggested that the members should go and inspect the ground themselves Mr. GILLESPIE: I think we have all seen it, and it is in a very bad state indeed. If we continue doing nothing the time will soon come when it will be taken out of our hands. The Local Government Board will come down and do it themselves.—Mr. GLOVER asked,if it was a nuisance, why did not the authorities put it right? The whole of the money was going to the pockets of the private persons be- longing to the church.—Mr. lizeeeseene said they could not keep it in a proper state. The coffins were down on .the rock in • some pieces, while he had actually seen funerals when the coffins had been put down id a foot of water.—Me. Beeemeetex observed that a proper system of drainage would remedy that.—Mr. GILLESPIE: I think it is a most unsuitable place for a burial ground.—Mr. GLOVER agreed with that idea.—Mr GILLES. PIE said the thing had beee talked about so much that he hoped the Local Government Board would come down and take it out of their hands. Then they would have done with it.—Mr. GLOVER remarked that he had simply been giving expression to his opinions.—The matter dropped; and as this was the only business toe meeting concluded.

ORMSKIRf CHURCH. MUNIFICENCE OF LORD AND LADY DERBY. The restoration of the Derby Chapel in Ormskirk Church has just been completed at the sole cost of the Earl and Countess of Derby, who have manifested their interest in the work by personal inspection. The vault beneath the chapel is now closed. Prior to the burial of the late Earl in 1869 it was the burial place of the Earls of Derby. It was built under the will of the third earl, and has been the subject of much research by antiquaries. The first Earl of Derby was buried at Burscough Priory, the s cond at the Monastery of Sion, Middlesex, and from the terms of the will of the third earl it may be safely assumed that a chapel was built and a vault made at Ormskirk in 1572, and that he and his suc- cessors in the direct line buried there lie in it. By it be ordered 'that his body should be buried at Orrnskirk, and that a chapel should be there erected, and a tomb (vault) prepared for that purpose agreeable to his dignity ; the ancient monastery of Burscough, where his ancestors were laid being totally demolished." He died 24th October, 1572, and his body lay in state at Lathom till December 4th following, while the work was being carried on. There are many effigies in the chapel. Those next the chancl are those of Henry, Earl of Derby, Lord of Man and the Isles, Lord High Steward of England, Lord Chamberlain of Chester, E.G., and his wife Elizabeth, &welter ef Clifford, Earl of Cum- berland. He was one of Queen Elizabeth's commissioners who witnessed the execution of Mary Queen of Scots, and bears upon his surcoat counterchanged the insignia of Man, and quarterly let and 4' h Stanley, 2nd Clifford (his wife), 3rd Lathom. Both Clifford and Lathom are wrong in blazonry, the latter haying eight plates instead of three, add the former being minus a 11=•53—most probably worn away. The tomb next this property belongs to the Bicker- gaffe Chapel, and is most probably that of Henry Stanley (of the Crosshall family), de jure Pxoris of Aughton and Bickerstaffe, 1515-98. The effigies next the front of the church are, no doubt, an Earl of Derby and his countess, the only charges decipherable being Man, Stanley, and Lathom. The effigy of the earl is much worn, but it bears the collar of the Garter. In the visitation book of Sir Wm. Dugdale, 1661, one of these effigies is sketched, bearing ap- parently on his shoulder the "cross engrailed" of Mohun ; but in other particulars incorrectly. In the work of restoration great care has been taken to preserve whatever of antiquity could be utilized ; and a more befitting Lancashire memorial to the great earls could not ' be desired.

SUICIDE BY LEAPING FROM A BRIDGE. Early on Thursday morning a young bookbinder named George Symington threw himself over the North Bridge, Edinburgh, and, falling upon the railway, was instantly killed. SHIP RUN Dowt:: Loss OF LIFE.—Two seamen landed in a boat near Dungenes,s on Wednesday night. They re- ported that their vessel, the Juliene, belonging to Norway, had been run down, and that they were the only survivors of a crew of 14. ' ,FALL FROM A SCAPTOLD.-0° Thursday, at West Kirby, eight miles from Birkenhexi, a number of workmen em- ployed on a scaffolding were precipitated to the ground. One man named William Dryland aces killed, another severely injured, while the rest escaped with bruises. TI RECTOR AND THE SALVATION ARIEY.—The Rev. J. Spittal, rector of Heywood, having complained to the Heywood Corporation against the annowance caus-d by the Salvation Army band playing past his church on Sundays, the Corporation resolved on Thursday to request that the playing should be stopped. i ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CAIkRIAGE.—A young i lady who had been found n a railway carriage in an 'insen- sible condition was charged at Brighton, on Thursday. with attempting to commit suicide. 'There was no doubt that she had endeavoured to I:ill herself with chloroform. The defendant resolutely declined to give any. account Of herself, and was therefore remanded to prison. THE LUTHER COMMEMORATION. Professor Salmond, who arrived at Wittenberg, on Wedneedav, from Scotland to take part in the Luther commemoration, is the bearer of cordial greetings from the Free Church of Scotland. Sym- pathetic messages are also brought by the Irish deputation on behalf of the Irish Pre3byterian Church, and hy PastO Just, of Bradford, as a delegate of the German Evangelic3l !community of that city and England generally.—The Croiyn Prince, as the representative of the Emperor of Germany, arrived at Wittenhurg on Thursday to take pa irt n th • commemoration Hisa ,Inuserial Highness placed a wreat!,. ,on the tomb Of Luther,-d ' Aftglv4r43 delivered an addrea!, in opening the Luther Hill. 1

div.p: Admiral Pierre, late commander of the French squadron off Madagascar, died at noon on Tuesday. LOCAL 'GOVERNMENT IN INDIA.—The Viceregal Council on Wednesday passed the bill for the, introduction of lucal self-government in the North-western Provinces. A Russian chapel was consacrated at Copenhagen on Sunday, the Emperor and Empress of Russia, the King and Queen of Greece, the Princess of Wales, and other members of the Danish Royal Family being present. FATAL RAILWAY COLLISION IN AMERICA. A terrible railway oollison has occurred at Long Island. Two trains crashed into each other with tremendous force, completely smashing several of the carriages and blocking all traffic. Three passengers were killed on the spot, and 30 others were injured, some very seriously. LORD COL'nIDGE IN AMERICA.--Lord Coleridge is said to have won the heart of Boston by a speech which he de- livered on Saturday. In concluding, his Lordship said that America and England were bound toget,.,er by God Himself in golden chains of mutual affection and mutual respect, and two nations so joined, he was firmly convinced, man would never put asunder. THE CROATIoN RIOTS: 15 PERSON'S KILLED AND MANY WOUNDED.—A telegram published at Pesti', on Wednesday, , announced that violent agitation prevailed on the military

frontier ot Jacoboraez, where the insurrectionary movement was most serious. The military were compelled to fire upon the dense mass of rioters, killing 15, and wounding many others more or less severely. ENGLAND, FRANCE, AND CHINA—The Paris Figaiv ot Tim, sit ly stated that Lord Lyons had a long interview with Cirtllethel-Lacour on Welneeday afternoon, in the course of weich the British Ambassador strongly urged the neces- sity of France considering the danger which would result for European commercial interests from an outbreak of hos- tilities between Franca and China. THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT.—At Bomb iv, Indian loyalty is manifesting itself in advance in connection with the ap- proaching arrival of the Duke of Connaught to take up his military command in India. The municipality of Bombay his voted 50,000 rupees to provide for giving the duke a fitting reception, and is prepared to double the amount if necessary. Of a Prince so highly honoured much will t,e expected. THE CATHOLIC CLERGY AND THE IRISH-AMERICAN AGITATORS.—A telegram from Rome, on Wednesday, says the questions to be examined at the approaching delibera- tions between the College of the Propaganda and a number of North-American Catholic Archbishops and Bishops will include the consideration of the attitude to be observed by the Roman Catholic clergy towards Irish agitators in the United States. EGYPT—Sir Evelyn Baring has assumed his functions as British diplomatic agent and consul-general, and he paid a visit to the Egyptian Ministers on Wednesday, but will not be officially received until the arrival of the Sultan's formal approval of his appointment.—Hicks*Pasha, whose expedi- tion started on the Bth September, telegraphs that, accord- ing to the statements of numerous deserters, the False Prophet's religious influence is broken. A band of ma- rauders have made an attack upon Tolks, near Suakim, but were driven back. A LILIPUTIAN WEDDING —The American newspapers re- port the wedding of Major Mite with Miss Maria Nail, the dwarfs well-known as the "Midgets." The ceremony was performed by special license upon the stage of the Bucking- ham Theatre by Judge Iloke rhe bridegroom gave his age as 30 years, and the bride 33. The lady, who is 31 inches high, was attired in a tshite satin dress, with court train with pearl ornaments and long white veil interwoven with orange blossoms. Major Mite, who was born in Mos- cow, and whose r-al name is Zinaris, is 42 inches high in his styes. THE NORTHERN PACIFIC RAILWAT.—At G-olspike, Mon- , tana, amidst the booming of cannon. and the plaudits of a large assemblage, Mr. Villiard with a silver sledge on Satur- day drove the last spike of the Northern Pacific Railway. A more brilliant gathering of foreigners was never witnessed in the United States. This marks the completion of the third-trans-continental thoroughfare. Mr. Villiard, it was stated, creates a new highway between Europe, America. and Asia. The Northern Pacific is the longest railway in the world. It stretches over 2,500 miles of territory, and crosses thirty degrees of longitude. MURDER OF FOUR CHILDREN : SUICIDE OF THE MURDERESS.—A Vienna telegrami dated Monday night, reports a domestic tragedy of an exceptionally terrible nature. The victims were a Frau Obrist, the wife or a gilder, and her two sons and daughters, whose ages ranged from ten to eighteen. On the room they occupied being entered in the morning all five were discovered to be dead from the effects of poison. The cause of this painful event is that the furniture of the family was to have been ilis- trained upon. The mother, it is thought, first took poison, the children following her example. AFFAIRS IN ZULULAND.—Cetewayo is reported to have taken refuge near Isaudula, with a scanty following. The Times correspondent at Durban says the King's authority is extinct. Dabulamanzi, Cetewayofs brother, and one of the meat warlike aid troublesome of the Zulu Chiefs, has been arrested with his son, Sirago's brother, and half a dozen fol- lowers, in the Tugela Valley. on the Charge of being in the colony without a pass from Mr. Osborn, the British Com- missioner in Zululand. It is believed that Dabulamanzi's objet in crossing the Tugela was to tamper with the loyal Natal Kaffirs. He and his followers have been lodged in

Greytown Prison. EXCITING SCENE IN A FRENCIT MENAGF.RIE.—An excit- ing event has occurred at Lille during the fair. When the amusements were at their height a fire broke out in a menrerie, caused by the explosion of a petroleum lamp. A fearful panic ensued. The animals became uncontrollable, and roared and screamed in a frightful way. Two leopards escaped from their cages, and added to the terrors of the panic-stricken crown of persons attending the fair. Adjoin- ing the managerie was a theatre in which a performance was going on before a large audience. A rush was made to the doors, and a calamity appeared inevitable, but the fire- men arrived and the flames were soon subdued. Although many persons were bruised and injured in the crush, no lives were lost. ' RIOT IN CANTON.—There has been a serious outbreak of anti-European feeling at Canton. Although the immediate cause was an affray with river-side " runners," there cm he no doubt that it is directly traceable to the feelings which have been excited among the Chinese by the ag- gressive policy of France. Several houses were burnt down with kerosene, and the aspect of affairs was so alarming that the European residents fled for safety to the steamers lying in the river. No European was killed, and tranquility was restored by the exertions of the Chinese troops. Gun- boats have been sent up the river from Hong Kong, but great indignation is felt at the absence during the crisis of anv European men of war. The operations of the French in Torquin are stopped for the present by the weather. A Paris newspaper states that the British Cabinet, having " sounded" the Governments of France and China, is pre- pared to effer its mediation for the setilement of the Tonquin frontier question and the other matters arisin4 out of it.

div.head: MERSEY AS-AN INDUSTRIAL
div.p: THE MERSEY AS-AN INDUSTRIAL
RIVER.

A writer in the Shipping World. an,l Merced of Commerce, for S?ptember. who deals with the Mersey as an industrial river, makes reference to the great and busy industries of Widnes and Runc,rn with its magnificent bridge ; and gives a graphic description of the river from its rise to the open sea:--"Probably the finest view of the Mersey is obtained from the hurricane-thck of some homeward-bound ocean liner, passing between the North and Rock lights. The passenger then sees on the one hand the bristling fort and long? sweep of sea-wall, and on the other the Rock Bat- tery bicked by the green Cheshire hills. It will, however, be well before attempting to describe the Mersey at the proud consummation of its career, when the weilth of nations is entrusted to its keeping, and the mercantile navies of half the world float upon its broad bosom, to fellow it in a panoramic manner from its humble source to its responsible maturity. The Mersey, in its Derbyshire home, is born of the union of the Goy and the Theme—both insignificant streams—and pursues its very unimportant way until it arrives at Stockport, and it re- mains unimportant until past Flixton, where, being joined b}P the Irwell, the augmented stream flows on to Warrington, passing between Widnes on the Lancashire side and Run- corn on the Cheshire bank. After this, being j.)ined by the waters of the Weaver and the Bollia, it widens out between Hale Head and Weston Point to become that important estuary of the sea which is known all the world over for its great 'port of Liverpool. ' Although Warrington is 21 miles east of Liverpool, it is on the Mersey, and being an undoubted factor in the industrial history of the river must have a word or two of description. It has a popolVion of some 50,000, and is the centre of the tanning trade of the north for heavy sole leather, there being some 30 or more tanneries for that description of leather, using from 8.000 to 10,000 hides per week. Almost all the soles supplied in army and police contracts are tanned there. Widnes and Runcorn may be dismissed with the remark that they produce alkali, good soap, and bad smells. Sailing onwards in the wider portion of the river, the Weaver hav- ing now joined its waters to those of the Mersey, we come, on the Lancashire side, to Garston, where there are exten- sive docks and excellent railway communication, and where the vessels connected with the Rouen trade are genefally berthed. From this point the grand series of docks of the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board commence on the Lanca- shire side."

AN IRREPRESSIBLE BUTCHER. Elizabeth Darlington, butcher, Bridge-street, was summoned before the St. Helens magistrates, on Friday, for having had an unjust scale in her possession.—Supt. Johnston said that from information he had received be went to Mrs. Darlington's shop on Satur- day night about eight o'clock, and inspected the scale in. question. There was a pound weight lying on it, and when this was removed the other end of the scale dropped down, .and it took about 4 drachms to bring it to a proper balance. The scale, besides, was not fit for use, as it was a very un- certain one.—The defendant, who had been three times previously convicted for like offences, was fined 401. and costs.

div.head: POLITICAL
div.p: POLITICAL

Mr. Hugh Birley, M.P. for Manchester in the Conserva- tive interest ditd on Sunday morning. Dr. Pankhurst has announced his determination to come forward as a candidate for the vacancy in the representation of Manchester caused by Mr. Birley's death. Sir Stafford Northcote and Mr. Raikes have consented to speak at a demonstration of the Conservatives of North Wales, which is to take place at Carnaivon, on the 22nd October. Mr. James Samuelson, the labour candidate for the repre- sentation of Liverpool, was one of the speakers at a meet- ing held in front of St. George's Hall, on. Saturday night, When a resolution was adopted in favour of an extension of the hours of polling to eight o'clock p.m. • Mr. Bradlaugh, speaking at Middleton, on Saturday, said he was going in November to ask the courts of law to in- terpret the law as it stood in the conflict between himself and the House of Commons, and that Course failing, he would interpret it himself. Hitherto his interpretation of the pri- vileges of the House of Commons had been right. At a meting of the 'Nation It Itedicti Federation, held at Westminster, on Tuesday evening, a delegate was appointed to attend the proposed Liberal Conference in Birmingham, with instructions to protest against the late Egyptian war, and to give notice that the National Radical Federation would decline to support the Liberal party in the future unless a genuine policy of peace, retrenchment, and re- form characterised the programme of the conference. Messrs. Bradlaugh arid Labouchere addressed their con- stituents at Northampton on Tuesday night. Mr, L 3.. bouchere reviewed the legislation of the past seseion, and commended the Agricultural Holdings, the Patents, and the Bankruptcy Bills as measures of practical utility. Mr. Bradlaugh said he should not allow Parliament to do any- thing till the House allowed him to sit. The Conservatives had thrown down the gauntlet, which he would crush with fingers stronger than iron. A vote of confidence was passed, after opposition from Councillor Corrington, who objected to Mr. Bradlaugh's expressed determination to meet force with force. He, therefore, refused to move a vote of con- fidence' although requested to do so by the chairman. The Hon. E. F. Leveson Gower addressed his constituents at Bodmin on Wednesday evening. He claimed that the Government still enjoyed the confidence of thecountry, and he believed their policy was improved. It was not true that the foreign policy of the present Government was the same as that of their predecessors. The Conservative policy tended to create difficulties, whereas the present Govern- ment's policy tended to solve them. They were sorry to have to go to Egypt, and would be glad to return therefrom. He trusted there would be no Chinese war, on grounds both of humanity and the prosperity of British trade. He claimed that several useful measures had been passed during the session, such as the Bankruptcy and Patents Bills, and the Agr;cultural Holdings Act.

I REL A.ND. DEATH OF THE LORD CHANCELLOR OF IRELAND.—The Lord Chancellor of Ireland (the Right Hon. Hugh Law) died on Monday morning. He had been ailing for some time. An Order in Council practically closing the Dublin Cattle Market and placing severe restricting on the trade in the metropolitan area was issued as a supplement to the Dublin Gazette on Saturday night. MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A GUARDSMAN—On Monday, the body of Sergeant Price, 3rd Battalion Grenadier Guards, was found in the river Liffey in an advanced state of de- composition, but without any signs of violence. He had been missing for three weeks. THREATEN!NG TO MURDER.—At Cork Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Alexander O'Gorman, brother of Major O'Gor- man, late member for Waterford, was sent to gaol for one month in default of finding bail for having threatened to shoot a man named Compton. ANOTHER OFFICIAL FOUND WANTING.—As a result of Mr. Michael Davitt's representation in regard to the dead pauper he found by the roadside near Loughrea, the Local Government Board has directed the Guardians to call upon the relieving officer to resign his post. DISCHARGE OF PRISONERS —The six men confined in Tullamore Gaol charged with the murder of Constable Brown, of Parsonstown, King's County, were discharged on Tuesday by order of the Government, there being no evi- dence forthcoming sufficient to sustain the charge against them. CRUELTY TO A GIRL.—At Cork, on Monday, a farmer, named Ahern, and his wife were sentenced to six months' imprisonment each for cruelly treating a girl 12 years old, daughter of the former, by not providing her with proper toed, and with fastening a chain on her leg to prevent her leaving the house. A rather fashionably-dressed woman about 40, who gave her name as Margaret J. Ingersole, and stated that she is from Cheshire, is in custody in Dublin charged with at- tempting to commit suicide by throwing herself through the window of the Civil Service Hotel, where she was stay- ing with two children. RAILWAY ACCIDENT—TWO foremen of platelayers, named Clancy and Daniels, whilst superintending some work on the line near Clonmel Station, on Monday, were knocked down and shockingly injured by a shunting train. Ilaniels died in the hospital, where Clancey now lies in a precarious condition, with both legs shockingly mangled. PRECAUTIONS AGAINST SPREAD OF CATTLE DISEASE.— The authorities at the Dublin cattle market took extraor- dinary precautions at Thursday's sales. Six veterinary surgeons were engaged, and 1,900 head of cattle were examined, which necessarily delayed business, but there was not a single case of disease discovered. THE BRUFF MURDER CONSPIRAM—The investigation into the charge of conspiracy to murder preferred against Dr. Connolly, Thomas Connolly, jun., and Kate Connolly was continued at Bruff, county Limerick, on Wednesday, when the case for the Crown closed. Kate Connolly was bailed; the other prisoners were remitted to the county gaol on remand. CRUELTY TO ORPHAN CHILDREN.—The Rev. Samuel George Cotton, rector and manager of the Caragh Orphanage, county Kildare, was on Tuesday fined £lO, with the alter- native of a month's imprisonment, for aggravated assaults on four children at the orphanage, wbona he chained to- gether with heavy logs of wood attached. Notice of appeal was given. THE MURDER OF CAREY : IMPORTANT EVIDENCE ANTICI- PATED.—Nine detecives left Dublin on Saturday morning for London, in connection, it is stated, with the forthcoming trial of O'Donnell for the murder of James Carey. They will be called to verify Carey's departure for South Africa, and it is said that sorae extraordinary facts connected there-

with will be elicited. A MAGISTRATE COMMITTED FOR FRAUD.—Mr. Connolly, a magistrate and landed proprietor, was charged at Tuna- more, on Saturday, with attempting to substantiate false claims under the Irish Arrears Act; also with suppressing certain facts, and being privy to their suppression ; and that he also was privy to the production of false evidence. Prisoner was committed for trial, bail being accepted. " Ma. CLIFFORD LLOYD.—Mr. Clifford Lloyd has issued his farewell addrees to the constabulary of the Western Division, congratulating then t 811 effleieiloy and zeal, and crediting them with the present peaceful condition of the district. It is expected that Colonel Forbes will succeed Mr. Lloyd. It is said that at Mr. Clifford Lloyd's sugges- tion the Government has consented to form the nucleus of a new police force in Egypt by engaging men from the Royal Irish Constabulary. WIFE MURDER. A prisoner, named Glasteen, was charged at the Dundrum sessions, near Cashel, with the wilful murder of his wife, Maria Glasteen, who had been suffering from consumption, when it was alleged the accused treated her with violence. The principal evidence was that of two children, who saw what had occurred through a chink in the door. The prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed for trial. He is a small farmer living about four miles from Dundrurn. Tina Intsn NATIONAL LEAGUE.—At the fortnightly meet- ing of the National Leagne, in Dublin, on Wednesday, Mr. T. Mayne, M presiding, Mr. Harrington, M.P., reported that a meeting of the Organising Committee bad been held, at which it was determined to alter the date of the meetings of committee, so that a report of the proceedings might be submitted to the central branch meetings. The chief busi- ness was the reVision of voters' lists. Subscriptions had been received from several local branches, and £B7 from America. Mr. Michael Davitt was present at the Organising Committee, but was suffering from a severe cold, but is not seriously ill. SANGUINE ANTICIPATIONS.—Messrs. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., Harrington, M.P., and gently, M.P., were present at a National League meeting on Sunday at Galway. A resolution of confidence in the leadership of Mr. Parnell having been passed, the hon. members delivered addresses. Mr. O'Connor observed that the question of self-government for Ireland would soon be taken out of the hands of the Irish party, and dealt with as a question to be quickly I settled by Parliament. Irish independence was not far L distant. Messrs. Kenny and Harrington spoke of the work done by the Irish party, the, former declaring that if seventy good members were returned, independence would soon be achieved. MR. MICHAEL Davitt visited Water- ford on Sunday, and received an enthusiastic greeting. He was presented with several addresses at the railway station, and then accompanied by bands and banners, proceeded to Ballybrieken Hill, where about thirty thousand people had gathered to hear his address. CREDITORS' MEETING AT Sr. H e second general meeting of the creditors of James Conlon, of 2Z qilk-dreet, and Market Hall, St. Helens, has ben held at the oftces of Messrs. Massey mid Hain', solititors, St. Helens. The resolutions passed at the first meeting .iccepting a composition of 43. in the poised, and appointing Mr. Eckersley, chartered accountant, Manchester, trustee to receive and distribute the same, were confirmed.

. . CRICIEET.—A match was played oe Wednesday in a field kindly lent by. Henry Fogg, Heti.. between the Middleton House team, raised bp Master 11. Fagg, and 11 of the senior boys attending the Prescot Board School. 'lhe Middleton, team were the first to bat, and were not disposed of until a .vod stand had been made for 42 tuns. 'I he scholars neat went in to bat, and darkness put an end to the game after 19 runs had been made. The bowling of Master Ft.gg de- serves special praise. The scholars hope to have the plea- sure of again meeting their opponents. AirAtrta' WITH A PONER.-,-TnoMaS Kivangh wa!, on Tuesday, charged at the St. Helens Folic,: Court, with hav- ing unlawfully wounded Cormick Powell.—Bo tl4 the pri- soner and prosecutor, it seemed, live in Jsines-street, and about 10 o'clock on Monday night their wives ware quarrell- ing with each other in the street. Powell went out ani was trying to separate them when Kavanagh rushed out aud "st.Ock him a violent blow on the bead with a poker. Powell fell to the ground and bled freely from wound about an inch song; which bad been inflicted on his forebevl.—At the court Powell said he did not wish to prosecute, and showed great reluctance to give evidence, but thc prisoner was com- mitted for trial at the sestf.ons.

SiIOCIEING OD FitAtt- ACCIDENT /0 ST. HELENS.—On Wednesday afternoon a shocking and f 4•11 accident occurred at Messrs. Gamble's cliemtest works at o,4.ar'd's Bridge, St. Helens. ' During the afternoon a latrahrer nimed Patrick Dunn was engaged filling a waggon, but awe being .missing for a short time he was found lying undeineath some Wag- gons which were in motion, having (widen-fly been run over. The skin and flesh wre torn from One of his legs in a most shocking manner, and the bone broken. Imniediate medical attention was procured, and the injured man waa removed to the Cottage hospital. The injuries, however, were so serious that he died about seven o'clock the same wening. It is supposed that his injuries had been r ceived owing to his falling asleep on the waggon way, 'and ut being per- ceived the waggons had been drawn over his br.dy.__

ANOTHER 'Ai-SAULT ON SALVATIONISTS AT ST. HELENS. —A young man named Robert Duffesy was, on Monday, charged at the St.' Helens Police Court with having as- saulted a; Salvationist named Jacob Spash.—The complain- ant said that on Sunday the Salvationists were proceeding in procession along Tontine-street whe snoieone knocked his hat down on his head He tuned round to see who it was and the prisoner was pointed out as the man who had done it. He therefore got hold of him and told someone to go for a policeman. While they were waiting for the officer the prisoner -kicked and struck him in a very violent man- ner, and several of his'companions attempt.d, to rescue but without success, as he was at length given into custody. Complainant said that his hat, which was worth 15s, was completely spoiled.—Corroborative evidence, which went to show that the Salvationists were meeting with a great deal of hostility in their campaign in St. llelene,.taeving been given, the prisoner was fined 5s ano. costs. STEALING NEWSPAPERS' AT Sr. HELENS.—A respectable looking man, named Thomas Crahan, was, on Wednesday, charged at the St. Helens Pol:cs Court with having stolen a parcel, cmtaining some newspapers and Bs. ld in money, from -a tramcar.—lt appeared that on Taesdav, a parcel of return newspapers had been sent by tramcar from Martha 'Pennington, a stationer, at Hay-deck. to the Liverpool Daily Post Office, St. Helens. On the tramcar drawing up oppo- site Mr. Wilcock's shop, Ormskirk-street, the conductor left the car a short time, and on returning he discovered that the parcel was missing. It also seemed that the prisouer had been seen to go into Mr. Wilcock'a backyard with a parcel under his arm similar to the one stolen, and after- wards a number of newspapers were found in the closet, but Bs. id. was gone. Prisoner was afterwards apprehended at Ilaydock.—The Mayor, who was on the Bench, said he thought there ought to be some more secure place for putting parcels than on the sat i in an open tramcar.—The prisoner, who said he desired to be tried at the sessions, was com- mitted for trial, bail being allowed. THE 2ena L.E. VOLUNTEERS AT Sr. THOMAS Cinntaft— On Sunday morning about 160 of the members of the 2nd L.E. Volunteers attended divine service at St. Thomas's Church, St. Helens. They mustered at the Drill Hall, Cropper's Hill, at a quarter to ten, and marched thence to the church under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Roth- well. The other officers present were Surgeon-Major Hall, Captain Ward, Captain Craik, and Lientenants Lyon, Roth- well, and Higgins (Huvton). The service was conducted by the Rev. Mr. Pigott with the exception of the lessons, which were read by Mr. Vincent, B.A. Previous to com- mencing his sermon Mr. Pigott welcomed the corps, and said he was pleased to see them there in such good numbers, and- trusted that as they had made a start in the way of a church parade they would have one at least once a year. At the 'close of the service the corps re-!ormed in Westfield-street, and was joined by Major Wilccck and Captain Duffy, who had been at a Catholic place of worship, and having accom- panied the Huyton contingent part of the way to the station, returned to the Drill Hall, where thy were dismissed..
ALLEGED BURGLAItY AT PAHR.—At the St. Helens Police- Court, on Mond iv, two young men, named Maurice II nley and Edward Maiev, were charged with breaking into the

house of Charles Whitfield and stealing a golel-watch and guard.—Whitfield said he was the landlord of a beerhouse in Ashcroft-street, Parr, but had only been in the house a week. About 11 o'clock on Sunday night the two prisoners °AMC to his house and got a gallon of beer' and again came back at half-past eleven, and one o'clock on Monday morning, and got some more beer. On each of these occasions they were served with the beer in the kitchen, in which the gold watch and guard, as well as some money, were lying on a table. As soon as the prisoiers left, complainant fastened the doors, Ste., and then fell asleep in the kitchen. About half-past one he heard a noise as if one of the window sashes were going down, but thinking it was only caused by the wind he took no particular notice of it, but on awaking at three o'clock he saw that the gold watch and chain were missing, the money, however, being left. He, in cons-quence, gave information to the police. The stolen articles were worth about £I.I.—P.C. Walsh spoke to having gone to the lodgings of the defendants in Twvford-street and apprehen- ding them. In Hauley's vest lie found the gold watch —No defence was made by the defeudants, except that Hanley said that he had been so drunk that he did not know whet he had been doing, and would certainly have taken the watch back in the morning on finding it in his pockets. They were both committed to the assizes. YOUNG WOMEN'S' FRIENDLY SOCIETY FOR PRESCOT.— On Wednesday afternoon a !fleeting of the young women belonging to the bible class was held in the Town Hall, Prescot. The class is conducted by Mrs. Mc'Naughton, wife of the respected vicar of the pariah. It had been an- nounced that the Countess of Lathotra and Mrs. Wyatt would address the young people. Her ladyship and Mrs. Wyatt were warmly welcomed by the following ladies, who, we must state, do much to promote the interests and well-being of the young women of Prescot: Mrs. McNeughton, Mrs. Penrhyn (Huyton Vicarage), Mrs. W. L. Evans' Mrs. Spenceley, Mrs. Driffield, Miss Driffield, Mrs. Henry Cross, Mrs. Lockwood, Miss Lockwood, Mrs. Arthur Evans, Mrs. Fielding, Mrs. T. Evans, Misses. Coales (2), Prescot. About SO young women acoempanied by their mothers assembled to listen to the advice and admonitions which their lady friend the Countess gave in such simplicity of language and manner that not a single word could be misunderstood by the listeners. After speaking almost ' half-en-bour, the Countess concluded her address by urging and encouraging every young person belonging to the class to the habits of thrift, industry, carefulness, and vigilance. , Mrs. Wyatt followed the Countess and detailed the path of duty young women especially ought to pursue in order to become useful members in the several stations of life to which they may be called. The class now adjourned to the large room in the bank building, where tea was provided. The ladies above mentioned kindly took an active part in making the event as pleasurable as possible. The formation of a Young Women's Friendly Society for Prescot dates from the visit of these two excellent ladies—the Countess of Latham and Miss Wyatt—and such an institution in Prescot will prove of inestimable worth. The concluding part of the day was spent in a service specielly held in the Parish Church. Many of the young women attended the service, which was conducted by the vicar, who was assisted by the Rev. F. Lee. An excellent and appropriate sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, vicar of Huyton. The rev. gentle- man took his text from Gal. vi., 2. Considering the efforts which are being made in the town of Prescot to promote the well-being of its young people, it perhaps may be expected ere long "That our sous may grow up as the young plants; and that our daughters may he as the polishea corners of the temple." He afterwards renewed the was imposed for the drunkenness, and lOs and costs for the assault.—A Young is:en named William Scott wascharged with similar offences to the above in Victoria-street, on Sunday evening.—P.C. He was cons, quently taken in charge when he 'aecame very violent and called upon the crowd to rescue him. RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending 26th March, 1884.—The Guanra..airs of the four of the RuNcorin UNION are desirous ef receiving TENDERS from parties willing ro CON- TRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil ; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces the price to include about 301bs. per week of the best batcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; Best Brand ( lsts) American or English Bacon ; Fish for inmates ; Potatoes; Wheat Straw ; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various Sizes, as per samples, to .be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; liouseCoal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting le, Per „mile. and Funerzls at per funeral. Parties tendering for tbe supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guarditans, how and when required. Tenders to be secompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not ,bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, lu Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other CAR be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's offilcBeB,Fr eodso "Tender for The on or before Monday, the let day of October, 3, ad ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 2nd October, 1883. at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. _ -
By order of the Board, LIII6.KBR, redshiim, 4th September, 1883. Clerk to the Guardians.

On WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 26th.— LYMM, CHESHIRE.— SALE OF VALUABLE FREEHOLD AND LEASEHOLD DWELLING-HOUSES, LAND, AND COTTAGES.—TO BE BOLD BY AULTION, by MR. THOMAS SUTTON (by order of the Trustees of the late Mr. George Forrest deceased), at the PLOUGH HOTEL, in LTMM, on WEDNESDAY, the 26th day of SEPTEMBER, 1883, at Five for Six o'clock in the afternoon, in the following or such other lots as may be detained upon at the time of sale, and sub;ect to condithins of sale to be then read, and which conditi ,ns can be seen at the offices of Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, solicitors, Warrington, 14 days prior to the sale, to- gether with tire indentures of lease referred to in Lots 1,2, and &.

Lot I.—All those Two Freehold DWELLING-HOUSE'. situate on Eagle-brow, Lymm, now in the respective occupa- tions of Miss Forrest and Mr. Thomas Dutton, as tenants thereof, together with the gardens behind the same. The gardens behind the houses contain about 31 perches of land, and are (with the gardens mentioned in Lot 2) leasehold for a term of 21 years from the 29th day of September, 1870, and are sold subject to an apportioned rent of Di, and to the coven- ants and conditions contained in an indenture of lease dated the 30th day of November, 1870. The rent of the house and garden occupied by Miss Forrest is £32 a year, and ef the house and garden occupied by Mr. Dutton is £22 a year. The freehold and leasehold portions are more particularly described in f he plans. LOT 2.—A1l those Two Freehold DWELLING-HOUSES, with the COTPAGE adjoining, and now in the respective occu- pations of Mr. Henry Everton, Mrs. Forrest, and Mrs. Joynson, situate on Eagle-brow, and adjoining to Lot 1, together with the Stable belonging thereto; and also all those leasehold gardens, situate behind the dwelling-houses and adjoining a portion of Let 1. and containing about 37 perches of land. The house and garden occupied by Mr. Everton are let at a rental of £4O per year. That occupied by Mrs. Forrest is valued at £l5 a year; and that occupied by Mrs Joynsou 3s per week. The leasehold gardens behind the houses (with the gardens mentioned in Lot 1) are held for the residue of a term of 21 years from the 29th day of September, 1870, and are sold sub- .

iect to Use rent of £l4, and to the covenants and conditions contained in an indenture of lease dated the 30th day of No- vember, 1870. The freehold and leasehold portions are more particularly described in the plans. The purchaser of Lot 2 will have to take an assignment of the lease of the 30th day of November, 187 G, being the lease of the whole of the leasehold gardens referred to in Lots 1 and 2, and shown on the plan, and must then grant an underiease to the purchaser of Lot 1 of the porti m referred to in that lot, at a mat of Ra per year. LOT those Six Leasehold COTTAGE:a, with the out- builchngs and yards belonging thereto, situate and being in Henry-street, in Lymm aforesaid, and now in the respective occupations of Messrs. Peter Moore. Henry Simpson, and others. This lot is held for a term of 99 years from the 24th , June. 1857, and is subject to the payment of the yearly rent of £8 lie. 10d., and to the covenants and conditions contained in an indenture of lease, dated the 24th June, 1357. The gross yearly rental of this lot is £49 Ss. LOT that Freehold Plot of LAND situate and being directly behind Lots 1,2, and 3, and commonly calledor known as the " Bowling Green." This plot contains about 2 roods and 22 perches of land, and adjoins the Bridgewater Canal, LOT 5.—A1l that valuable Freehold DWELLING-HOUSE and GARDEN,containing about 2 roods and 15 perches of land, statute measure, situate and being at Rush Green, in Lymm, fronting the high road from Lymm to Warburton, and now in the occupation of Mr. William Ogden, as tenant thereof, at a yearly rent of £l3. This plot has a gcod frontage to the high road, and affords a valuable building site.: LOT 6.—A1l those Seven Freehold COTTAGES, situate on

Rush Green aforesaid, and adjoining Lot 5, and now in the re- spective occupations of Messrs. Thomas Wilson, Thomas Brad- burn, and others as tenants thereof. The gross yearly rental of this lot is £5555. The passage between this lot and Lot 7is to be a common passage to both Lots 6 and 7. loT .—All those Two Freehold COTTAGES, CUTTING SHOPS, and GARDEN, situate on Rush Green aforesaid, and on the southerly sides of Lots 5 and 6, and now in the respec- tive occupations of Messrs. William Allman, Francis Bradburn, and others, as tenants thereof. The gross yearly rental of this lot is £33 17s 4d, The passage between this lot and Lot 6is to be a common passage to both Lots 8 and 7. LOT 8 —The Reversion of and in all that Freehold COTTAGE. with the Two GARDENS thereto, and situate on Rush Green aforesaid, and to the south of and adjoining Lot 7. This lot contains about 1 rood 38i perches of land, statute measure, or thereabouts, and is sold subject to the estate and interestthere- in of Mr. John Forster, of Rush Green, Lymm, for the life of ' Mr. Thomas Percival, of Appleton, in the county of Chester. Mr, Thomas Percival is about 71 years of age. There are valu- able watercress beds on this lot. Zcheols, 690 660 (being under 7 years of age) without individual examination, and 2,252,454 (above 7) on passing a satisfactory examina- lien in reading, writing, and arithmetic; 61,056 were actually presented for collective arid 2,119,374 for individual examination, and while of these last 1,378,175 passed the pre- scribed test without failure in any one of the three subjects, 119-zz scholars out of every 100 examined passed in reading, 81 92 in writing, and 77.27 in arithmetic. These figures are very encouraging, and show an improvement on the previous year's returns. The accom- modation has increased by i 48,689 schdol Places, the scholars on the register by 114,250, the average attendance by 151,616, and the number of children individually ex- -4,lllined by 123,676. There is, we are glad to a corresponding increase in the number Passes. These results could, of course, only be obtained by a vigilant application of the Compulsory clauses of the Act, and, although much has been done by this means, much yet remains to be accomplished. These results are also in a measure due to our drawing extensively upon the rates and upon voluntary effort, The voluntary contributions during the .Yciar amounted to £724,846, from 270,253 'ltoscribers ; and the contributions from the tes reached £808,121, an advance of ~'69,384 on the previous year. The receipts 4°m school pence show an increase °ll, the previous year of £76,273 ; the Government grants in aid of ‘4.l.ay schools have advanced on xBBl-2 4,°111 15s. Bjd.to 155. to ihd. per head. The night schools examined during the year were in number; 33,135 scholars above twelve years of age were on an average in attendance each night; 34492 scholars were qualified for examination by having made the required number of attendances during `ne night school session. Of these, 25,370 Were actually examined, and out of every roo SehOlars so examined 89 68 passed in reading, 9.'07 in writing, and 4.9.27 in arithmetic. Mr. Inatthew Arnold, one of the inspectors, calls for a better class of these evening schools, Which are admittedly a great aid to education, and he points out that there is in them a lack pf organisation, which it should not be diffi- cult to remedy. Another Inspector calls at- tention to the fact that the Salvation Army aave in some places proved more attractive "tan the evening ,ichools, which we regret to !ee have in consequence collapsed. A de- Dateable point in connection with the educa- tion question, and one which has given rise '0 Much bitterness from time to time, is that vhich has reference to the financial results Of the working of the day schools of certain etasses. From the present report it appears !hat the expenditure per average attendance in voluntary schools in England and Wales 1.: t 14s. 634 d. ; in the Board Schools it is IS, 61,4 d., or very nearly 7s. more. On ,Lue other hand the grant earned per scholar 441 average attendance was in the voluntary 1C21991§ 15s, and in Board Schools t v - 2d., Or sd. /more. The highest e*endi- tlilire Was in thsi, London Board Schools, and the Ic'wEnt in the Roman Catholic Schools; amount of grant earned, however, was `LigheSt in the Birmingham Board Schools, lowest in the Rohian Catholic Schools. Y e have frequently heard a great outcry from °ur Church friends about the sin of denomi- °ationalists transferiing their schools to the re of School Boards. But Churchmen 'PPear to be the greatest 'sinners in this re- sPect, for we find that since 1875 upwards 1,000 schools have been handed over to school boards, and of this r,OOO no less than 711 were the property of the Church. Fifty- ;even schools were in this way transferred aSt year, and of these 46 belonged to the Church' of England. A very gratifying fea- ture of the report is the fact that the number of half-time scholars is on the decrease, only 177,125 being presented to the inspectors year; it is scarcely so pleasing to read tnat out of the 2.119,374 scholars examined many as 1,062,625, being over ten years of age, ought to have been presented in stand- Ards 4-6, but only 591,238 were so presented; tvfhile 471.387 or 44.36 percent. were presen- cl in standards suited for children of seven, eight, and nine years of age. The proportion scholars presented in standards 4.-6 was in voluntary schools 28.87, and in board schools 26'93. The statistics, we regret to say, show, compared with last year, a considerable off in the number of schools in which 'I), ecific subjects are taught; and another 'errient of dissatisfaction is this, that, so soon bY passing the prescribed standard children are freed from the obligation of attending school and are entitled to go to work, they at once removed. It is very desirable :at if passible means should be devised in srder to prevent so many scholars leaving :11001 under such circumstances, and at so arlY an age. We are glad to find the re- 4111rieration of teachers is on the increase. In , 11,.!7(21 the average salary of a certificated -.aster was Lgi I 2S. 9d., now it .is £ll9 6d., that of a schoolmistress in 1870 was 16s. id., and now it is £72 os. d. The 3rPenditure on behalf of education is on the Increase. The sum expended by school °Dards in England and Wales during the year inider review was £+,215,773, as compared nc/1h £3 521,838 in the previous year. So •Ig, however; as the quality of the education Parted continues to improve, and it is more ,Yedely diffused year by year, the expenditure !s not likely to give much cause for complaint ;nasrnuch as it is sure to be returned in the (Tproved habits and condition of the people. 11 the whole the report is a most satisfactory 2?p, and deserving the careful study of all 7,D0 are interested in so important a work as 44t education of the young.

MR. BANTOCK PIERPOINT announces his annual grand concert for the second week in November—probaby -on the 13th. THE REV. GROWN HACK lectured on "The Bible; the word of God," before the members of Camden Mutual Im- provement Class on Friday last week. MOSS BANK WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNNS —The Rey. J. Hathersall preached the anniversary sermons on Sanday, when callections were made in aid of the trust fund. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELICTION has been fixed to take place on the 23rd October, and naminations may be made up te four o'clock on the 12th October. The Board is composed of 11 membere, and each ratepayer has a likc number of votes, which he may distribute amongst the can- didates as he thinks fit RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS' ELEcrioss.—The official de- claration of the poll shows the result of the election as published on Thursday to be slightly incorrect. The fol- lowing is the correct list :—R. Shaw, 416; Dr. Steele, 400; F. Fairhurst, 386; P. Speakman, 370; H. White, 376; W. J. Shore, 346; Dr. MacDougall, 299. CAMDEN CHAPEL, RuNconfe, after being closed several weeks for repairs and alterations, which have cost LTO, was re-opened on Sunday last, when sermons were preached by the Rev. R. Harper, of Widnes. A children's service was conducted in the afternoon by Mr. H. Randle and Mr. Geddes, of Oldham. A WIDNES MAN DROWNED.—The other morntng the dead body of Michael Jordan, 36 years of age, of Sankey- street, Widnes, was found in the St. Helens Canal at that place. Deceased was employed at Messrs. Pilkington's chemical works, and on Monday last he left the manufac- tory at about four in the afternoon. He proceeded to the Market Hotel, where he had some drink with a man named Martin Donlan. The latter states that deceased left the house at eight o'clock at night, in "a perfectly sober state." He was not seen afterwards until his body was discovered in the canal, into which, it is supposed, he must have fallen, whilst on his way home. LOVE ADVENTURE OF A WIDNES MAN IN ST. HELENS. —al young Irishman, named Terence Loftus, who hailed from West Bank-road, Widnes, on Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, brought a charge of having stolen some money from his person against a young woman, named Catherine Ryan.—Leftus, it seemed, aloag with a companion, had been indulging in a public-house in Liverpool-road, on Saturday, the prisoner and another woman being in their company. He felt rather "drowsy and sick," he said, and went into a back-yard, and was shortly after followed by the prisoner. Whilst there he felt the prisoner's hand in his pocket, and afterwards on going into the public-house he discovered that some money was missing therefrom.— Loftus made his statement in a very cautious and anything but a clear manner, and without asking for any further evi- dence the Bench dismissed the charge. A WIDNNS BUTCHER HEAVILY FlNED.—Before Sir Thomas Earl and Mr. Heal at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Christian Bower, pork butcher, Victoria-road, was summoned to answer a charge of havitg unjust weights in his possession.—Supt. Barker said he visited the defen- dant's shop on Monday, and examined his weights. He found a 71b. weight 1 drachms light, a 41b. and !lb. weight each drachm light, and a Ilb. weight 1 drachm light. The defendant's wife showed him a certificate that the weights were tested in January last, but that was a long time foe weights to remain untested in a business like the defen- dant's. The defendaat had been previously fined for a siiilar offence.—The Bench imposed a fine of £1 10s., and costs 12.—Defendant: I cannot pay it. I can't afford it.— Mr. Lewin: Sit down then. The magistrates will issue a distraint warrant against your goods.—Subsequently a per- son would have paid the fine, but defendant forcibly pre- vented him. Russconti BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Cemetery, on Wednesday, under the presidency of the vice-chairman, Mr. George Moss. The were also present Messrs. Coleburn, James Handley, W. Whittaker, P. Briscoe, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). It was reported that the interments for five months ending August 25th were 135; corresponding period last year 138. The fees received during the Babe period amounted to £135 2s 8d; last year, £127 133 8d; increase £7 9s. The Finance Committee reported that they had appointed Mr. James Handley their chairman for the ensuing year. The month's cash account had been examined, and they recommended ac- counts amounting to £l7 14s 6d for payment. The receipts for the past month were £2B Ils 10d, and the payments for wages £9 Bs, a balance of £l9 3s 104 having been paid in= the bank, It WO recenitnended th!tt s rest on loans fall ink dud on the 25th September, amounting to £5B 15s be paid. It was resolved that a call be made upon the over- seers in December as follows :—Sinking fund, £120; interest and current expenses, £80; total, .£2oo.—Mr. Handley moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Coleburn se- conded the motion, which was carried. DISORDERLY WOMEN AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday, at Run- corn Police Court, Mary Ferrier Was charged in custody with using profane and obscene language, and also with assaulting P.C. Robinson while in the execution of his duty.—P.C. Smith said about ten minutes past eleven on the previous night he was on duty in High-street, when he heard a disturbance, and proceeding to the spot, found the defendant shouting most obscene and profane language. He ordered her away, and she struck him a violent blow on the face, and several times on the breast. She also kicked him. He then took her into custody, but she lay down in the road, and it was with great diffiulty she was conveyed to the police station with the aid of P.C. Smith. As the prisoner was a bad character. the Bench fined her a and costs 7s 4d, or a month's imprisonment on the first charge, and sen- tenced her to a month's hard labour OR the second.—Sarah Blower, a woman of bad character, was on the evidence of P.S. McMichael, cunvicted of using profane language in High-street on June 18th, and sentenced to pay a penalty of £1 and costs 17s 4d, or go to gaol for one month.—Mary Nash, ten old woman, Was fined 5s and costs 17s 4d, for being drunk and disorderly in Cooper-street on the 21st August. FRAUD ON A RUNCORN TR&DEIMAN —Before Mr. Ches. Reynolds, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Henry Hum- phries, about 18 years of age, was brought up on remand charged with having on the &la inst. unlawfully and fraudu- lently obtained from Arnold Unsworth, boot and shoe maker and clothier, High-street, a pair of trousers, a coat, vest, a pair of shoes, a cap, and 10s. From the evidence it seemed that the prisoner was cook on board the schooner sane, of Preston, which is lying in the Weston Canal. On Saturday ; morning he entered Mr. Unsworth's shop and handed Mr. Unsworth letter, which asked him to supply the bearer with a good suit of clothes, and a sovereign to pay his ex- penses to Liverpool. The writer promised to afterwards settle with Mr. Unswortit. The note was signed Captain James Spencer, and as Mr. Unsworth was acquainted with that person, he, without critically scanning the letter, sup- plied the article.% and gave the prisoner 101. 'Oa Tuesday he saw the mate do the vessel, and then discovered that the letter was a forgery. He at once issued a warrant for the prisoner's apprehension, which was effected at his father's house at Penn, in Staffordshire, by Inspector Hollingwortb. The prisoner admitted that he had forged the letter, but added that he was going back to the vessel, and could have "worked it eff."—The prisoner was committed to take his trial at Knutsford Sessions

WIDNES CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMZERANCE SOCIETY.. —At the Mission-room, Alforde-street, on Monday evening, an entertainment was given by the members of the Siinm's Cross Juvenile Branch of the Church of England Temper- ance Society. The room had been decorated with appropri- ate mottoes, presented by Mr. Benbow, of Mersey-road, and choice plants adorned the platform. There was a crowded audience. The Vicar of Whines, the Rev. J. Wright- Williams, presided, and delivered a short address. The following members took part in the entertainment: J. Bate, Lizzie E. Gleave, N. Pilling, Minnie Gillow, Gilbert Thomas, J. and C. Bate, Lavinia Crick, Minnie Gibson, Francis Edwards, Annie Thomas, and Arthur Welland. The dialogue, "The doctor's prescription," was given in capital style by Master J. Bate, and Misset S. E. Hirst, Maggie Raw, and F. Edwards; and another entitled, "The first glass did it," was well recited by Misses Maggie Raw, Minnie Gillow, and S. E. Hirst. During the evening Mts Williams presented the following children with prizes for regular attendance and good conduct: J. Bate, Emma Booth, Lavinia Crick, Annie Cave, F. Edwards, M. Gillow, James Pilling, Maud Singleton, Annie Thomas, F. Warbur- ton, S. Prescott, John Woods, Ellen Forrest, Mary Sale, Mary Taylor, M. Faulkner, M. Gibson, and E. 11. Howarth. The Vicar tendered the acknowledgments of the society to Mr. Bate for lending the piano for the evening's entertain- ment, to Mr. Benbow for his present, and to Mr. A. Edwards for printing the' programmes. A collection in aid of St. Paul's Church building fund concluded the pro- I ceedingz. A WARNING TO FARMERS: A WIDNES CASE. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Beesley, a farm labourer, was charged with committing a breach of the Highway Act by working a steam thrashing machine within such a distance of the highway .as to be a danger to horses and cattle.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, defended. —P.C. Lamont said about a quarter past five on Thursday, the 30th ult., he saw a threshing machine within three and a half feet of the carriage way in Norlands-road. The machine was on a field belonging to Mr. Shuttleworth, and the defendant was in charge of it.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, for the defence, stated that the machine belonged to Mr. Whitfield, of Union Farm, Bold, who had it for six or eight years. The defendant had been in his service 17 or 1E years, and during

the whole of that time had had charge a a-etearq threshini machine. He saidte had never heard that it was an offence to erect thb machine near the highway, and for several years be had erected the machine at the saine place on Mr. Sbuttleworth's Wm. He had also threshed at similar places on other farms. He contended that the 4.ct only required that the machine -should not be a danger to horses and cat- tle, ad this had been provided against by the hiring of a man ill ho stood in the road, and stopped any horses and conveyances that pasted. The machine was then stopped. and the conveyances allowed to pa s 4 He put it to the Bench tkat this was not a case for a penalty, but that. they would say he had suffered enough in having ts engage a solieiter. He called Jonathan Day, who de- posed that he was hired to conduct vehicles past the machine, which was stopped on such occasions. Only three vehicles passed during the day. Mr. T, Shuttleworth said he lived at Nor- land-road Farm. He had farmed it 30 years. Ever since the steam threshing machine was introflucefl he had been in the habit of putting it in the place where it was seen by the constable. It could not have been moved further. If be bad known that a screen was necessary he should have had one erected.—Sir Thomas Earle (the chaitman) said the Bench were of opinion an offence had been committed, though not a serious one. It was well that fanners should understand that they could not put up engines near the highway.—The defendant was ftned 26. Cod, and costs 75. ed.
