THE FENIAN INCIDENT AT We-pmts.—At a meeting of the members of the Loyal Orange Lodge No. 495, Liverpool, 'a resolution was passed to tender their thanks to Inspector Barnett, of the Widnes police force and his men for the cool and determined manner in which they behaved in repressing a disloyal movement, and in saving the flag of England from insult. It was signed on behalf of the Worthy Dis- trict Master by the secretary. The particulars of the inci- dent referred to were reported last week. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL —A special sub-committee of the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal had a long con- ference on Tuesday with their engineer and others as to the plans to be adopted in the bill to be introduced into Par- liament in the next session. Several alternative schemes and several alterations of the original scheme were examined and discussed. It was decided to adhere to the original scheme in its main features. Various alterations were, how- ever, resolved upon, which, it was believed by the com- mittee, would have the effect of improving the navigation and the scheme as a whole, and at the same time remove much of the opposition hitherto encountered. WIDNES FOOTBALL Cum.—A general meeting of the members of this club was held in the Norton Arms, Lugsdale-road, on Thursday evening, Mr. W. Ireland pre- sided. There was a good attendance of members, amongst whom were Messrs. E. H. Harrison, J. Burgess, T. Hindley, A. Brolvn, H. Cookson, J. McCririe F. Smith, W. Smith, F. Sampson, and J. Smith (secretary.) The Secretary read a report which stated that the following gentlemen had ac- c3pted the office of vice-president :—Revs. George Bond, M.A., W. H. Duggan • Messrs. H. W. Deacon, C. E. Barlow, and J. McDonald. Unfortunately the club lost the support of Mr. Duggan through that gentleman having left the town. Ths committee regretted to report the resignation of Mr. J. P. Kershaw, hon. treasurer, but although the valuable services of that gentleman would be lost as head of the finance, he would be retained on the committee. An agree- ment had been made with Mr. Blessington for the use of his field at a rental of £5, and field expenses amonnting to £l. The next charity match has been fixed for December 29th. Übe following sab-committees have been appointed:— Field: Messrs. J. J. Latham, H. Cookson, J. Burgess, E. M. Harrison, and E. M. Davies; finance: Messrs. T. Hingley, J. Burgess, and E. M. Davies.—The report was unanimously adopted.—On the motion of Mr. Burgess, seconded by Mr. , Smith, Mr. H. Cookson was appointed treasurer.—The Chairman urged upon the members to be regular in atten- dance at practices, so tkat the captain would be able to choose a strong representative team to face the one Mr. I Sutton would bring during the season. It would include I several county and international players.—This concluded the business. ASSAULT oN A SHIP'S CAPTAIN AT RllNCORN.—Yester- day, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. Charles Reynolds , and Mr. John Brundrit, Thomas Whitchurch, a young man, I was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 10th September, unlawfully assaulted Joseph Dingle. Dingle is captain of the vessel Fanny, at present lying at Weston ' Docks, and the defendant had been in his employ as a sea- man. On Monday he sent for the defendant in his cabin to settle with him for the voyage. The defendant did not receive the wages he expected, and commenced to use abusive language to the captain, who thereupon ordered him out of the cabin. Defendant then challenged him on I deck to fight. While they were going up the ladder the defendant kicked him on the head, shoulders, and arms; and the captain seized hold of his leg to hold him. On deck the captain was compelled to " clinch " with the de- fendant in his own defence, but used no more violence than was necessary.—Captain Thomas Hawker, master of the Fame, and Charles Broad, mate of the same vessel, corrobo- rated this statement.—Defendant denied that he committed a the assault, but alleged that the captain tore his trousers , and shirt from him. He called Hans Ernest Knaop, mate , of the Fanny, and Charles Obsen, A. 8., on the Fanny, who stated that they saw the defendant and the cap- tain struggling on the the deck, the latter striking the former in the face with his fist.— Before deciding this case the Bench decided to hear a claim by Whitchurch against Dingle for £2 3s, being the balance of wages due to him.—Whitcharch stated he shipped with the captain at London as A. B. for a voyage to Weston Point at the wages of £3 5s per month. He had worked on the vessel a month and nine days.—The captain admitted that he had net paid the complainant able r seaman's wages because he had been unable to perform the duties. He had had to turn him away from tip irtteol, and '1 it had he;;; , ver nae on him and th mate when they had og ttfo Wind On the vessel, lie considered that such sea- Td e I men ought to be stopped by checking their wages in pro- portion to what they were worth. lie believed that a great I many lives were lost and property as well through such I people as the defendant shipping as A.B. In answer to Mr. I Reynolds, the captain said he had made no entry in the log.—Edward Stokes, seaman on the Fanny, deposed to the complainant's incompetency.—The Bench considered the assault proved, and fined Whitchurch 2Cs, and costs 14s Bd,. or in default a month's imprisonment with hard labour. They made an order upon the captain for £2 Os 9d, the I balance of the wages claimed. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—There was a good average attendance on 'Change on Tuesday, but , only a quiet market so far as actual business was concerned. I Makers, however, are still kept tolerably well engaged, and ' there is no perceptible pressure to sell at lower rates. Pig iron makers are still delivering pretty heavily against old contracts, and these, with the small orders coining forward, keep them going. Lancashire makers are firm at 45s to 45s 6d, and in district iron, although more of the inferior brands might be bought for less money, the average quoted rates remain at 44s 101 to 45s 10d, less 21 for forge and foundry Lincolnshire delivered here. The hematite trade continues exceedingly quiet; nominally, prices are unchauged ; but the tendency is towards weakness. Manufactured iron makers are mostly kept busy with orders for prompt delivery, and in some instances there is rather a pres,ure of present business, which has induced one of the local firms to ad- vance their quoted list rates for bars 2s 81 per ton. This, however, is altogether exceptional, and does not represent a realised advance on actual sales, for actual business prices do not more than m iintain the late basis of £6 28 61 to £6 5s for bars; £6 12s 61 for hoops ; and £8 5s to £8 7s 61 for sheets, deiivered into the Manchester district, and there is no great disposition to buy forward even at these figures. Business in tho coal trade continues fairly active for the time .of the year, and the pits are being kept going about full time, with the output generally going away. To some extent, howeyer, the upward movement at the commence- ment of the month has tendert to check the demand, and so far as the advance on pit prices is •concerned, it has scarcely been fully in detained. On the Manchester side, where the leading local firms have not gone beyond an ad- vance on the delivered rates, leaving the pit prices un- changed, there has been a giving way on the part of sellers from those districts where the pit prices had been put up, but in West Lancashire and the districts which are depen- dent upon the Wigan coalfield for their supplies 6d to Is per ton above last month's prices is being obtained. Generally the better classes of round coal are moving off fairly well for house-fire purposes, and for the common classes of round coal there is a moderately good demand. Engine classes of fuel are, however, still difficult to sell; burgy moves off only slowly, and slack is plentiful, the common sorts being a drug, and for the above classes of fuel prices are with difficulty maintained at late rates. Shipping is moderately active, but sellers have not been able to establish any very material advance in prices. The average quoted rates at the " pit mouth remain at about 103 for best coals, 83 for seconds, fis to 6.3 61 for common coal, 4s 6d to 53 for burgy, 3s 63 to 4s for the better qualities of slack, with common sorts to be bought at about 23 91 to 33 3d per ton. For shipment steam coal delivered at Gerston or Liverpool averages 7s 91, and the good qualities of house coal 93 3d to Os 61 per ton.
FARNINORTH AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

The annual show of the Farnworth Agricultural Society will be held on Tharsday next, at the show field, Farnworth. So far the prospects of the exhibition are exceedingly good, and tine ieather is all that will be needed to make it as successful as in former years. In every class but the cattle he entries are as numerous as usual.; the dogs are expected to be a magnificent lot. Considering the alarming extent to which foot-and-mouth disease has spread in the kingdm, the falling of in the entries for cattle is not to be wondered at, but it is reassuring to know that the society's district is free from the disease, and there is no obstacle to the exhibi- tion of the animals that have been entered. The prizes offered for competition amount to £SC)O, exclu.ive of a number of fine silver cups. A public luncheon will be held in the show .field at two o'clock. Mr. E. Whitley, M.P., of Liverpool, will preside.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER
THE OUTER TEMPLE. - RATTLES AND REVOL- VERS. - LONDON FILLING. - MISS KATE VAUGHAN.-ANOTHER THEATRICAL MANAGER. -FIREWORKS AND WATERFALLS. - FLOWERS AT FUNERALS. - LONDON GAS LAMPS.- SOVEREIGNS.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

lln one of Thackeray's novels there is mention made of a set of chambers in the "Outer Temple." The nomenclature reads like the invention of the novelist, but it is at least a fiction founded on a fact. There really was an Outer Temple; the gate which leads into the subway opppsite the Law Courts suggesting the old division by the initials O.T. The passage is just west of Palsgrove Place, and the question of initials was some time ago an important one in fixing the value of rents in the neighbourhood. The Temple lies in the city. The E.C. line strikes south from where Temple Bar used to be. The Outer Temple would have lain west of that line. Palsgrove Place' would have made excellen lawyers' chambers but for the misfortune that it lay at the wrong side of the instal boundary. When the postal letters were introduced the authorities were very arbitrary in their rules about them. Documents which had the initials took precedence of those that had not them, and where they were wrongly adopted there was a delay of a post. The result was that all that network of streets that originally was part of the T-mple, and was largely used by the bar for. cham- bers, got into disrepute. The barrister should have Temple in his address. That was do rigeur, but these streets were not in the Temple according to the Postmaster. Letters and briefs were delayed, and the Outer Temple became an im- possibility. Now so little importance is attached to the address that the Solicitor-General's chambers are not in the Temple at all; postal initials are practically disregarded.

From a meeting held by the superintendents of police at Scotland-yard this week, it seems there really is sueh a thing as a policeman's rattle. I have never heard one myself, nor have I ever met any one who did. The constables seem ner- vous about revolvers,and are not very anxious about rattles. The true solution of the difficulty is to increase the number of plain-clothes policemen and to makg their beats quite un- certain. All other Government officials engaged in the work of detection are quite incalculable in their m3vements. If a negligent schoolmaster or a fraudulent tradesman had the same advantages as the burglar he would never be detected. However, no one is in such danger of the armed burglars as the suburban constable and his apathy about being supplied with firearms looks as if he thought the pre- sent scare was overdone.

Loudon is beginning to fill, the shops in Regent-street are doing well, two or three of the theatres collect big houses, and the Fisheries on Wednesday were quite gay :with fashionable people. The explanation is that this week we are between two seasons. Hamburg, Krensnach, Wiesbaden, Land the whole tribe of Rhenal watering places have shut up their shops and their heuses. The English came late to them this season, and though they came late they did not stay long. I hear that the Hamburg people are grumbling even more than their wont at the worst season since the Franco-Prussian war. And now what may be called the English season has begun. People are all trooping home, and a week fn London is necessary to refit for a fresh tour. To-day the arrivals by the Calais boat were 274. By the way, it is astonishing what a preference there is for early hours on the part of the English abroad. The second ex- press seryice leaving Paris at the reasonable hotlr of tta and getting in about hail-psi seven had not halt-the number of passengers, while the Brussels express only carried 41.

We have lost in Kate Vaughan a beautiful dancer, and notwithstanding what all the critics say, I do not think we have gained anything very good as. an actress. She has been for some years so indisputably the best dancer—indeed the only -graceful dancer on the London boards—that people forget her antecedents. She was once a mere music-hall dancer, famed for her agility. Refinement was not then so much thought of as now. The admired school of dancing wasrather acrobatic. Suppleness and a capacity for con- tortion were what delighted audiences who paid a florin for their stalls. All the same, it was a good school; and the best dancers we have have come from it. I suppose next to Kate Vaughan the most lady-like dancer now on the stage is Ada Wilson. She has only juit made her fame, but she takes rank dis- tinctly as a dancer, not as an acrobat. Most of the business that so delights the Mashers of the Gaiety might just as well be done by men, or indeed by machinery. It is wonder- fully flexible, and it is in time to the music, but it is not Idancing in the sense that Kate Vaughan and Ada Wilson's performances are dances. Yet Ada Wilson was a ballet girl lat the Canterbury. Miss Vaughan carried with her im- personation the same grace which made her dancing so ; delightful, but she wants force and variety, and indeed the dramatic instinct altogether. Her loss to the Gaiety is very considerable. It is the first break in a team that have worked together for many years. Connie Gilchrist does not lin the least fill her place. She is very p;quante or very I perky, according to your own view of her, but her dancing is unrefined. It is not so much musical as music hally. And yet, when she had t'w chance she showed she might have made a very good actress. Her "Libby dear" in the " Almighty dollar" was inimitable. She could have done the Country Girl alatest better ',tun Kate Vaughan but she can't do KAte's parts in burlesque.

I bear that Lady Monclaton is going to join the Eetr- bohn Trees, and both Alto take, a theatre and try—if not lost—their fortune. Lady Monckton is in excellent comedy actress—a sort of young Mrs. Stirling or younger Mrs. Stirling, with a touch of Maria Wilton's hoydenish humour mired up with her genteel comedy capacity. I think she is as yet only known as an amateur, but she has acted very often at Sir Percy Shelley's theatre in Chelsea, and occasionally for charities at the Gaiety. She takes the same kind of parts as Mrs. Kendal affects, and plays them with more breadth and humour. Mrs. Beer- bohn Tree has b'ossomed out into an actress finite suddenly. She is now engaged with her hus- band at the Globe, but as yet there is more promise than performance. Beerbohn Tree hirnsslf is a born actsr. He IS an actor just the way Toole is an actor. He cannot help himself. I've seen him in the Strand follow a friend of his and adopting exactly the whine of a London beggar solicit alms, which his friend, without looking round, would re- 'f ese. lie would go on begging till at last the other would turn round angrily and dad Mr. Tree blandlg walking be- hind him in the most faultless mornicg costume. •

it is a horrible idea to think of ths Rhine being added to the list of natural objects which are treated scenically, and-suhjected to the vulgarity of lime light ,and Bengal lire. It is a kind of well-deserved Nemesis that the guests at Schaffhausen this ye3r have suffered a great deal from rheumatism, as I arn also told that the visit to the Cobseun exhibited for five francs under a blaze of Bengal fire, in- variably develops malaria amongst some of the English and American guests. It was, perhaps, well enongh to exhibi the Giessbach by pyrotechnic light, but the :Falls of the Rhiceought to have been respected. I suppose it is neces- sary to make Nature suit all tastes. There were a number of Cook's tourists at Schaffhausen this year.

I hear that the subject of funeral reform will be started from afresh point of view. The meaningless pomp and ex- pense are what have recently been attacked. The decorations are now coining in for their share of criticism—l mean the floral decorations. These have latterly become entirely conventional. They are sent just as Christmas canto are sent, not so much from fooling as because it is thought fashionable to send them. There are of coarse certain .oc- essions when the fashion, even if it be no more, should be observed. Her Majesty the other day sent a wreath of roses and lilies to Frohsdorf. But amongst private people the usage has -become a tax. It means but little and it costs a very great deal. I remember seeing the funeral cortege of Madame Blanc, the widow of the owner of the gaming tables at Monaco, pass up the streets of Paris literally heaped over and laden with fl Avers. This kind of floral grief has become not so much a tax as a tyranny, and it will continue tall acme person high in rank discredits it. It may be that as we used to see after the announcement of a wedding "no cards," so we may see to an invitation to a funeral "no flowers." This winter there will be fought in London a novel kind of battle of the standards. As the combatants will be vestrimen, it may be surmised that the battle will not be very chivalric. Indeed, the standards arc not banners but brackets. The gas-lamps of the West End are admitted to be intolerably shabby. Indeed, they are more than shabby; they are dangerously insufficient. We have gJt such fine big globes now that the old standards cannot support them. I hear a great effort will be made to try and get them all as much as poseible of the oame pattern. Workmen are now

busy at the corner of Icorthurciberland-avenue, opposite the Grand Hotel, putting up very_ handsome standards. But these are only tentative; that is they will certainly be adopted for their present site, but it is not yet settled whether the other end of the avenue will h:e turui•Med with similar lights. It is clear that something most be dine for the piece of ground opposite Apslev House. Even when the crutches are taken from. under ths Duke's statue, and he goes into the melting pot, the site will he one of the most important in London. At present it is very well lit, but the lamp-posts are obviously only temporarily put up, and probably whatever is adopted there will be repeated all along

One of the London police magistrates has come out with a very good suggestion about spurious coins. His remark has only reference to the gold coinage. He says we have too many sovereigns, or rather too many sorts of sovereigns. There is the red gold alloyed with copper, and the yellow gold alloyed with silver; and there is the George and Dragon sovereign, and the more common pattern, and lastly, there is the Australian sovereign. The tradesman gets per- plexed, and really judges by the weight and the ring. lam told milling is the coiner's chief difficulty, and yet most of the gold pieces of other countries have a motto stamped on the edge. All the French coins have, and so have the Belgian, and most of the Italian. The Austrians use the edge, and so latterly do the Russians. One point that is liable to be overlooked in dealing with questions of bad coins is that in theory the crown is the loser, but in reality it is the public wko are the holders of the coin. If the Mint and the Treasury combined cannot put down coining it is rather hard that the innocent "holders for value" should have to pay for it. With the silver coinage one does not mind, but it is rather hard on a tradesman who finds two bad sovereigns in his till.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COM- MISSIONERS.

The first meeting of the Board since the election was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. J. Meadowcroft pre- sided, and there were present—Dr. Steele, Messrs. T. Nor- man, Dobson, White, Fairhurst, W. Whittaker, Shaw, Lake, Pritchard, Briscoe, P. Speakman, Williams, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), and M. Barker (sur- veyor).

div.head: LATE MR. TIIOIIIB COOK, OF HALTON.
div.p: THE LATE MR. TIIOIIIB COOK, OF HALTON.

The remains of Mr. Thomaa Cook, of L'alton, were in- terred on Tuesday, at Runcorn Parish Church, with every mark of respect. With the death of Mr. Cook a long and useful life has been closed, and respected and full of years the deceased has passed away. Mr. Cook, who had reached the ripe age of 75, ,came to reside at Halton Z 5 years ago, and actively interested himself in many social reforms in his own village and,the adjoining town of Runcorn. His sympathies always lay with the Oddfellew Order, with which he was associated before hiaresidence in ilaiton. He took a prominent pact in the formation of several local lodges, which are now useful and ,prospereus izstitutions. He had held various official positions, which his ex- perience and shrewdnesa enabled him to fill with credit. The deceased, however, was not one of those men Woo regard the Oddfellow movement from a cceunercial standpoint alone. He never werlooked eke importanze of the Order as an assistance in dime' of sickness among the working classes, but while atriving to promote financial prosperity, he sought to unite aye brotherhood in a bond of mutual respect and affection. This was always his aim, and his example left its impress upon the lodges with which he stood associated. For some years the &. ceased held an official position with the Wesleyan Metho- dist Society at Halton, but on account of feeble health re- linquished it some years ago. The funeral, as above stated, took place on Tuesday. In the first carriage there were the Rev. John Lockwood, vicar of Halton; Mr. George Crute, and Mr. Robert Wright, Mr. William Croley, and Mr. Geo. Rodgers representing the local Oddfellows' lodges. The next carriage contained Mr. John Cook Mr. Charles Cook, Mr. Jno. Lancaster, Mr. Wesley Cook (sons), and Mr. Win. Cook (brother to the deceased). In the next carriage were Mr. B. Roberts, Mr. J. Caygill and Mr. Lewis (sous-in-lavv), Mr. T. Cook (nephew), and Mr. John J.lckson. The bearers were Mr. John Wesley Haddock, Mr. S. Coventry, Mr. Thomas Cooke, and Mr. Barrow. The burial service was read by the Rev. John Lockwood, the funeral arrangements being in iho bads of Mr. S. Yarwood.

div.p: THE ELECTION: AN BXPLANATIoN WANTED.

Mr. BRISCOE declared the result of the election, an the new members took their seats in the usual form.—Dr. STEELE moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, that the return- ing officer's expenses, amounting to £l2 us. for the elec- tion, be paid.—Mr. Donsow said perhaps the returning officer would give an explanation of the error in the declara- tion of the poll. The officials had plenty of time to give a correct report.—The Lew CLERK: The final return was never corrected. It was only a rough accourit of the elec- tion that was corrected, and not the final report that the returning officer signed.—Mr. BROOKES explained that there were two pages in the polling book, and only the total of one page was brought into the summary that was first. published. In posting up the final summary afterwards, it was found that this page had been omitted.—The LAW CLERK: But the final return was never corrected.—Mr. BROOKES: No; it was not the official declaration of the poll that was issued after four o'clock.—The motion was then carried. TNE COMMITTEES.—MR. HANDLEY AND THE FREE LIBRARY
CollflflrrEE.

The next business yas the appointment of committees.— Dr. STEELE said he had often thought that if the Free Library Committee was composed entirely of members of the Board or entirely of outaiders, it would be an advantage. However, as it was now he thought it better to leave the names as far as possible what they were heretofore, and begged to move that the Library Committee consist of the Chair- man, Dr. Steele, Messrs. P. Briscoe, F. A. Lake, P. Speakman, and R. Shaw as Commissioners, and the Rev. Canon Bar- clay, Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. John Simpson, G. Rhodes, and T. Riley non-commissioners. He placed his own name

there because he took great interest in the Library.—Mr. F. A. LAKE You leave Mr. Handley out.—Dr. STEELE : I cannot help it.—Mr. LAKE : Of course you must leave some one out.—Dr. STEELE : I think it desirable that Mr. Riley should be on. I think he represents the working class—the class for which the library is intended. Mr. &Law thought the committee consisted of too many mem- bers, and wished his name left out.—Dr. STEELE substituted MI:. Lightbarn's name because he was not on any other committee.—Mr. NORMAN seconded the proposition.—Mr. LAKE thought Mr. Handley ought to be a member of the committee. It was an awkward matter to strike anybody's name out, because all the members mentioned he should like to see on the committee, especially the outsiders, but Mr. Handley took such a large part in the formation of the library, and took such an intense interest in it now, that he certainly ought to be placed upon it even if they had to strike the name of someone else out. He therefore proposed Mr. Handley in place of Mr. Rhodes. Personally he should very much like Mr. Rhodes to have a seat on the committee, but that gentleman had retired from the Board and had an objection to take a greater part in public matters than he could help, and would feel relieved if Mr. Handley's name was substituted for his own. Mr. BRISCOE seconded the amendment.—Mr. NORMAN, as seconder of the resolution, would be pleased to see Mr. Handley a member of the corn- mittee.—Dr. STEELE had no objection to Mr. Handley's name, and after Mr. Lake's remarks, he would accept it in place of Mr. Rhodes.—The resolution was then passed. The other committees were appointed as follows CANAL BOATS' AND HOSPITAL; Messrs. W. Fisher, S. Taylor. P. Briscoe, T. Norman, W. Whittaker, P. Speakman, F. Fairhurst, and H. White.

PERFORMANCE OF THE "FLOWER QUEEN" AT RUNCORN. The charming cantata, "The Flower Queen, or the coro- nation of the Rose," retains its hold upon the affections of the people of Runcorn. Three years ago, and again in 1881, it was performed before crowded audiences, and 013 Wednesday evening last, the third occasion of its represen- tation in the town, the Public Hall was filled with an ad- miring and appreciative company. The reasons for its suc- cess are not far to seek. To a poetical composition of pure sentiments and graceful style, is the added charm of beautiful Choral music, and solos and songs in bright and pleasing numbers, while the whole is set off by scenic effects of no mean order. A detailed description of the piece is not needed, as a lengthened account has pre- , , Yiously been published in The Examiner. The argument, , I as prefaced on the programme, is briefly that the Flowers 1 I meet in a secluded dell in the forest to choose their Queen. A person discontented with the world seeks, in the same I place, retirement from its cares and disappointments. The Flowers tell of love and duty; and the Recluse—learning that, to fill the station allotted by Providence is to be happy —resolves to turn again to usefulness and contentment among his fellow creatures. Frances Jane Crosby has woven this simple plot into a delightful story, which lulls itself to a variety of artistic treatment, and we must com- pliment Mr. Handley, the talented conductor, upon the suc- cess which has attended his latest production of the cantata. The performance, with the ex- ception of a few slight blemishes, which only the exacting critic would seriously regard, was well sustained throughout, and the individual " flowers" and the chorus won the praise of all by the finished grace with which they filled their parts. With the exception of Miss Eborall, the" Queen Elect," and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint, the "Recluse," the performers were all amateurs, a fact which ; adds considerably to the merit of the representation. The' secluded dell, where the meeting of the flowers takes place, was admirably I:C.".:Vtrayed, and when the screen was drawn aside, revealing the grouped flowers singing the chorus "We are the flowers, the fair young flowers," surrounded by luxuriant plants, and beautiful flowers arranged with exqui- site taste and skill, there was a hearty outburst of applause. The costumes of the fair performers agreed well with their characters, and profusely adorned with flowers, added brightness to the scene. To Mr. G. Rhodes belongs the credit of designing and carrying out these decorations, for which he also to a great SHOCKING DROWNING CASE AT extent provided the inaterials,although Mrs. C. We have rreviously noticed the excellent per- formance of the chorus, and having stated that Miss Fannie Handley presided at tire piano, Mr. John Ravenscroft at the harmonium, and that there was an efficient orchestral baud, it only remains to be added that Mr. Handley weilded the baton with his usual =proficiency. The performance was repeated on Thursday evening, when the Public Hall was again crowded. The cantata passed off in admirable style, everything working with the greatest smoothness. THE " CIIAMTION WALKER "AT EARLESTOWN.—D a ring the present week, a large number of persons resident in Earles• town and Newton, have been considerably amused at the daily peregrinations of a person calling himself 'The Cham- pion Walker" who professes to be engaged on the some- what arduous task of walking 2,000 miles in 1,000 hours. What conditions or what inducement is held put to the fel- low, who is apparently attempting the task, are not quite clear, but the collections which are made in certain public- houses, may possibly account in some measure for hie lengthy walk. The " walker " frequently patrols the road from the Blue Lion, Newton, to the Oddfellows' Arms, Earlestown, and as before stated, his passage through the latter town, particularly in the evening, attracts consider- able notice and attention, the juveniles being the meat ardent admizers and followers of the " ped. " , ORDERS FOB MatrrENiNcß.—.-Before Messrs. R. Hough- ton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqe., at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, Richard Carr was summoned by Joseph Caldwell, relieving officer, for neglecting to maintain his wife at present confined in Whittingham Asylum. Mr. Caldwell seated that the defen- dant's earnings were about .£2 per week, and he had three children working. His wife was costing the Guardians 18s. per week, but they etily asked for an order for ss. per week. The Bench made an order for that amount.—John Dickinson was summoned for neglecting to maintain his father and maher. According to the statement of Mr. Cald- well, the earnings of the defendant would average about £1 per week, and the Guardians asked for 2s. weekly. An order was made —An order was also made upon Paul Critchley to pay the sum of is 81 per week towards the maintenance of his mother, who is over 80 years of age and chargeable to the common fund of the Union. There were three sotis who contributed the amount stated, but the defendant was £5 in arrears.—Henry Wildman was sum- moned for neglecting to maintain his father. Mr. Cedwell stated that the defendant's father was over 70 years of age, and the Board of Guardians allowed him 5s per week. Four sons each repaid is per week, but the defendant re- fused to do so. The defendant said he had had 15 weeks' illness, and he had a wife and family to support. He was quite willing to pay, but be had been unable to do so for some time. He supposed the relieving officer was a limb of the law, and was sure to show his authority. As Shakespere said, "He is droved in a little brief authority," and he wanted to show what he could do. The magistrates Imade an order for the defendant to contribute is per week.

A RISKY EXPERIMEN'T.—Captain Drerar, who started on Thursday night from Dover for Folkstone ix exeri- mental tugboat, has not sinca been heard of. FAREWELL ADDRESS TO THE MARQUIS OF Lortim—A farewell address was presented to the Marquis of Lorne and Princess Louise by the Municipality of Toronto, on Thursday. MR. PARNELL'S ESTATE.—The Dublin Express yesterday says :—We understand that Mr. Parnell has recently paid off the charges on his Wicklow estate, amounting to £13,000, by a cheque on the National Bank. FEARFUL FALL OF A STEEPLE JACK.—Whi:e Alexandra Williamson, a steeple jack, was engaged in repairing a chimney-stack near Boness, on Thursday, he fell to the ground, a distance of 200 feet, and was killed on the spot. A tOLT AND COWS AFFECTED BY HYDROPHOBIA.— At Cahirconliss, Ireland, a colt and five cows have been bitten by a mad dog. The colt has sines died, and the cows are in so pitiable a condition that they will b 3 slaughtered.

NEWRY CONSERVATIVES have resolved to present Sir Stafford Northcote with an address on his visit to Belfast. A prize fight, believed to be for a hunlred pounds, toA place at Orpington, Kent, yesterday, the pugilists mines being unknown._ . .

Oiirasoß IN IRELAND.—A labourer, nlmed P,Atrick Kely, was waylaid and stabbed on Thursday night when return- ing from Tullamore Fair, by a p3rty of men. No hops are entertained of his recovery. The police as 311rching for the assailants.

Foot-and-mouth disease is spreading throughout North- amptonshire, Huntingdonshire, and C.infordgeshire in an alarming degree. The whole of the Isle of Ely, in Cirn- bridgeshire, comprising several towns .td many villages, has been declared an infected area.

MANCHESTER ELECTION.—A—bubI in correspondent tele- graphs:—lt is now certain that the Irish National League will take no active part in the Manchester election, the seat being regarded as a certainty for the Conservative candidate. Dr. Pankhurst will reeeive the Irish vote.

SERIOUS BOILER EXPLOSION.—YesterdAy morning a boiler explosion occurred on the premises of Mr. Hurley, Lutterworth, near Leicester. The buildin;, together with the tall chimney, were reduced to a heap of rains, and the debris was scattered in all directions, portions of the boiler falling in the adjoining streets. Three parsons were in- jured; one seriously. pillow SMALLPDX IS SPREAD. At Birmingham, where smallpox is still very prevalent, a man was summoned yes- terday for sending the clothing of a smallpox patient to a pawnbroker's shop, where it was taken in pledge, and mixed with other garments. The man's only defence was that "he did not mean to do any harm." The magistrates ill-. posed a fine of 103. and costs.

- SERIOUS FIGHTING IN TONQUIN : HEAVY LOSSES. -- A. telegram from Hong Kong, yesterday, says :—An engage- ment lasting eight hours, has been fought between the French troops and a body of Black Flags at Phokhai, be- tween Hanoi and Sontag. The French had two officers and 50 men killed and wounded. The loss of the Black Flans is estimated at between 500 and 600 men. THE LUTHER COMHEMORATION.—III connection with the Lather commemoration it is reported that amongst the descendants of the great Reformer wesent at Wittemberg are Lieutenant Fletcher Luther, of the British Navy, and Dr. Luther, of Belfast. The authorities at the British Museum recognise the cclebration by exhibiting numerous books, manuscripts, and other relics of Reforma- tion times.

Dnowzrzu Ix A WASIIII7I3.—Au inquest was held at Blackburn, yesterday, touching the death of Elizabeth Pearce, aged one year and eight months, daughter of a moulder. The child, when playing in the backyard of the house of a woman named Walsh, who nursed her while her mother was at the mill, fell into ,a washtub, containing about a gallon of water, and was drowned. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

All doubts as to the safety of Mr. Simmons, the wronaut who ascended at Hastings, on Thursday, with the intention of crossing the Channel, were set at rest yesterday evening by the publication of a telegram received in the afternoon from the Cherbourg correspondent of the Central News, stating that the balloon and its occupants, Mr. Simmons, and Mr. Small a Hastings photographer, landed safely at Cape la Hague, at midnight. SHOCKING WITH OF A BOLTON TRADESIVOMAN.—An elderly tradeswoman, named Charlotte Marshall, was found dead and terribly disfigured at the bottom of come cellar- steps near her residence, All Saint's-street, Bolton, yesterday morning. The deceased was one of the most prominent butchers in the town. She was seen going home about eleven o'clock on Thursday night, and evidently fell down the open cellar way. There is no suspicion of foul play. DISCOVERY OF DYNAMITE:CARTRIDGES NEAR L:ORK.—At lan early hour yesterday morning, acting on iafortr?ation, Sub-inspector Starkie and Constable Bulwer went to Kil- berry, en the outskirts of the city of Cork, and discovered 190 cartridges of dynamite near an old fort. They were bud' a few inches underneath the surface, and appeared to have been there a considerable time, as the paper in which they were folded was rotten. An informer pointed out the place of concealment. LORD DUFFERIN RECALLED TO CONSTANTINOPLE.—The Pall Mall Gazette says :—We are informed that Lord Duf- feria has been suddenly recalled to Constantinople. It is nearly a year sines Lord Dufferin left the Bosphorous, and although his full holiday has not yet expired, her Majesty's Government appears to have thought that under existing circumstances it would be well if the British Amhaseader at the Porte was again at his post. Lord Dufferin will leave for Constantinople on Wednesday next via Marseilles. Coneasrote AT SEA.—Eeirly yesterday morning the steam- ship Hardwick, of West Hartlepool fer Sunderland in bal- last, was towed into Scarborough in a sinking condition, having been in collision yesterday morning, in a thick fog, about twelve miles north of Flamborough Head, with the steamship Crcesus, of Middlesborough for Bilbao. She was cut down below the water's edge, and, the sea pouring in, sail had to be placed over the rent. A fireman on board at- tempted to jump on to the Crce3us, but was killed.

- CHARGE OF AIDING TO DEFRAUD CREDITORS - At Macclesfield, yesterday, John Henry Wood, prtc:er and stationer, was charged, on the prOsecution of the Treasury, with aiding and abetting George Brownson, tailor ard draner, to defraud his creditors.—Counsel for the Treasury said he would prove some of the most impudent frauds ever perpetrated. The evidence showed Wood-made a false claim on the estates, tore leaves out of the ledge, and con- cealed goods belonging to the creditors. The prisoner remanded.

The prisoner bad gone and f rom- Lon- don through Glasow to Coll, in the Rebride-,, then to Belfast, returning to Glasgow, and sabsequa"atty. proceeding to London. Post Office Detectives Ru.mbold and Buller :h, traced the prisoner, from a West End otel to Walworh, P./0 was recovered. , and on Thursday arrested him. £5

PANIC IN A Sour g YORESIIIPA four o'clock yesterday morning ans alarming accident, followed employed on the night shift, by a panic amongst the MP:, occurred at Church-hole Colliery, Dodworth, which gave rise to the rumour that the workings were on fire. A large steam pipe which conveys the steam from the surfacs to the undnground leaulage engines burst, causing the steam to rush thron;in the air currents and workings. The work- m'en, being panic stricken, rushed , to the pit bettom, and. were drawn out of the colliery. DISLOYALIY te DUBLIN—In Dublin on Thursday night, at the *meting convened by Mr. Porter, of the "Loyal . _ _ _

National Association for the Revival of Ireland's Legislalive Independence "exception was taken to the use of the term. "loyal "in the tile of the association by a man named Ward, who was subsequently chaired around the room. Two resolutions were proposed, bet the expression of loyalty to the Queen in one of them evoked groars and hisses. A voice in the crowd said "Parnell ruled' Ireland," and the. Chairman, attempting to proceed, hoped they would not act so foolishly as to repudiate loyalty to the Queen. This ob- servation was met by the question "Who is she ?",and a lad, who covered one of his eyes with a cloth, said, She is not much respected about the vicinity of Northampt9n.o Shortly after, nearly all present left, the man Ward being cheered down the street. ALARMING BrBSIDENCE IN CHESHIRE : PROPPING UP I TOWN HALL.—Tho Northwich Town Hall is in such a damaged condition in consequence of subsidences caused by continual extracts of brine at the large salt works near at hand, that the local magistrates recerrly issued ae, order to the lessees to take it down or to repair or otherwise Secure The building. The lessees decline to =Ns in the matter, and on the local board now devolves the responsibility of protecting the Public. If a portion of the Town Hall is taken down the entire building will inevitably collapse, it is 83 cracked and split up by uneven stibsidences. There is no power to rebuild the Town Rall,and the magistrates refused an application to amend their order by inserting the word "rebuild." The only alternative is tl temporarilY secere the building by what is popularly known throughout the salt district as propping, and this will probably be attempted immediately.

THE WALTHAMSTOW MURDER. At the Central Criminal Court, yesterday, William Goul- stone, blacksmith, aged 25, was tried for the murder of i& five Children—three of whom be drowned in a c's.ern, and afterwards killed his twin babies by repeateJlv striking them on the bead with a hammer. For the prosecution, a number of witnesses were examined whose evidence clearly proved prisoner's guilt. For Otte defence. a Plea of insanity was set up, and witnesses were called who testified that In both branches of prisoner's family there was hereditary in- sanity, and that his mother and several other relations had been confined as lunatics. The jury, however, after only fifteen minutes absence., found a verdict of guilty; and prisoner, who protested his innocence, was sentenced to death.

ATTACK ON THE HUYTON VOLUN- TEERS AT KNOTTY ASH, The first march out of the newly-formed Huyton Com- pany of the 2nd Lancashire Engineers Volunteers (Captain Ross's) has been marked in an unexpectel manner. They mustered between ninety and a hundred, at their quarters, the Queen's Arms, near Huyton station, on Saturday after- noon, and formed under the command of Lieut. Higgin at half-past five o'clopk, headed by their band from St. Helens. They marched through Roby and Broad Green to Knotty Ash, fellowed by a numerous crowd from Huyton and Whiston. Refreshment was provided for them on the bowl- ing green of the Knotty Ash Hotol. Whilst regailing them- elver. it seems a disturbance arose in another part of the hotel L'etween some of their followers and others of the neleUeurhood. On re-assembling and ready to march, two-Pea-faring men named Jack Morris and Harry Ireland, belonging to Lfeyton, were set on by half a dozen men; three of their friends in the Engineers thereupon left the ranks to aid them, and the efforts made by Lieuteeant Higgin to restore discipline, com- menced what threatened to be a serious riot. Some left the front ranks under the impression that their officer was being maltreated. A degree of order having been ac- complished, a start was made, the band playing a popular air, which is supposed to have been mistaken for a party tune. However, the Irish element of the neighbourhood mustered in great numbers men and women execrating m the and pelting them with stones. When about a mile had been marched under these difficulties a big, stalwart Irishman made a dash at one of the bandsmen; a halt was called, then ensued *general fight; the ranks broke up, the first assailant was pinned to the wall by three or four rifle butts and muzzles; sticks, stones, and rifles were made free tise of; one Volunteer (Sapper Henry Eastleam) drew his bayonet and struck a man on the ground, but he was Immediately seized by Lieutenant Higgin, and his arms and acccutrements taken from him. Energetic efforts were Made to restore order, and ultimately headquarters were reached about nine o'clock, with no more serious injuries than a few cuts and bruises. In addition to the officer minted, there were present Sergeant-Major Edwards, Ser- geant Drill-Instructor Goss, Sergeants Herbert, Bernard, '—einwrigebt, and Tomes. Eistham, it is stated, was ordered , "end in his uniform, and this he did on Monday even-

HAVE MADE ME. Stephen had gone, but his heart quickly revolted against so leaving his mother, and he returned to her. Even in the brief time that had elapsed while he was away from the Countess, he had changed his expression— recovered his ordinary attitude—and was able to say with a smile,— "It's very absurd this taking of things seriously; but as I don't often err in that way, I suppose you can forgive me 2"

"Yes, if you will listen !" "If I do, remember it is simply because you ask me !" As he said this, he placed both his hands on the table, and leaned over it, so near to her, that she felt certain what- ever he might say, he was deeply interested in the sub- ject, and bent on th 3 sttidy of lacr tell-tale features the while. " Yon said it was a question of honour. Suppose I could find a way honourably to settle that, and leave it no- longer a question ?" " Mother, Ido nof care for such flights of fancy. They are like those of my shuttlecock, easy to send up, but cer- tain to come quickly to the ground." "But if I do what I say?" "Then—yes, then I'll think of it." "You like her ? ' "Very much—when I can find time." "Do you cemsider her good looking ?" "No." "Stephen, you amaze me!" " Ah, that's because you don't wait to the end. i going to add—because she is so much more." "I think her loyely !" "Tastes differ." " But yours?" "Minds its own business. Once mare, mother, I tell you
I was

I an; quite sure this is not mine." "What, not even if the young lady differed from that opinion ?" Startled, a little confused, but anxious before everything else to keep his mother from any progress in the delicate path she had chop, Stephen answered brusquely, almost rudely. "As I don't think the young lady has any one settled opinion of her own, she is scarcely entitled to meddle with that belonging to anybody else." "For so young a man you seem strangely harsh in your judgment"! "I suppose it's through not getting tamed by conflict with the world, whi,th you know you didn't approve of." It was too mach. The Countess rose in anger and deep distress, and was about with passionate vehemence to say a few words, and resign for ever the things for which she alone now cared to live ; but Stephen moved in turn, antici- pated her, and said with faltering voice— "l am sorry. I will be more careful. Tell me what you wish. I will not, if I can help it, again interrupt you." lie then 3W:A by her side, his face turned a little away. "You are poor. And whatever I can do for yon will not make you rich. Miss Vandeleur's fortune would. That is one thing." "She is a lovely girl, not yet knowing her own heart and mind, with much of the brightness of youth, and of high spirits, fond of the despotism which beauty tends to create, but no sort of evil in her, and no faults but such as time. experience, and above all the care and love of a worthy hus- band, will no doubt remove." "When she came here I told her in the plainest words, to consider herself free."
"Did you tell my brother that ? " sharply interposed Stephen. "No."

"Why not?" "Because he would have thought my act had been done in hostility to him. And I did not tell you for the opposite reason, that it might have led to baseless dreams. In fine the young lady herself was a stranger to me in all essen- tials; and therefore I did no more than was required to put her at ease, and relieve her from an embarrassing posi- tion which she had done nothing to create." " And why do you tell me now ?" Such was the ques- tion the Countess waited to hear, and wanted, but it came not.

Stephen_ was strangely silent, but locked so much more troubled than pleased, that the Countess, striving to guess what was passing in his heart, concluded that his habit of self-depreciation, if partly assumed to antitipate unfavour- able opinion from others, had ended by making him believe in his low estimates of himself.
"And what practically do you wish me to do ?" he said, breaking the long silence, when he found his mother would not.

"Be respectful and attentive to her, which at present you are not. Study her in a kindly spirit. Don't frighten her by a random and caustic speech just after opening her heart by a kind one." "will that suffice to win Miss Vandelear?" , "Na, or else I suppose yen wculd say she is not worth winning ?" Stephen smiled as if his mother was not far wrong there, but there was little of sunshine in his smile as he asked: " What else then ?" " May I tell you frankly ?" "Yes." "You have been the Youth, you now must be the man ; with a man's dignity of aim, of methods, and behaviour. Your delete must somehow be paid, and it must not be possible henceforth for the world to say you are hunted by duns; that you take your friends from the meanest and most worthless outcasts of society, or allow them to take you; that—oh Stephen, how shall I tell you? The word profligate has even been applied to you!" "By whom? But I know. The Earl! You dare not deny it! He lies! I beg his pardon—he is a great personage, and can only be mistaken." "I was sure of it. And he will be so. too." "I can wait." "Will you, my vary dear bey, think all this over and --" "Let me recollect. Miss Vandeleur is to have the care and love of a worthy husband, and et to have her faults cured. And you do me the honour to think that in order to win so enviable a prize I have only to be attentive, and avoid frightening her on the one hand, and only to take care on the other that I become conspicuous alike for dig- nity and virtue. Unhappily there is one difficulty." "None that we may not together conquer!" "And yet it is together the difficulty has grown. Mother, lam fit for no such programme. lam but that which you yourself have made me!" The Countess gazed at him but for a single moment, then rose, and in intense feeling was about to go away without another word being spoken, but she stopped at the door to say— " Madman! Blind Mail:lan that you are! not to see that whether your charge be true or false, I have been de- voting all that remains to me of life to undo the evil work ! " The last word had scarcely left her lips before Stephen was about to speak, but saw she bad left hint

div.head: CHAPTER XVI.—" HE IS WHAT HE Loolcs."
div.p: CHAPTER XVI.—" HE IS WHAT HE Loolcs."

Stephen, for some time after his mother's departure, gazed at the open door trying to sAtisfy himself that he had done rightly, but not feeling very successful. Was she, as she said, devoting her last days of life to undoing the mischief that had been wrought? Had he spoken too strongly, when for the first time he spoke at all out of the overflowing bitterness of his heart?

These and similar questions troubled him. But he felt he must put them away with the strong hand, if he was to carry out his long-pondered design of making an effectual change; and try whether he had the strength and manliness to work out his own redemption, after leading such a self- indulged life. In this dissatisfied mood alike with himself and his mother, but feeling his heart reproach him so strongly with regard to her that he would be sure to fall back on the old stage of things, if he did not shut out for a time that dis- turbing element, he moved gloomily from the room, and descended the staircase; but stopped on the way, musing, to look out of an open window that copamanded a street along one side of the house. Suddenly his attention was drawn to Gentleman Jack on the opposite side, and who had caught sight of him, and was signalling to him in so conspicuous 1 manner as would speedily attract the attention of everybody near, if not stopped. With something like an oath, Stephen waved his hand in answer to warn him away; and Gentleman Jack, not know- ing but there might be obstacles to a meeting just then, ceased his demonstrations; and moved off to act in another matter of scarcely less importance to him, but which to mot men would have been paramount. The reader will remember that Gentleman Jack, while waiting in the hall after their last meeting, had seen a lady pass in, whose face, appearance, and mlnners brought home to him an alarming idea as to her personality.

This made a meeting with her more necessary than ever. But how to compass this he knew not, except by hanging abolt the neighbourhood. So he waited, thinking if he did not cstch her he might watch for Stephen. , His patience and temper were sorely tried with her delay, and with , anticipations of the unpleasantness of their meeting if it really was his wife, and he had to confront her, in order that she might not interfere with his present occu- pations at liarlaxton. He looked at a neighbouring clock. Already an hour and a half had passed, And Mrs. Davies had not emerged. Was it possible she was telling her story, their story to the Countess, and so the one thing he had to guard against was settled against him beforehand? He knew it was not a story to bommend itself, so far as he was concerned, to ordinary commonplace minds or hearts. And then' too, thoe esisses are so Very numerous! And besides that, so very unimaginative that they cannot place themselves in the position, or understand the motives and temptations of a man of a different order like himself. She was but a pretty, dreamy, farmer's daughter, while he was a gentleman. And he Lrld only married her because, while taken ,with hr good -, looks, he found she was so (Reims of a trite gentleman for her husband,that he pro- rosed, and was instantly accepted. And then after full trial

His volunteer promise decided her. "If I allow you to come in, it is merely to prevent a scene—a scandal—before the whole street." "No better motives could there be; so allwr me to follow you, as your very humble servant." He took off his hat, smiled, and bowed to her in a demonstrative manner. She led the way into the parlour, drew down the blinds, but left the door ajar; so that no passers-by could see them, while they might readily hear, if there should be any loud speaking. Then she seated herself on one side of a little table, while he took a chair on the other. She was the first to speak: "I do not think it advisable that anything we may say to each other should be overheard, while perhaps to you it may be more than advisable; and therefore it will be well to speak low and quickly, and so come to an end." Noticing in his angry thoughts her sinister remark about the "more than advisable," but repressing all reference to it, Gentleman Jack addressed himself cautiously to the business of discovering, first, whether she had been in the hall, and then or now identified him; and, secondly, what was her business there. She on her part was with equal anxiety wondering whether he had seen her leave Lord Harlaston's, and there- fore might know where in future to seek and worry her— perhaps destroy her rising prospects. "As I was passing along the street I saw you come out from Lord Harlaxton's," said Gentleman Jack, concealing for the moment his own connection with the mansion, and one of its inmates. Mrs. Davis was obviously disturbed, but knowing not what to say, said nothing, and left him to takeelais own course. - "Will you be surprised to hear that my most intimate friend resides in that house, and is no unimportant mem- ber? I refer to the Honourable Stephen Chandos Fronde," and once more, the speaker delighted himself with the son- orous roll of the words. This, if true, was a still more serious fact for Mrs. Davis to learn; but again she was silent, feeling it still more difficult to speak. • "And I may now tell you that I was waiting by appoint- ment in the hall to see my friend when you came and sat near me; and something moved me to feel a strange inter- est in you before I discovered how natural that was, in the discovery as you pissed me, I looked on my own ever to be respected wife!" "And what does all this come to ?" at last said Mrs. Davis, with breath that might have been borrowed from an east wind, so sitter and so penetrating was it. " Why do this. Supposing that you are henceforward an inmate of Harlaxton House, and I am so unfortunately placed that you do not care to reveal to any—which. means every—body there our relations, that then it is my duty to re-assure you, and to say that nothing in the world shall escape me in my visits there to compromise you." "I think you do not usually care for one-sided bar- gains—so what is the price I am to pay for your attitude ?" she asked. "No price at all, because for you to be equally silent about me, springs naturally from your own view." " That is all you ask from me ?" " AB."
CHAPTER XVIIL-MOMENTS OF DINGER.
The interview between Stephen and his mother, which had brought him to seriously contemplate an immediate and secret departure from his home, had been even more terrible in its conclusion for her.

" So ends inv dream !" she murmured to herself, as she paced to and fro the corridor. " All is lost. I have now nothing to, live for but to watch the progress of the wreck, and my own disgrace and humiliation !" Seeing him pass from her room in his way to the stair- case—making no attempt again to speak to her, or modify his language—the incident, slight as it was, gave new ft poignancy and danger to all her thoughts. " He has stricken, and now abandons me !" she thought, as she re-entered her room, sat down on the nearest chair, and for a little space was silent ; reviewing all the features .of the position in the light of her own desperate state, and halt frantic thoughts and imaginings. Suddenly she became conscious of what she was doing: and by clasping with both hands her breast, tried to still the beatings of her heart, which began to give their old solemn warning._

In so doing she touched the ruby heart-shaped gem that lay there, tool it in her fingers, looked at it, and in another moment broke out in low, hysterical cries ; revealing such passionate distress and anguish, that for a time it seemed as if her every sense was helping to rush her into some mad outbreak tending to swift destruction. And when that state ceased, it was only to let her subside into one of greater danger, by its quietly reckless abandonment of all natural sifegaards and tendencies to self-preserva, tion.

0, my sister!" thus ran her thoughts, " when I forced this poison-chalice from thy desperate hands, didst thou ever afterwards fear lest I, too, might be tempted? Thou still had me to guard thee from the fatal draught. I stand alone. No sister, husband, and now no son•to help or save! Can I live dishonoured? Why, that is death indeed, without death's peaceful balm. One drop from this ends all. 0, sweet heaven, forgive the madness of a breaking heart ! "
She opened the secret receptacle, smelt the contents, as if to fortify her own resolve, by the deleterious odour, stopped, and dallied as it were with death.

It was at that moment when death or life seemed to hang before her vision as the scales of some supernatural balance, which the slightest mental touch one aide or the other might in an instaiat bring to an end, that she heard the voice of Stephen cuing to her in gentle tones from the threshold of the door behind, which he had just opened, unheard— " Mother !"

Jr was magical. The ruby heart WAS instantly closed; a prayer in the wildest agitation went up to God for mercy from that other, living and suffering heart; and was fol- lowed by the consciousness she was saved at least from tke wickedness of suicide. And then swiftly succeeded a sense of the imperious necessity that he should not know. Striving to compose hersclf before allowing him to see her face, Stephen—unconscious of the awful crisis his mother had passed through, and thinking her seeming attitude of reserve showed simply her continuing anger and resentment, spoke and looke.a more calmly than he would otherwise have done.

"Listen, then. If you keep your word to me, and I see nothing in your behaviour to others that would compel me to give warning I agree. And here then we part." She rose, and he did the same. Then thinking it necessary there should be no miscon- ception in his mind as to her true feeling, and state of mind, she added,— "But if you violate either of those conditions I shall at once seek the Countess, tell her who and what you are, and abide the consequences." "You are a brave woman, and I only wish I cauld stand aside to see another man have the benefit of your frank courage, instead of me; but as that is not possible, why shouldn't we make the best of things? As strangers we are to be, and compelled no doubt often to meet, why shouldn't we as strangers take advantage of oar new relation, and make such meetings as agreeable as we can; as I believe is the custom with all well-regulated people the world over? So there, to begin," said he, holding out his band. She took no notice of the gesture, but passing him, went towards the street door at the very moment her landlady was in the passage • who saw them both leave the room, and separate at the door without any ordinary form of courtesy. The moment he had passed away, Mrs. Davis turned to the landlady, and said, "You saw that man ?" "Yes, my dear. And I own I don't like his looks, not to mention his clothes." "You will know him again ?" "Anywhere. I'd pick him out of a thousand." "Then, please, hold no converse with him if he comes again, and under no circumstances admit him to see me. He is what he looks!" CHAPTER WHICH GENTLEMAN JACK GETS AN INSTALMENT OF FORTrNE'S DEBT TO HIM. Stimulated by the success with his wife, Gentleman Jack returned to the pursuit of Stephen, and again caught sight of him, as has been previously shown. Not troubling himself with any more appeals across the street, he hurried towards the gate which happened to be open. Stephen on his part, also hurried his footsteps, to see that he was kept out. Swiftly as Stephen moved, Gentleman Jack was the win- ner of the impromptu race • and pushing the servants aside who obstructed him, with the assertion— " Mr. Stephen has called me, and is waiting for me," he got into the Hall, and thence into the Saloon, where he met Stephen face to face. "Jack," at once began the latter, stifling the anger and annoyance he felt, "You asked my advice. I give it briefly. Do as I mean to do—turn over a new leaf! There's half a sovereign to help. And so, farewell !" He went to the door leading to the Hall, opened it, and waited Gentleman Jack's departure. That personage took the money, looked at it, pocketed it, and then changing his whole manner, and the ordinary tones of his voice, he asked, menacingly, "And is that all you have got to say to me ?" "Well, I could add something if you provoked me," was Stephen's reply. "It wouldn't be wise. I came here in the best of tempers, but I too can be provoked." " Really ! How ?" "By your forgetting my present difficulty in your work !" " Mine, you scoundrel!" "..h, bad words are often- like the prickly shell of the chestnut, with much goodness inside for the hand deter- mined to get it out. Let me ask you one question : What sort of life do you suppose I have been leading since you have known me ? " "Well, to put it mildly, a bad one." "But spent mainly in your service, as your minister and tool. Half a friend in counsel, half a spaniel to fetch and carry. I don't think I was quite an angel of virtue before we became acquainted, but if I have gone to the bed since then, who has helped me on the road by making it pleasant and profitable? Look ye, Mr. Chandos Stephen Fronde, it mayn't be a pleasant thing to say, but it's a true and whole- some one, it is you who have helped to make me what I am!"

" Mother ! I will do what you wish. But trifler as tam, I can neither trifle myselt nor Miss Vandeleur into marriage without our both knowing well what we are about." "That is all I tFiser wished! " said the Countess, turning towards him a face suddenly illumined. "Oh, Stephen," she said, in accents that trembled with her excitement and agitation, "you know not what lies in your words—the relief, the comfort, the boundless hope alai joy they call forth!"
She rose to meet and embrac6 him, but so tottered on the way that she would have fallen had not Stephen seen the danger, caught, and supported iltr.

"-Mother.--devarest mother, how you tremble! And yolr face looks so strangely. You have been ill again, and you are striving to conceal it from me." "No, no, no! I an only too happy, and that makes me afraid. I hive been so wretched. Have had such bad thoughts. But now I could laugh!" And as if to prove the truth of her words, she did laugh hysterically, perhaps giving way to the instinctive impulse in order to disguise her state, and keep Stephen from suspecting what she had been thinking to do, and but for his coming, might perhaps have accompl;shed,

"Pray, ha cam," he said, in loving, earnest tones. "I will presently, but my relief, my happiness, is so great that it must find vent!" and no longer able to maintain even a show ef calmness she again broke out in violent hysteric mirth before she could stop herself; while Stephen, attributing everything to his own action in first causing his mother bitter disappointment, and then to the reaction through his present attitude, thought it wisest to let nature have her own way, and then all would soon be well.

And, so to, the Countess justified his expectation. Be- lieving, and rightly so, he had no suspicion of what it was that really so affected her, she gradually recovered her equanimity, and after a few minutes said, with a smile, Well, now to seek Miss Vandeleur !"

But instead of finding her, they found a note—saying a friend had called, and finding her unwell, and out of spirits, had insisted upon taking her off for a few days. Mother and son pondered over this unexpected delay to their plank but could decide upon nothing, but the necessity of allowing Ms s Vandeleur to clear it up in her own time and fashion.

BENEFIT FOOTBALL MATCH AT EARLESTOWN. --•••• In ex-
ceedingly favourable weather a match at football was

played- -on the 'Vulcan ground on Saturday . afternoon last, between the Vulcan and Newton Rugby Clubs, the proceeds being devoted to ' the relief of :a young man named A. Platt, residing at the Vulcan. Platt ,was not injured by playing at football as was erroneously stated in our last issue, but it was found neces- sary to amputate his foot from purely natural causes, and his fellow-workmen and companions, anxious to do their best for him, organised the match in question as the means of raking a sum of money to be given to him. It is pleas- ing to learn that the movement was well supported, and the ' large attendance of spectators testified to their liberality. As all the expenses in connection with the match were defrayed by the Vulcan team, the promoters have been enabled to raise about £lO 123 for Platt. The teams were captained by S. Williams (Newton) and H. F. Gooch (Vulcan). The former won the toss, and de- cided to play with the wind, sun, and ground in his favour. Gooch kicked off for Vulcan about four o'clock, and the leather WAS well returned by Mee. The Newtonians seri- ously endangered the Vulcan goal for some considerable time, the backs playing well up, and ably supporting the forwards. Up to half-time the visitors held an unmistake- able advantage, but only succeeded in securing a touch. down. On the cbange of ends the game was contested with renewed determination by both teams, the Vulcan contin- gent showing some capital play. They scored a touch-in- goal, but as no other point was registered, the match, which was an interesting one throughout, resulted in a draw. The following were the players :—Newton : W. Lane, full-back; S. Williams (captain) ; G. McCor- mick, • and W. Mee, three-quarter-backs; G. Lane, and T. Egan, half-backs; %V. Pennington J. Boardman, S. Rimmer, J. Naylor. A. Watkins, J. Fergu- son, T. Braddock, T. Ferguson, T. Fairelough, and H. Lip- trot, forwards. Vulcan: T. Slater, full•back ; T. Massey, W. Porteous, and J. Williams, three-quarter-backs; .J. "Hunter," and J. Harrison, half-backs; A. Lucy, H. F. Gooch (captain), J. Bolas, T. Owen' H. Snelson, J: Glli- brand, T. Holt, A. Catterali, J. Nichols, and J. MairbOurr e,. forwards. The umpireswere Mears. J. Fitzgerald (Newto a) and C. Singkton (Vulcau); and Mr.- R. H. Wright &ads- • fiscteriary offlaiated as referee.

ALTRINCHAM. CREDITORS' . MEETING.—A statutory meeting of the creditors of James Harriscn, of George-street, Altrincharn, hosier and hatter, was held on Wednesday, at the eaces of Messrs. Mann and Hooke, solicitors, Manchester. The state- ment of affairs- read by Mr. Edward Lawton, chartered accountant, showed liabilities to unsecured creditors £217, and assets £227: Liquidation was resolved upon, and Mr. Lawton and Mr. Shoolhred were appointed trustees- with a committee of inspection. Messrs. Maun and Rocke were entrusted with the registration. CROFT.

CHILDREN'S.TREAT.—This annual treat, which is Looked forward to with the greatest delight by the chiddren and young people in the village, took place on Saturday under the most favourable circumstances. The weather, though vezy showery in the morning, began to clear up about noon' and was very fine during the afternoon and evening, though rather cold. The treat was this year again carried out under the patronage and management of the School Board, who appointed Mr. George Beimelow (assistant overseer) hon. treasurer, and Mr. Alfred Dixon (schoeLattendance officer) hen. secretary. These gentlemen collected subscrip- tions from the ratepayers of the toweship, and others in- terested in the schools of the district, on behalf of the treat ; and it is -eery gratifying to state that they were highly successful in their undertaking. About one o'clock the children began to assemble at the Board School, and about a quarter to two some 350 children and friends had arrived, when a procession was formed, which was headed by a flag (carried by Mr. Silas Clough), and three membera of the School Board, namely, the Rev. T. P. Kirkham' M.A., F.R.S. (cbairman and clerk), and Messrs. Richard Turner (vice- chairman) and James Gooden ; the other two members, Messrs. James Hatton and Lewis Birchall, being unavoid- ably absent, as well as the hen treasurer, bat they were !present later on. Then came the Lowton Brass Band in full, uniform, and afterwards the children and young friends, who paraded the village under the superintendence of the hon. secretary, wit® was kindly assisted by Miss I Ball, Miss Stretch, and Messrs. Frederick William ! Ball (schoolmaster), John Waywell, John Clough, William Knowles, and Edward Monks, making a most pleasing appearance—the members of the School Board, hon. secretary, and assistant superintendents wear- ing white favours, and the children carrying flags and wear- I ing beautiful flowers. The children were highly praised ,1 for their clean, neat, and orderly appearance by a large I number of people who had gathered together in various places along the route. On their return to the school, after the march, the number present was increased by about 100 children and friends who were unable to join the processiots, and at half-past three the children sat down to an excellent I tea provided in the school-room, under the superintendence of Mr. Robert Sharpies, which they thoroughly enjoyed. I Subsequently nuts and sweets were distributed amongst them. Immediately afterwards the friends and the mem- bers of the band were provided with tea, after which they all adjourned to a field, kindly lent by Mr. Birchall, whore various games and sports were engaged in, including cricket, football, fiat racing, three-leg racing, egg-and-spoon racing, eec. The band played an excellent selection of music for dancing, dm., in a highly creditable manner (under the conductorship of Mr. Thomas. Booth, the band-master) until dusk, when the children returned to the school, and the band having played the National Anthem the proceedings terminated, all being highly pleased with the afternoon's enjoyment. Great credit is due to the School Board, hon. treasurer, hon. secre- tary, schoolmaster, teachers, and others (who kindly gave their assistance in making the tea, cutting up the provisions, presiding at the tea tables, and waiting during the tea) for the excellent manner in which they carried out the arrange- ments. The number present was considerably more than was expected, in consequence of a large number of persons purchasing tickets at the door, but all were accommodated. It is estimated that there were over GOO persons on the field during the evening, and, it being the wakes, a few nut and other stalls were erected on the play-ground attached to the school, which did a good business. We regret to-say that this year there were not the usual hobby horses, swing- boats, dec., which was a great disappointment to the children, who usually patronise them to a Ercat extent.

. SEWERAGE SCHEME FOR DITTON.-The Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority have had before them the plans of a , new sewer proposed to be constructed for the purpose of draining the township of Ditton. It is intended to construct the sewer four feet by three, which size will ba.large enough to drain the entire union if that should at any time be neces- sary. The total cost will be borne by the Broughton Copper Works, the L. and N.-W. Railway Company, and Major Cross, who only ask that the Sanitary Authority shall take over the sewer when it is constructed. The Authority have agreed to accept the sewer when made. ORDINATION OF PRIESTS -Early on Saturday morning, Dr. B. O'Reilly, Roman Catholic; Bishop of Liverpool, con- ferred the order of priesthood upon 13 members of the Society of Jesus at St. Michael's Church, Ditton. The ord- mandi have passed through a course of theological training at the Ditron College, and will now be despatched to mis- sions in various parts of the world. The sacred edifice had been beautifull# adorned with.flowers for the occasion. The musical part of the impressive service was of the usual high class. On Sunday high ones was celebrated, the newly ordained priests officiating. Toe Rev. A. M. de /Liza Radlitz, S J. in the afternoon preached a sermon from the text "All things are of God, who hath reconciled us unto Himself by Christ, and has given to us the ministry of re- conciliation." All the services were largely attended. THE TROL-BLES OF A DITTON FARMER.-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, James Monaghan and Michael Kelly, boys, were summoned on a charge of Wil- fully damaging the property of Mr. Alcum Cowley, farmer, Ditton.-Mr. Cowley said his crops had been very much damaged by men and boys trespassing on the ground and trampling the crops down. He had suffered nearly £5 worth of damage to one field of turnips alone.-P.C. Lemont stated that at half-past six on Sunday night be SaTY the prisoners enter the complainant's potato field and pluck bp a inir...l!?r reiurnd !filo the road with several in their hands, but when they saw him they dropped them and ran. He afterwards found that they left about a dozen loose on the field.-A fine of ss. and costs, 7s. 64, was imposed on each defendant, in addition to 21. 61. damage; in default of payment to go to gaol ten days. F,LIX ro N. Fruxrox ATHLETIC FESTIVAL. - The second annual "athletic festival, which had been postponed from the pre- vious week, was brought to a successful conclusion on Satur- day. The weather was favourable, and the arrangements, under N.C.A. rules, satisfac'orily carried out by Mr. S. Cooke, the secretary, assisted by a committee and officials. The handicapping was good, several of the contests result- ing in yery close finishes. The attendance was but moderate. MARRIAGE AT HALEWOOD.-At the Parish Church, Hale- wocd, on Siturday, Mr. W. S. Graves, of Dowsefield, Aller- ton, of the firm of S. R. Graves and Son, shipowners, Liver- pool, and one of the reprqsentatives of West Derby Ward, was married to Miss Fanny Charlotte "Neiism?: eldest daughter of Mr. Robert Neilson, one of the county Justices, and formerly chairman of the Liverpool Tramways Com- pany.

ANNIVERSARY OF THE UNITED METHODIST CHAPEL, HIGH-STEEET.—On Sunday thc Rev. J. B. Stoneman, of Manchester, preached two sermons in the High-street Chapel to very good congregations, especially in the even. ing. On Monday Mr. Stoneman delivered his lecture on "Croakers." From the report read at the meeting it is found that £2OO As been paid off from the £950 left on the premises last year, leaving a present debt of £750, towards which there is a balance due to the credit of the trustees of more than £4O for next year. WINSFORD SALT TRADE.—An unusually large export for the past month (August) has kept stock down and prices hardening. In a good many instances the annexed list has been outstripped by a sixpence. The make is becoming more circumscribed as the brine sources keep low, and their limit of supply has been fully reached. A fair winter trade is in prospect, as the dull season has passed without ac- cumulating stocks.
