Shswirg excess of ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. The Northwich Local Board decided on Thursday by ten votes to six in favour of applying for a charter of incorpora- tiorr. 0 CHESTER AND ITS WATER SIIPPLY.—In obedience to an invitation from the Waterworks Company, several of the members of the Chester Town Council visited the upper works at Great Boughton, Chester, on Thursday, to "inspect the alterati ens and additions undertaken to perfect the supply of water to the city." SUICIDE OF A CHESHIRE MAGISTRATE.—Mr. J. D. Em- merson, J.P., of Peover, near Knutsford. committed suicide at an early hour on Thursday morning. During the night he had complained of being ill, and about six o'clock Mrs. Ernmerson gave him a cup of tea. She then left the room, and on returning shortly afterwards was horrified on finding that her husband had cut hie throat. Death resulted immediately. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT CHESTER CATHEDRAL.—Mr. James Doyle, a gentleman living at 18, Leson Park, Dub- lin, was visiting Chester Cathedral on Wednesday evening, in company with two other gentlemen, when he suddenly fell backwards in a fit, and his head coming into violent con- tact with the stone floor, he sustained such dreadful in- juries that he died on Thursday morning in Chester In- firmary without having recovered consciousness. Telt INCORPORATION OF ALTRINCHAm.—In accordance with an order of the Privy Council, the inhabitants of Altrincham are about to take steps to secure the incorpora- tien of the town and district. The order, which is issued by the Lord President of the Council, calls attention to the Municipal Corporations Act of this year, by which similar corporations are to be dissolved. The Act, however, excludes Altrincham from those to be abolished. How SMALL-FOX IS SPREAD.—John Moss, landlord of the Blomfield Anns, Chester, was on Tuesday fined 20.3 by the magistrates of that city for removing his son, who was suffering from small-pox, from Liverpool to Chester with- out adopting proper precautions. The lad, who had since died, was conveyed to his home under the defendant's charge in a railway carriage and a hackney coach, notwithstand- ing that a Liverpool physician had advised that he should be taken to hospital. A CHILD BURIED ALIVE.—On Satureay, at noon, number of children were playing in a sand pit at Upton, near Chester, when an immense quantity of earth fell upon them. A young man, named Davies, who saw the occur- rence rushed to the spat, and by dint of great exertions dug out one child. He had just come to the head of a second, named Basnett, when another fall occurred, completely burying it and knocking down Davies and partly covering him. The child was extricated, but died almeee lramee diately. CHORAL FESTIVAL AT NANTWICH.—On Wednesday night the twenty-first annnal festival of the Nantwich Choral Association was held in the Parish Church. There were over 500 voices, representing 19 choirs, from Crewe, Nie•- wich, Middlewich, Wrenbury, Audlem, Wheelock, Winsfo et, Warminglaam, Holmes Chapel, atc. The rectors of most of these parishes took part in the services. The Rev. Highton, Stewart, precentor of Cheater Cathedral, presided at the organ, and Mr. Harris, organist of Nantwich Church, con- ducted. The church was beautifully decorated, and the , festival pronounced a great success. ANOTHER IRISH LABOURER ATTACHED.—At Sandbach Sessions, on Wednesday, James Burgess and John Lowe were charged with an unprovoked assault on Patrick Con- nolly, an Irish farm labourer.—Connolly stated that he was walking along the road at Middlewich on Saturday night, when the prisoners, without any cause whatever, set upon him. One of them struck him with his fists and knocked him down with a stick, and then both kicked him as he lay on the ground.—Mr. Latham said they would not have English fellows assaulting an Irishman in this manner. Burgess would be fined 203. and costs, and Lowe 10s. and costs. MELANCHOLY BOATING ACCIDENT.—A boat accident with surroundings of a peculiarly melancholy character occurred on the Dee on Tuesday night. Mr. English, the son of a Liverpool merchant, took a boat for a row on the river, be- ing accompanied by Mies Lockwood, of Chester, to whom he bad become engaged on the previous day. They pro- ceeded with safety until they were opposite the White Horse Hotel, when from some uuexplained cause the boat capsized, and both Mr. English and Miss Lockwood were drowned before rtny assistance ceuld be obtained. At an inquest held on Wednesday night a verdict of "Accidental death" Was returned. SANDBACH BREWSTER SESSIONS.—At these sessions, on Wednesday, Superintendent Hindlay submitted his annual renort witL reference to the cenduct of the licensed victual- lers and beer retailers in the division during the year. There were 80 licensed victuallers, 43 beersellers, and 24 others whe sold off the premises, total 153, which gave an average of 202 of the population te each license, Three licensed victuallers had been proceeded against during the year, and one convicted ; two beersellers had been proceeded against, and both convicted ; and 244 pnsons had been convicted of drunkenness.—A new license was applied for by Thomas Antrobus to sell beer at Middlewich. It was refused. The Bench also refused to grant the renewal of a license for the " Halfway" Inn, Tetton, asked for on behalf of Jane Davies, Mr. G. W. Lath= (the chairman) remarking that there were enough licenses without it. FOAL Snow AT CHESTER.—The Chester Farmers' Club on Wednesday held a foil show at Chester. It was attended by close upon 1,000 farmers. There were three classes in which prizes were offered—one for colts, the second for Kies, and the last for the champion animal in the show. In the colt clese Mr. J Kellett, of Overpool, took the first prize of £8 with a brown Colt by Pointsman. The second prize of £4 went to Mr. C. W. Potts of Heron Bridge, Chester, for a roan colt, also by PoitArtan. In the class for filly foals the prize of £8 went to the Duke of West- minster for a bay by What's Wanted, which is a stud book horse. The second prize of £4 was taken by Mr. Willis, of Beeston, for a brown filly; and the third of £2 to Mr. W. Pickering, of Poulton, for a bey by Boston. The champion prize of five guineas for the best colt in the yard was won, after a keen contest, by the Duke of Westminster, while the second prize of two guineas was taken by Mr. Kellett's colt. SINGULAR TRANSACTIONS BY A CHESHIRE CLERGY- MAN.—A case was heard at the Chester County Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Horatio Lloyd, judge, in which Daniel Keating. a horse dealer, of Armagh, sought to re- cover from the Rev. E H. Barton, of Kelsall, the sum of £lO. It appeared that at the March horse fair at Chester Mr. Barton purchased a horse from the plaintiff far £45, in payment for which he gave the plaintiff a cheque on the Manchester and Liverpool District Bank. Plaintiff, seeing that the defendant was a clergyman, accepted the cheque and handed over the horse. The cheque' however, on being presented, was dishonoured, and plaintiff went ever to Kel- salt and informed defendant of the fact. The latter replied that he should have had some money coming to him from some relations, but he had been disappointed. He asked. plaintiff to take back the horse,' and this plaintiff consented to do conditionally upon his receiving ZlO for his trouble in the matter. Defendant, agreeing to this, gave him a second cheque in payment of the £lO, at the same time assuring the plaintiff that this cheque was all right, and would be honoured. When it was presented, however, it was returned marked "No effects." The present action was therefore brought to recover the £lO, and it was said that defendant had a counter claim in _respect to some horse c'oths; but as he did not appear, *judgment went against defendant by default in both cases.

"SEVENTEEN TIMES FINED FOR NOTHING."—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Michael Rock, Earles- town, a well-known "visitor" at the court, was samMoned for being drunk at Earlestown, on the 26th August.—On being askeA if he was guilty or not defendant replied, "1 think so, sir; if I open my mouth now they take me."—The Chairman said there was a long list against the defendant, who had been before the Bench on 17 occasions.—The defendant: And I have been every time for nothing, sir. (Laughter.)—He was fined 10s. and costs, and acknowledged it with a "Thank you, sir." EARLESTOWN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.— The open- ing, game for the ensuing season, in cohnection with the Eirlestown Association Football Club, was played on Sat- urday evening last, cn the new ground at Wargrave Moss. There was a pretty fair number of spectators in attendance. The match was between the let and 2nd teams, and owing to considerable additions to the list of members and a re- arrangement of the teams, some interest was taken in the encounter. During the first half the play was of an even ' character, both sides showing promise of future improve- ment. Neither team scored in the first three-quarters of an hour ; but after the change of ends the first team quickly showed their superiority and not many minutes elapsed before they scored. pp to the call of time the "seniors" pressed their opponenest and won the match by five goals to none, the points being .scored by Duxbury (two), Simm (two). and Dagnall (one). . A SECRET INQUIRY: REPORTERS EXCLUDED. One of the most extraordinary occurrences that has Oki° place at Newton Town Hall was witnessed on Saturdel, when the representatives of the Press, who had attended t° report the petty sessional proceedings, were forcible' Pre.' vented from entering a room in which a portion of the PIZ ceedings were held.. Among the numereus prisoners to ""ea tried, was one man against whom a certain indecent chlrlt° had been brought, and when the case came on, the ntegit. trates, Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and st. MCcorquodale, with their clerk, Mr. Bucliton, of ton, retired to an ante-room it being understood that tbe evidence would not be given before the large number of Per sons present in the court-room. There were three reporteret in attendance, and when the case was celled, they were ob°c. to enter the room, but were prevented by Superintendli Warring 7 Weir. The latter stated that the reporters Nytt not be admitted, but on those gentlemen remarking til; they had a right to be present as representing die POI Superintendent Weir gave orders to his subordinateeuto stop anyone from entering. The reporters, unheeding t"o advice, made an attempt to gain admission by pushing oPeo the door, but Superintendent Weir in a hasty manner tcee them to leave, and said if they persisted in their action t' would give orders for them to be cleared from the precisnct of the court. He called upon the police to remove the re; porters; and the foremest of them was seized by an ofaCtie and forcibly ejected from the entrance to the Superintendent Weir further instructing the ofgc`-t to see that the representatives of the •Press were Id away from the door. The reporters then put forWs, a plea that they were anxious to talk to the Bench, but tbc,', were unable to do this—the police officers refusing to cottc% the message. Nothing daunted, the representatives of tu., Press quickly wrote out a note heering the words porters wish to speak to the magistrates.," and bandroe to a police officer asked for it to be given to the magistrateo In reply thereto, the Bench stated they would be willing meet one reporter ; and accordingly one representative the Press entered the room. He informed the megletiit,,,e that the reporters wished to enter the room, but the 3,A.; spectot and one of the officers would not allow them to so.—Mr. Gillespie replied that it was only a preliminartP.; quiry into the matter.—The Representative of- the Pfe6e said he and the other reporters hid simply come -tberess,; right which they claimed, thinking that the evidence was:a be taken in the usual way.—Mr. Ruckton (the clerk) et, they had no right. The evidence was to be taken in usual way, but it was really a preliminary inquiry.---• Gillespie observed that under the circumstances they on,qlo not allow the reporters to come in; and Mr. McCarquena4 remarked that at Dublin inquiries were frequent;ii held with closed doors. The reporter tb retired; and after consulting with his feller - pressmen, the following was written :—" Gentlentc/1 —I have consulted with the other reporters Ice we are perfectly unanimous that we are entitled and bevel right to be present at this inquiry, having obtained It advice on the .matter. We respectfully insist uponl.o right, and hereby protest against our expulsion. regard to the remarks respecting inquiries at Dublin it -"et necessary to obtain a special Act of Parliantefi and we think the argument cannot be aPpriblcis in this case. Yours respectfully," dtc. written message was given to the - officer at the o'ss'ilt and he was requested to deliver it to the magistratee ; wee he absolutely refused- to do so, and even tried to prevetle reporter from knocking at the door. The reporter succeei; in doing this, however, and the " protest" was hande:l6 Superintendent Weir, by whom thee door was spened. 6 representatives of the Press afterwards waited for to considerable time, bat they heard nothine further abolltlo matter, and they accordingly retired.

An Earlestown correspondent writes in referee to this episode as follows:—This exclusion of g representatives of the Press from such an inquiry aPtelbje up a very important question, and one affecting La rieita and privileges of the public. It is wilet"ne or not the reporters, in the exercise of their dal, ie behalf and in the interests of the public at large, al ie legally prevented from taking the evidence submitted.,,, support of a serious charge against any person; and 31; what is more important, whether or not it is a lawful 841' r. practically convict anyone on evidence not given in the log of those who may have an interest in the case. GrPt.,,,l for the sake of argument that magistrates have the and right to order criminal proceedings to he C° to ducted with closed dows, would it not: soil, a be more in accordance with the dictates eel justice that anyone charged with an offoT should be tried not behind the barred doors of sole but in a "free and open court," to quote the words of Summary Jurisdiction Act? If this were done, then person, if guilty of the offence with which he or she 107, he charged, would feel the "sting of his conscience" 0148 than if he were convicted in private; while if he shouluepg innocent—and many a person under similar circurnstari:o"o has been proved to be innocent—then all the more fea,'„e exists why he should have an unfettered chance of shoWZ it, and an uncrippled opportunity of publicly redeeming ?, character, blasted and blighted by being hurried 0114 heinous Charge before a magistrate. It may be all ve`i well to talk about consulting the interests; A morality by excluding the public from eg-e trials, but surely there is no justifiable reabel% why the duly eccredited servants of the Peee should be debarred from being in attendance. They be trusted to exercise a wis.r discretion in the matter of lishing evidence, and it seems a most high-handed and "iThe potic proceeding to exclude them from the hearing. Summary Jurisdiction Act may not state in definite terwoo that representatives of the Press shall be admitted, 110,..rt0t the other hand, dots it say that they shall be prohiule. it from being present. But it does say that any person agai";o whom a charge is brought shall be tried in a "free and let court," an 1 if the magistrates act otherwise their corlufiof is contrary to the spirit and meaning of the Act. Maniere your readers may probably remember that the reporters WA, excluded in a similar manner a few montbS acri and it is for the public to say whether or not theY willing to allow trials bzhind crosed door& Unless an 11051110 takeable and energetic protest is lodged against it there /lab; no telling where it will end. This view of the case was put f3rth in a letter which appeared in your columns is time ago, and from which the following is taken r, is an act which I think is most despotic and uncalled 00 and those whom I have spoken to upon the subject condefil..l it as e most hiF,h-handed and arbitrary proceeding. It be said that the charge WaS One ette:i o i[self 'W,t5 cient to justify the sccret proceedings, but I would more serious and the more damning against a man's acter a charge is, all the more reason exists why he aMte,, have an uofettered chance to publicly prove hi a innocaeto and why his companions and feltoe- countrymen shcLot have the opportunity of hearing what has to be Sllci 1253.1,4 t him as well as on his behalf. If they are not to have W',o", I claim for them, then the people of this country are e,Lto fronted with a state of things which takes us back allli9s`cal the days of the Inquisition with all its fee.,r'Oci evils and wickedness. Men of England ! DO rur see your danger? Will you allow one of ;lumber to be dragged off on one of the most aboalllfeo charges, hurried before a magistrate, and confronted persons who, with closed doors, swear almost his Ye/ (for character in many cases means "life ") away? lolib next be the turn of arAy one of us, and we may be dealt,w, to in a similar fashion. In an open court we should he anri, convince the public, and our fellow countrymen of 00....,r)a nocence, but in a room, alone with witnesses who i'm'ees swear anything with the knowledge that their utter would not go forth elsewhere, we should have no chaneee'eee say then, arise, and look after your liberties, which D'of been purchased by the blood of your forefathers. i‘C,tif, man is assumed to be innocent until he is proved to be gti" and what right, I would ask, has anyone hurry off an " innocent " man, and in secrecy accusa of a horrible crime. Is this liberty? Is this justica 0 say " No." Let us have no more secret inquiries; JeCJ have no more "dark " inquisitions; but open, free, a public accusations, and then there will be a chance of eve one being dealt with in accordance with the dicertes of law and of justice.

The Evening Eapress, alluding to the exclusion of re:t porters at Newton on Saturday last, says :—" furning °lff the reporters was an amusing incident at the Newton Fl Sessions, and the police probably thought it a capital Jl3/ot to put down the Press at the direction of-the' justices. ; •ty there is a principle Involved in the matter. lhe publicitie given to magisterial and other similar proceedings ill,es• most real of all safegutuds which British liberty posse- 0, If the magistrates have power to try prisoners in secrstire the Newton Bench claim, how long is liberty likely °we main safe? Magisterial discretion is one of those unkned quantities which are always more puzzling than useful, iler, It has often appeared that this so-called discretion cised in a very indiscreet fashiou. In his "T4ble ri Cowper says : Let magistrates alert perform their parts. Not skulk or put on a prudential mask. This is counsel which the Newton justices would till' well to study. It is their business to well and tr,,;ir try criminals and other offenders, but it is no pot of duty to screen either offences or offenders from public If the evidence to be adduced before them is I,lrelY !La! unfit for feminine ears or the ears of children, such nei—tbe may easily be excluded from the court without affecting„-e publicity of the proceedings. But the Newton Bench tii• preferred to try a case of criminal assault in secret—i.nf-tho gating the circumstances in a private room, from whicilied• public were excluded and the reporters fo,c'hlv eXPe,,Ag Is this the law? If it is, an alteration will be 511e7,00 demanded. If the justices can expel reporters at to sweet will, in the exercise of that uncertain discretioPtber which we have referred, they may also try in private ° tbe classes of crime. While public liberty is imperilleol; the discretion of the Bench may also be exercised to cl"b' sblY delinquencies of prodigal favourites of fortune. ProDocb the evidence given on Saturday before the Newton „t tb° was unfit for printing, but of this the Press and II" magistrates should be left to judge."

Sneyd Kynnesley) to the Education Department there ap- pears the subjoined remarks with reference to the schools in the Runcorn district :—" Questions of supplying deficien- cies of accommodation fortunately occupy but little time in this district. Birkenhead, Hope, and Runcorn are the three exceptions. The Runcorn School Board has twice proposed to build one or more schools in the town; but in both instances they have found on inquiry that the exist- ing accommodation was sufficient. PRESENTATION TO THE PASTOR. In connection with this church a congregational tea party was held in the school-room, on Monday evening, and was in every way a success. About 300 persons took their seats at the tables, which had been handsomely decorated with choice plants and flowers, and the repast was thoroughly enjoyed. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Mutch, Miss Parker, Miss McHugh, Mrs. Costello, Mrs. Williamson, and others. Sabsequently the tables were cleared away, and a meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. Father Fenelley, the pastor of the church. He was supported on the platform by Messrs. J. Harty, Edward Hill, J. Mutch, T. Wil- liamson, 41. Kelly, and S. W. Goodall. Advan- tage was taken of the gathering to present the rev. father, who has ministered to the spiritual necessities of the Catho- lics of Runcorn for the past six years, with an address and purse of gold, as a token of the respect and esteem in which he is held by the members of his numerous congregation. Mr. J. Harty was secretary and treasurer of the committee which had originated the testimonial. Every praise is due to Mr. E. Hill for his labours in connection with the presentation and in organising the tea party.—Mr. Harty, in presenting the purse of gold, read the following address, which, he remarked, accurately represented the feelings and sentiraents which permeated the congregation : " To the Rev. William Fenelley.—Rev. and Dear Sir,—We have assembled here this evening, impelled by many con- siderations, to convey to you an assurance of the profound esteem in which you are held by us, who are committed to your spiritual care, and to offer you our heartfelt thanks with this humble tribute as a small acknowledgment of

of your services and sacrifices amongst us. Ticough we cannot hope within the scope of this address to enumerate your many claims upon our affection, nor to dwell as we would wish to do upon your maw" endearing qualities, yet as a typical minister of our holy religion teaching holiness of life by example, a promoter and supporter of every good cause, we beg most humbly to pledge our deep love for, and unalterable attachment to, your reverence. Actuated by these motives we gather round you, and as a feeble memo- rial of our affection, we offer you this small token, however inadequate, in testimony of the abundance of our kindliest feelings.—We are, reverend and dear sir."—Addressing the rev. chairman, Mr. Harty then said: For my part I may say that, having had the opportunity with;e tho loot ...pi. of months to partly sound the deep affection which wells up in the hearts of your people in Runcorn, I am very jealous; for here in this small room I see around me the horny-handed gentlemen who contributed the shilling and the sixpence with the sweat of poverty, I might say, upon them, which have made this testimonial as substantial as it is. I have no doubt that now in the evening of your long and honourable life, which I hope may be peaceful and happy to the close, it will be a consolation to you to reflect that leal hearts and true beat for you in Runcorn. (Applause.) And when the time comes, as I suppose in the natural course of events it will come, when we must part, the regret, I am satisfied, will be mutual. But I hope that neither time nor dietance will separate us in spirit—(hear, bear)—and may our hearth in friendship always shake hands. (Applause.)—On rising to acknowledge the present, the Rev. Father Fenelly ap- peared to be much affected with the heartiness of his recep- tion. He thanked the members of the congregation for the way in which they had gathered around him, and consider- ing they were so poor, for the valuable testimonial ttbat had been given him with so many kindly expressions of affec- tion. He adverted at some length upon church and school matters, which, he said, were in very good working order. (Applause.) A great many people found fault with them for not building -a new church, but they were very poor, and where were the funds to come from? He thought the church was large enough, and if money could be raised to build anything, he should prefer to erect some new schools. (Applause.) He had a great aversion to incurring debt—the church was already heavily burdened enough—but if they could procure funds he would gladly undertake anything that the congregation would suggest. (Applause.) After again thanking the congregation, the Chairman resumed his seat, and Mr. Edwd. Hill spoke a few well-chosen words suit- able to the occasion, concluding by proposing a hearty vote of thanks to Irish National. Foresters' Band, which had discoursed sweet music during the evening under the presi- dency of Sergeant Ryan, and to the brothers Mulvaney for their comic entertainment, which had added gristly to the enjoyments of the evening. The vote was heartily accorded, ieed. and the meeting termn

SHOCKING CRUELTY TO HORSES AT NEWTON.—Before R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquadale, Esqs., at the Newton Petty Sessions, on , Sa.tuniay, Abraham Parker, of Turton, was summoned for ill-treating a pony at Newton on the 23rd August.—ln- Spector Campbell, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, deposed that he saw the defendant ridimg a pony at Newton fair, and leading another at the same time. He had a spur on his right foot, and with it he "ripped" into the pony's side and used it very cruelly. Blood was dropping from the pony's side to the floor. He , (witness) followed the defendant, and on stopping him found ' that a piece of the animal's side, about the size of a hand, was covered with blood, as well as the spur and heel of the defendant's boot—Another inspector of the society gave corroborative evidence.—P.S. Commins (stationed at New- ton) also corroborated. The defendant said it was a veiv -stupid pony, but he did not ill- treat it to the extent that had been described. He called a witness, who said there were only three drops of blood on the horse's side.—The defendant was fined 20s. and coste.—Henry Smith, of Manchester, was summoned for causing a horse to he worked in an unfit state at Newton on the 20th June last. —lnspector Campbell deposed that on the firs..lay of Newton races he saw the de- fendant, along with a man named Scholes, in charge of three i horses and a large 'bus. The centre horse was fearfully lame on both hind legs, and was going along with great difficulty. He found two large wounds on its body, from which matter was issuing; and altogether he never saw an animal in such a state. When it was released and turned into a field it stood shivering and shaking in a most pitiable state. He had been nine years in the society and he never saw a horse worked in such a shocking condition. The de- fendant was summoned to appear, but as he did not do so a warrant for his apprehension was granted. When he (wit- ness) went to the defendant's residence the defendant escaped by the back door and had since given them con- siderable trouble. He surrendered himself that morning.— The Bench imposed a fine of 20e. and costs. EPPS'S COCOA.—GRATEFUL .AND COMFORTING. It is by the judicious use of such articles of diet that a constitution may be gradually built up until strong enough to resist every tendency to disease. SERIOUS OUTBREAK OF SMALL-PDX. A HOSPITAL TO EX ERECTED. The minutes of the Health Committee contained the Medical Officer's report which showed that during August there were 80 births-384 per 1,000; and 45 deaths-21eG per 1,000. The deaths included 22 children under one year and five between one and five years. Zy:notic diseases caused 10 deaths-or 4.8 per 1,000. The Nuisance Inspector reported that there were five fresh cases of scarlet fever during the month and one proved fatal. There were now seven cases of small pox in John-street, Lugsdale. The tenants of two houses adjoining those where most of the cases were, had been removed at the Board's expense. Dis- infecting was constantly attended to; and he requested in- structions as to remuneration for attendance on sick people. The medical officer had vaccinated and re-vaccinated several adults and children in John-street. The committee were of opinion that a hospital for infectious diseases for this district was necessary, and recommended that they be authorised to select a site for the purpose of erecting a suit- able structure. The Surveyor was instructed to prepare for next Board meeting plans and estimates for a temporary hospital to accommodate ten or twelve persons, which it was proposed should be erected in the Ditton gas yard. The Inspector was instruc- ted to arrange payment for attendance on small- pox patients.—Dr. O'Kmaree, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the first case of small-pox occurred three months ago, and there had been nine since. They were nearly all in one locality, and it was apprehended that there ...might be an epidemic of small-pox in the township. To obviete a contingency of that kind the committee proposed to erect a temporary hospital. Mr. Higginson had drawn three plans to carry out the proposal, accommodation to be provided for twelve patients. The first plan showed two wards with six beds in each ward, and a nurse's room in addition. The second plan only provided for two wards, and no nurse's room, while the third sketch provided for four wards to hold three beds each. The structure would be of wood, and the committee asked for permission to proceed -at once with the work. The committee intended to put the building upon their own land in the gas yard on Ditton- road, and as it would only be temporary the objection which the medical officer at one time raised to that site would not -be serious.—Mr.Dtrrrore: What is the contemplated cost?— Dr. O'KHEFFE: I don't know until the tenders are opened. —Mt, DIMON was apprehensive that the erection would entail great expense upon the ratepayers. He did not see why the Board should be called upon to enter upon this .matter so urgently. They bad had small-pox in the town before, and as they had got nearly to the end of summer,there was no reason why they should not get the disease under. The population had not increased and with strict inspection he believed the disease could be stamped out without going to 'the expense suggested.—Mr. Hotroarrox said he presumed that Mr. Dutton was not aware of the spread of the disease in the higher part of the distriet. It he was he would not say anything against tbe urgency of this temporary hospi- tal.—the CHAIRMAN : I think Dr. O'Keeffe will be able to answer that question.—Dr. OICEEFFE said he had observed .on a former occasion that small-pox was nearly as dreadful a disease as cholera, and if it became epidemic there was very little doubt it would decimate the population. But in addition to that they had got orders from the Local Government Board to prepare for the invasion of cholera amongst them, whether It came up in ships from the Sloyne or occurred in the township. It was incumbent upon the Board to make pro- vision, and that immediately for any infectious disease that might come amongst them. As they had been for a long time without hoepital or any provision at all of that kind, it was desirous that they should be provided with one, and by the Public Health Act, 1875, they were allowed to ex- pend a certain amount of money for this object. The com- mittee were not desirous to spend the funds of theeßoard in an extravagant manner, and anything that they did for the benefit of the health of the public of the township would be .done in as ezononaical a manner as they possibly could. If they did not provide the accommodetion required, the Local Government Board would reprimand them, and make the provision themselves at the expense of the ratepayers ef Widnes, so that he thought they bad better anticipate them. The accommodation was absolutely necessary, and they bad ,
FINANCE.

The Finance Committee's minutes stated instructions had been given to apply for anotuer instalment of £5,000 re main sewer. Various accounts were recom- mended for payment.—On the proposal of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. WRIGHT, the minutes were passed. TRH GAS COMMITTEE.—PASSAGE BETWEEN SIR, PANICHURST AND MR. MIDWOOD.

The GAS ENGINEER reported to the Gas and Water Com- mittee that the rainfall for August had been 235 inches. There had been 47,214,617 gallons of water pumped, and 45,565,301 gallons delivered, an increase on the previous year of 25 46 per cent. There had been 2,916,000 cubic feet of gas made, and 3,150,000 cubic feet delivered, a decrease of 6.63 on the corresponding month last year. The illumi- nating power of the gas was 16.56 candles. On the 31st August Mr. W. Farrell, of Runcorn, wrote respecting water he had usAl at the repairs of some houses in Travis-3treet. The Engineer stated that he had traced other persons using the Board's water without authority. It was decided to in- vite these persons to meet the committee, and also to issue placards warning the public against using the town's water without authority. It was recommended that the tender of Messrs. J. W. Wareing and Co. of £2 163 0.1 per ton for tar, and that of Messrs. Hardman and Co. for gas liquor be ac- cepted.—Mr. PANICHURST moved the confirmation of the minutes. Gas liquor was such a drug in the market that there were no buyers, and the price obtained for it this year was much below last year's price.—Mr. HANDLEY seconded. and observed that the low price of this article would make a difference of several hundred pounds in the revenue of the gasworks for the next 12 months.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that other works besides gasworks produced the liquor, and hence the market was overstocked.—Mr. MIDIVOOD asked if the contracts had been granted in a proper manner. Mr. PANKEIHRST replied that everything had been fair and open. He thought it was an unfair question indeed for the chair- man of the Highway Committee to ask another chairman. —Mr. MIDWOOD: The chairman of the Highway Committee has nothing to do with it at all. It is another matter alto- gether. Mr. Panklaurst has no right to raise the Highway Committee.—Mr PANKHURST : I think it an unfair question. It must be a great want of confidence in the committee.— Mr. MID WOOD said he did not wish Mr. Pankhurst to take offence in any way. But last year the tenders were sent in and opened, and then the gentleman who had the contract last year was allowed to come into the room and fill his tender afterwards.—The CHAIRMAN: You can hardly expect that it was done with the cognizance of the chairman of the committee, and whatever was done last year cannot be taken as a test of what has been done this year.—Mr. MIDNYOOD : I ask if it was done this year.—Mr. PANICHURST : Nothing of the sort; the tenders were sent in properly filled in. The mistake last year was that the tender was sent in txt filled up, and it was sent back to be filled up. This year it was sent in proper form,—The minutes passed.
This concluded the business.

GAMING WITH DICE AT T—HATTO HEATIL—Six youths, named James Fairclough, Aaron Halt, Tnomas Traverse, Joseph Ashton, Hitchin, and Sheffield were on Friday charged with gaming with dice on the Sunday previous.— Sergeant Sherratt said that on Sunday morning he was pass- ing a shed near the public footpath at Thatto Heath when he heard voices within. On looking through one of the doors he saw the defendants gaming with dice.—The defen- dants pleaded guilty, and were mulcted in fines of 2s GI and ' ss' and costs. AN EARLESTOWN GINGER BEER MERCHANT AND HIS Honsu.—On Tuesday, at the Northwich Petty Sessions, Wm. Elson, ginger beer manufacturer, of Earlestown, was charged with allowing a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit state at Witton, Northwicb, on the 15th ult.—Mr. Osman Harper, inspector for the R.S.P.C.A., found a boy. named Jones, driving a horse attached to a ginger beer cart belonging to Mr. Elson. The horse was very lame in both fore feet, and one was bandaged with tar and cord. The foot had a sandcrack in it, and the horse was altogether unfit to come 16 miles with a cart, or go back that dis• tance.—Robert Ritchen, jun., of Newton-le-Willows, the blacksmith who shoed this horse, said the pitchcord was not put round the horse's foot to hide anything from the inspector, but to prevent sar.d from getting into it. He could assure the Bench that de- fendant took as much care of his horse as a young fellow did of his sweetheart.—As the Bench did not think the case was a bad one, defendant was let off with a fine of 203., in- cluding costs. PRESENTATION TO AN EARLESTOWN TEACHER —A very pleasant and enjoyable gathering was held in St. John's school, Market-street, Earlestown, on Monday evening, when Miss A. Baybutt was presented with a practical token of the respect and esteem in which she was held by the teachers of the school. Miss Baybutt has not only been connected with the Sunday school for some considerable time past, but for the last nine years she has assiduously and satisfactorily performed the duties of a pupil teacher in the day school. , She has become endeared to the scholars over whom she was placed in charge; and her sister teachers of the Sun- day school have not been slow to mark their esteem and respect for her. A nice party of the teachers sat down to an excellent tea in the schoolroom, after which the chair was occupied by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar, among other gentlemen present being the Rev. Fl E. &lath (curate), Mr. H. J. Darman (organist), and Mr. J. Jones (librarian). The Rev. T. B. Matthews presented to Miss Baybutt, on behalf of the teachers and parents of the chil- dren in the day school, a handsome timepiece; while in the name of the Sunday school teachers he banded to her an ex- cellent writing desk. In making the presentations, Mr Matthews referred to Miss Baybutt's long connection with the schools; spoke of her earnest and &voted labours during that period, and said she was about to sever her con- nection with the school for other fields of labour; a (ac• ' which no one regretted more than be (the vicar) did. He afterwarcis commented at some length on Suralay school work and its object, pointing out the nec,ssity for earnest- ness among those who engaged in ii.—Addresses were also given by the gennemen nal-ned, the evening bcing spent in an enjoyable manner.

On Wednesday evening Councillor GREGSON delivered another address, and the meeting was presided over by Mr. D. Garnett. There was a fair attendance, and besides the chairman and Councillor Gregson there were also on the platform Mr. J. Green and Mr. W. Roberts. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said he was sure that it must be a matter of thankfulness to all in that room, and more particularly to those who had stood by the principles of total abstinence for the last quarter of a cen- tury or over, that public opinion had been turned to the side of the temperance cause in such a degree during the last few years. They were sometimes apt to forget time pioneers of this cause, sometimes apt to forget altogether those who had borne the heat and burden of the day; and that night he felt it not only a pleasure but a privilege—and he hoped all present did as well—that they were able to listen to a gentleman who was one of the first who had to stand the scourge of ridicule in those days because he dared to be a Daniel and dared to stand alone. It was equally a pleasure to know that in the very humble circumstances of the pioueers of this cause there were still living gentlemen who bad attained considerable eminence in the spheres in which they bad worked. He could mention several gentlemen whom he knew. He might refer to the Mayor of Scar- bo.rough, to a gentleman who was the Mayor of Chester, and to three other gentlemen who were or had been mayors of the boroughs is which they lived. Many of those gentlemen had sprung from the ranks of the working class, and he took it that they owed their position to embracing temperance principles. He was glad that the work was now almost accomplished. At the same time, if they read the news- paper reports and carefully looked round themselves, they found that even in the borough of Warrington there was a great deal of work to be done by them. He thought there was something for everybody to do. On the other hand the pat%

total duties of Dissenting ministers are confined within the circle of their own congregations, and for the discharge of these duties they frequently find a difficulty in getting paid. Under these circumstances I venture to assert that the working men of England, Wales, and Scotland will pause before they allow the inestimable blessings which a State Church confers to be ruthlessly torn from them. If it be said that the State has no right to prescribe a form of public worship and to support it, lanswer that the State is as much justified in doing that as itis justified in prescribing the education which shall be given in our elementary schools. It Dissenters think that they are deprived of privileges which Churchmen enjoy, let me remind them that it is their own fault. They elected to leave the fold, they were not driven from it, and they have no right now to grumble. There is no attempt or even desire to interfere with them, and that freedom to worship as they please, which they claim for themselves, it ill becomes them to deny to others. For some reason not quite apparent the name of the respected vicar of Holy Trinity has been unnecessarily dragged into this controversy; I should very much like the Revs. J. Warnock, E. Moore, and J. Yonge to relate their experiences of Dissent, and to state the extent of the freedom which they are supposed to enjoy. Dare they preach as they would like? Are they not rather obrged, just in propoition as they value their situations, to study their every word and action? Have they not cliques and coteries to serve, and are they not at thedictation of the kirk session, elders, deacons, or whatever else the potentates at their several little Bethels are called ? Methinks they often fervently play to be de- , livered from their bondage. They know not what liberty of I which they boast so much is. I observe that nearly, all Mr. Westbrook's opponents have an eye to the loaves and fishes. New, on this point let me say this : That venerable friend of Warrington, Sir Gilbert Greenall, has, out of his own private means, provided a site and built and endowed, —or is, at any rate, about to endow—at Walton a church which, like all others, will be open to every parishioner. Will any man, or any body of men, with pretensions :to honesty, advocate the confiscation of that building and the appropriation of that endowment to other purposes? If so, I call them robbers, and the advocate or advocates of such a policy I would not trust within arms' length of my pocket. —Yours, A CHURCHMAN.

Warrington, September, 1853. Sir,—The "deal hand " in Nonconformist charches seems to afford Mr. Westbrook a good, clear-throated crow, worthy of chanticleer himself. NOW it ought to he plain to any lair and intelligent man that no individual outside a Noßconformist Church has the slightest right to interfere with or concern himself about those self-contained and v•iluntary religious organisations—no more than he should concern himself as to who may be the baker or the butcher serving his neighbour. And why str,? Because the Non- conformist makes his own choice as to who shall minister to him in religious matters, and he spontaneously pays out of his own pocket for such services. Then, shows Mr. Westbrook, why do those who are not Churchmen inter-

, fere witii the Church? Plainly, as .he knows, bacau3e as citizens NVES are all compelled to be, legally, members of the Church ; and because it, as a national institution, touches every individual socially, pecuniarily, religiously, and our civil liberty as well as our religious freedom are potentially at its mercy, or affected by its temper or interests. The voluntary payment of ministers is a sensible and honest arrangement, I think, well calculated to prevent social dis- cord. At the same time be it said, that where the " dead hind" controls, those who accept its leading must lawfully abide by it. But, Mr, Westbrook, with a lack of candour not worthy of any controversialist, quietly assumes that there is no "dead hand" holding the Church of Eng- land In its grip! It is, demonstrably, the hand that is in the tomb and the voice which is in the I grave—the dogmas, the rubrics, the canons of contentious ' priests of bye-gone ages—whose lively presence, at the pre- sent moment, is the cause of the fierce turbulence and rend- ing antagonisms in the Church. Proof in abundance is every day forthcoming. Here is the latest. At the Winchester Diocesan Conference, the Rev. Canon Wilson said, referring to the Prayer-book, that "the circumstances of the time made it desirable that they should have greater freedom." Mr. M. Portal said, that "the act. of uniformity resembled a strait waistcoat, and to an energetic clergyman it was like a bearing rein and a kicking strap to a high-spirited horse." But I am wasting your space in supplying evidence of the fact, that the Church groans under the control of the "dead hand." B.A. P.S.—ln my last letter a printer's error turned latter into better in the following sentence No one who knows the facts ought to flaunt the advantages the favoured class (the Church) have enjoyed to the disablement of the latter (the Nonconformists.") The invidiousness occasioned by the error make= me desirous of correcting it.

div.head: BENEFIT FOOTBALL MATCH.
div.p: THE BENEFIT FOOTBALL MATCH.

Sir,--in your notice of the Rugby football niatch for the benefit of A. Platt, played on Saturday last, Bth inst., you state that an accident, which necessitated amputation of the foot, was the result of football. This is not correct, as the amputation NVR9 owing to purely natural causes, Mr. Platt never having played football. As I think Otis mistake may augment the feeling as to the dangerous nature of the game, already held by a portion of the public, would you kindly give publicity to this correction, and oblige.—Yours re- spectfully,
JAMES NICHdhUli, Hon. Sec. V.F.C.
THE OVERSEER AND THEIR ASSISTANT.

A meeting of the Over era for Warrington was held at the offices, Town Hall, on Thursday evening, under ths presidency of Akerman Kean, the other members present being Messrs. A. Mackie and John Harrison, with Mr. J. L. Tunstall (deputy assistant overseer.)—Couucillor MACKIE reported the interview Mr. Blackhayst and himself had with the Board of Guardians respecting the assistant over- seer. He said they were of course able to tell the Guar- dians that they had no personal or private interest in the matter whatever, and that the Overseers only object was in the first place to secure the best gentleman they could get as an assistant overseer, and at the same time do the best, as far as they wall could, for the venerable gentleman who had served them so long. (Hear, hear.) The feeling of the Guardians was vary general in favour of the course which the Overseers recommended. He understood, however, that there had been some further discussion on the matter at a meeting at which he was not present, but be thought the Guardians expected that Mr. Pilling would now take some step by placing his resignation in the hands of the Board, who, as they knew, had to do with the matter. If Mr. Pilling was so advised it would be for the Guardians to make the selection of his successor, and he was very much gratified to find an almost unanimous—in fact, he might call it a perfectly unanimously—feeling in favour of Mr. Tunstall, who he might say—and he was sure the Overseers would say it also—had so faithfully—and not only faithfully (for an ignorant person might be very faithful), but intelligently managed the matters of that Board. (Hear, hear.) However, it was a question entirely between Mr. Pilling, the Guardians, and Mr. Tunstall. He was sorry that some remarks had been made, he believed at some of the meetings, almost implying that they (the Overseers) had gone about the matter secretly and has- till. He need scarcely say that there was no foundation in that; that it was really the want of better information that had led any ger.tleman to make that remark; and that, having gone as far as they had, they could go no further except giving their hearty good wishes and their support to those who now had the power of making the selection should Mr. Pilling be advieed to go further in the matter. (Hear, hear.) Whether Mr. Pilling was so advised or not he could not tell, but whether he would not be compelled to retire by the report of the Poor Law auditor calling attention to the continued inability of that gentleman, he thought the Overseers had done their duty to the public, and only an act of courtesy and good feeling in moving in the way in which they had done so as to secure a successor who, he thought, had made an offer of a very liberal allowance to Mr. Pilling during his lifetime. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN said when they considered carefully the minutes which had been read, and the remarks of the Local Government Board upon the sub- ject, he was sure that if the gentlemen referred to had been in possession of proper information they would never have made the remarks they had done. They were all anxious as Overseers that Mr. Pilling's interests should be considered as far as possible, but at the same time when they were called upon by higher authorities to act in the matter, there was no alternative but to do so. They were anxious to act in the best possble way, and he felt quite sure if they sought the whole town through for a man for the position the Overseers could not find a better man to succeed Mr. Pilling than Mr. Tunstall. The auditors had expressed themselves in that direction, and they had declared to him more than once that they considered Mr. Tunstall the best man they had ever come In contact with as an assistant overseer, and that if the overseers had , to make a change they could not do better than let the mantle fall upon him. He should be very sorry for it to go abroad that he was in favour of Mr. Tunstall more than any- one else who might seek the position, but he was satisfied ' as far as his knowledge went there was no man better quali- fied to fill the post. He was of wonderful assistance to the Overseers; he had the law at his finger ends, as he had dur- ing the time he bad been in the office made the law his sub- ject of study; and he was ready at all times to give them such advice as would lead them in the right direction. Mr. Tunstall had never been wrong, and he was as r. Mackie had said, both faithful and intelligent. Therefore he thought Dr. Maceie and Mr. Blackburst had done their work very well, and had laid the matter before the Guar- dians in such a light that they seemed to be unanimously of opinion that the time had come when some change should be made. He had no doubt when that change took place Mr. Pilling, who WO an old and faithful servant of the Cor- poration, would be considered. He thanked Dr. Mackie and Mr. Blackhurst for having laid the matter before the Guar- dians, and said he had no doubt it would have the effect they anticipated when the deputation was appointed.—Mr. HARRISON remarked that the overseers had done the best thing they could, and it now rested with Mr. Filling's advisers to take some action.—Mr. TIINSTA.LL said he would like to be allowed to say he was very much obliged to them for the observations they had made regard- ing him. He was only afraid they had overstated the case. He bad done his best, and he would do the same as long as he was there.—The CHAIRMAN called attention to a speech by Alderman Davies, who had a good deal to do with Mr. Tunetall, when a dispute took place in regard to the assess- ment of the gas works. Alderman Davies, he said, declared in the Council Chamber that Mr. Tunstall was the beat man for the post that ever he had mot with, and he :said whatever 'lie Overseers did they should stick to him.—The subject then dropped.

div.p: Xetteus to the editor.
THE ANNUAL LICENSING MEETING.

Sir,—Your correspondent "A Ratepayer" is labouring under a mistake. There has been no departure this year from the usual practice with respect to giving notices of the annual licensing sessions. Notice by placard or advertise- ment has never been given of the sessions for the renewal of licenses, nor is any such notice legally necessary. Had the gentlemen who wished to memorialise the magistrates made enquiry at my office they could have obtained any informa- tion they required. Notice of the " renewal " sessions (the "annual brewster sessions") was sent by the Chief-Con- stable to every magistrate in the borough. according t• enstom.—Yours, , IL B. WHITE. Borough Magistrates' Clerk's Office, Warrington, Bth Sept., 1883.

div.head: EARLY CLOSING.
div.p: EARLY CLOSING.

Ste,—ln collecting statistics as to the position of the early closing movement in the provinces, we find that in a very large proportion of the towns in England and Wales there is among the varions shopkeepers a half holiday, or an early closing, on some day of the week. But we do not find this to be the else at Warrington. Permit me to direct the attention of your readers to this fact. Wherever the mid-week closing has been obtained, whether in London or the country, it has been the means of greatly relieving the assistants, as well as the employers, and has not been the cause of any appreciable inconvenience to the pablic. In- deed, it is not unfrequently the case that the public go heartily with the movement, and readily evince their ay:II- /Why with it. Our Association will gladly help with ad- vice, and in other ways, any movement which may be originated in your district for securing this great boon. Applications addressed to ma for specimen bills, pl wards, agreement-forms, etc. (with stimps for postage), will receive immediate attention.-1 am, sir, yours faithfully, JAMES A. STACEY, Secretary. Early Closing Assiciation. 100, Fleet-street, London, E.O September, 1883.

Messrs. Joseph IL and W. P. Baiges, share brokers. I'4, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Sept. 13th) :

Several influences have acted on the markets during the past week, and as they have seen irregular so have the movements in stocks, the general result being adverse almost all round; but with finer weather the reduction in the bank rate, and the absence of any great difficulties at the settlement, a better feel- ing is apparent this afternoon. Foreign stocks are firm, those quoted here producing no instance where lower figures are marked, whilst most have moved upwards to a greater or less degree. Egyptian stocks are foremost with a rise of 1 in the Daira Danish, It in the prof and in the truifieds. Mexican railway at Tics have been tie chief feature of the week, the onslaught on their values being continued, and sa'es forcing figures down as low as 814. From this point they have sharply recovered, closing (at official time) 84 89i, or only about 41 per cent, below last Thursday's close. General trade advices do not warrant any stir in miscellane .us shares, and there is none to chronicle. Business passing during the week in the aggregate is small, th nigh probably a little above the average for some weeks past, COAL, IRON, itC , AND KlNlNG„—Rather more dealings are reported than for several weeks past, and quotations show a rather m,re healthy appearance on balance of alterations, the changes for and against being pretty evenly balanced. HUYTON CRICIERT CLOW—The concluding match of the season as played last Saturday, at Warrington, and ended in favour of the home team, making the fourth loss to Huyton, of a season which has been a most successful one; good cricket has developed in the young blood which is calculated to firmly establish the good position that the club has hitherto held in the county.

A RUNAWAY SOLDIER ROBBING A DRUNKEN MAN AT COLLINS GREEN.-At the Newton Petty Sessions on Satur- day last, before R. Houghton, T. S. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqrs, Patrick McQuire, dressed in" regimentals" was charged wjth stealing from the person of Michael Cain a er lever watch and a silver guard, together of the value of 11555. The evidence showed that on the 13th August the prosecutor, who resides at Burton- wood, partook of drink rather freely and stopped at the house of a friend at Collins Green until about half-past eleven at night. He then left for home—about a mile and a half distant—but on his way sat or fell down on the road s'de and in a short time was fast asleep. About one o'clock the following morning he was awoke by his sister and mother, who had come in search of him, and shortly after- wards he missed his silver lever watch and guard. He had them on him when he left the friend's house. The police were informed of the occurrence, and after enquiries had been made into the matter it was ascertained that the prisoner bad sold the articles for 9s. ad to a Mrs. Patin, wife of a labourer, residing near to a cousin of the prisoner on the following morning after the robbery. He told his cousin and Mrs. Palin that he bad bought the watch and chain for 4-ss. from a man who was on tramp ; and on being asked where he had got the money from be replied that he had won a lot at cards, and had also got the remainder by selling some of his clothes.—P.C. Grundy apprehended the man at Orford Barracks Warrington, and on being charged with the offence he said be had bought it from a man at St. Helens whom be did not know. He added that he gave 4s. 9d. for it. He also stated that he had broken out of the Barracks at Warrington and walked to St. Helens.—The prisoner was committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions at Kirk- dale.—Sergeat Cambridge here stepped forward, and kr.lid : I am sent hers by the commanding officer of the Sth arid 40th Regiments to watch the case on behalf the military authori- ties, and also to tell your worships that the prisoner burs a , very indifftrent character.
